items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #3372. This is a community tracker for small, independently claimable improvements to flaky tests.

## The problem

Recent PR CI contains assertions that race background work and an intermittent hang that can occupy a runner for almost six hours. These failures consume contributor time and make unrelated PRs harder to validate.

The initial triage reviewed GitHub Actions `Test` runs from September 13-23, 2026 and recent `k3-unit-tests` failures. These are selected examples, not a complete inventory or a measured repository-wide flake rate. The test code was checked against `dev` at [21571dae80c6](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/commit/21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160).

The initial tasks cover:

- **Health-monitor exit:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a thread-exit assertion; two PRs have same-checkout failed/passed attempts.
- **Health-monitor fallback/recovery:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a state assertion; failure logs show fallback completing after the assertion.
- **RESP wait diagnostics:** a same-checkout rerun passes after an almost-six-hour hang near the RESP test boundary. The exact blocked operation remains unproven; this task adds bounded waits and diagnostics, not a speculative production fix.

## Initial tasks

- [x] #5314: Synchronize health-monitor exception-driven exit
- [ ] #5315: Synchronize health-monitor fallback/recovery phases
- [ ] #5316: Bound RESP waits and add stalled-operation diagnostics

## September 22–29 follow-up tasks

The follow-up scan covered **September 22, 2026 04:31 UTC through September 29, 2026 04:31 UTC**. It inspected 1,338 GitHub Actions run records across `Test`, `CPU Device Tests`, and `Operator: CI`, and 2,106 Buildkite build records across the active LMCache pipelines, then examined relevant failed jobs and retry logs. These inventory counts are not a repository-wide flake rate or a claim that every failed log was exhaustively analyzed.

Each new task below includes a failed/passed pair within the **same `dev` Buildkite build**, with the same LMCache checkout and vLLM/torch versions. PR-head-only matches with an unverified base merge, dependency/version changes between attempts, and one-off failures were not used as confirmation.

- [ ] #5402: Make `vllm_bench` inputs reproducible across retries and retain the comparison settings/results. Build #5340 changes from 7.34% slower than baseline to 0.62% faster without a source change.
- [ ] #5403: Preserve separate baseline/LMCache raw timings for `long_doc_qa`. Build #5294 changes from 50.3% TTFT improvement (fail) to 70.4% (pass); #5291 provides a second pair.
- [ ] #5404: Retain L2 data-flow diagnostics after `long_doc_qa_l2` performance failures. Build #5287 changes from 1.49x TTFT speedup (fail) to 1.54x (pass).

These are independently claimable **reproducibility and diagnostics improvements for confirmed intermittent test verdicts**. They deliberately keep the existing performance/data-flow assertions. Completing a diagnostic task does not establish that the underlying timing instability is fixed; report any remaining root-cause work separately.

Contributors can develop the scoped regression coverage with CPU-only command stubs. End-to-end validation uses two CUDA GPUs and the exact CI workload; each child provides a self-contained historical reproduction recipe. A maintainer can help with GPU validation. The CPU environment below applies to the initial #5314–#5316 tasks, not these GPU workload runs.

Existing health-monitor/RESP tasks and ongoing MQ, distributed-storage, and observability work were checked to avoid duplicate newcomer assignments. Intermittent model-output mismatches were not turned into generic timing-hardening tasks or described as harmless flakes.

## Claim one sub-issue

Use the native **Sub-issues** list below. Start with either health-monitor task if this is your first test contribution; the RESP task benefits from familiarity with Python futures and event loops.

These tasks are primarily meant to help new contributors learn the LMCache contribution workflow. Please claim **only one sub-issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned task or an open PR in this tracker, finish that one before taking another, and leave the remaining tasks for other new contributors.

1. Pick one unassigned sub-issue and check its comments for an existing claim.
2. Comment `/claim` or "I'd like to work on this" **on that sub-issue**, so a maintainer can coordinate assignment. Please do not claim the parent tracker itself.
3. Keep one task per PR, target `dev`, and follow [the onboarding guide](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md).
4. Sign off every commit (`git commit -s`), run `pre-commit run --all-files`, and include exact test commands and results in the PR.

## Shared CPU test setup (initial tasks)

The initial #5314–#5316 tasks do not require a GPU, model download, or external Redis server. Use Linux x86_64 with Git, a C/C++ build toolchain, FFmpeg, and Python 3.12 with venv support. The RESP tests use an in-memory mocked client. Allow sufficient disk space for PyTorch/vLLM dependencies. The full pre-commit checks also need Rust/Cargo with rustfmt and clippy.

Run this in a fresh working directory. The explicit revision is the **triage reference**; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install 'vllm==0.30.0' 'torch==2.13.0'
python -m pip install -r requirements/build.txt -r requirements/test.txt -r requirements/common.txt
NO_GPU_EXT=1 python -m pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
python -m pip install pre-commit
export PYTHONHASHSEED=0
python -m pip freeze > ci-repro-requirements.txt
```

items.title: GGUF convert support for Vibevoice
items.author: amin-jhn
items.body_excerpt: Hey there! I am trying to convert my fine-tuned vibevoice into a gguf format for inference but cant find proper code or converter any where. The architecture is currently unsupported to any known converter like llama.cpp but I have already seen many variation of gguf-formated vibevoice. Can anyone help me with that?

comments.author: pwilkin
comments.body:
So the status currently is that there's no support for VibeVoice in llama.cpp (but llama.cpp *does* support TTS architectures, it's a question of somebody adding support for that specific model). 

What you have seen are probably repacks done by calcuis in his weirdly named "gguf-org project", but that project is not affiliated with ggml-org nor with llama.cpp in any way and from what I've analyzed the contents of those files, they are simply direct repacks of the original SafeTensors files, but with layers that are known to be quantizable by GGML converted to the respective quant format (with a side effect being that only a small percentage of the tensors that *should* be quantizable are really quantized, since the GGUF library does not know that for example `model.acoustic_tokenizer.decoder.stages.0.0.ffn.linear1.weight` should be a quantizable tensor). He then converts them back to F32 before running, so it's not a real GGML architecture, just a repack - not a very efficient one at that, since he unpacks all the quants to F32, so the memory usage will be the same as with the original model, just the quality will be lower (for example, the ComfyUI-GGUF solution, which supports GGUF quantization, does it by properly patching methods and dequantizing tensors on the fly as they're being used, so even though it does not utilize native quantized kernels for MAT_MUL like GGUF does, it actually allows to run those quants with a lower memory footprint).

TL;DR: You can try doing a repack in the same way, using `quantize` from the `gguf-py` library (a decent LLM coder will probably write that for you), but real VibeVoice support requires adding a proper MTMD model.

comments.author: amin-jhn
comments.body: Thank you so much for your detailed response!

comments.author: Ra5hidIslam
comments.body:
Hey @amin-jhn and @pwilkin,

Following up on pwilkin's suggestion, I went ahead and wrote a Python script using gguf-py that successfully repacks and quantizes the VibeVoice SafeTensors into a Q8_0 GGUF file.

While I know this doesn't close the issue (since it still needs the native C++ MTMD model support mapped out for llama.cpp), this script should fully solve the repackaging hurdle for anyone trying to run a compressed version through custom frontends like ComfyUI in the meantime.


```python

import argparse
import numpy as np
import torch
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import gguf
from gguf.quants import quantize
from gguf.constants import GGMLQuantizationType

def pad_tensor(tensor_np: np.ndarray, block_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pads the last dimension of a 2D tensor to be a multiple of block_size."""
    rows, cols = tensor_np.shape
    if cols % block_size == 0:
        return tensor_np
    
    padding_needed = block_size - (cols % block_size)
    print(f"  --> Padding tensor: {cols} -> {cols + padding_needed} columns")
    return np.pad(tensor_np, ((0, 0), (0, padding_needed)), mode='constant', constant_values=0)

def vibevoice_repack_with_padding(path_input: str, path_output: str):
    print(f"Loading Safetensors from {path_input}...")
    try:
        tensors_loaded = load_file(path_input)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error loading file: {e}")
        return
        
    print("Initializing GGUF writer...")
    writer_gguf = gguf.GGUFWriter(path_output, arch="vibevoice")
    writer_gguf.add_string("general.name", "vibevoice")

    tensor_count = 0
    quantized_count = 0
    BLOCK_SIZE = 32 

    for tensor_name, tensor_data in tensors_loaded.items():
        tensor_np = tensor_data.cpu().float().numpy()
        
        is_2d_weight = len(tensor_np.shape) == 2 and "weight" in tensor_name
        
        if is_2d_weight:
            # 1. Pad to multiple of 32
            tensor_padded = pad_tensor(tensor_np, block_size=BLOCK_SIZE)
            
            # 2. Quantize into a structured array
            q_type = GGMLQuantizationType.Q8_0
            quantized_struct = quantize(tensor_padded, q_type)
            
            # 3. Cast the structured array to raw bytes
            quantized_bytes = quantized_struct.view(np.uint8)
            
            # 4. Add to GGUF using ONLY the raw bytes
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(
                name=tensor_name,
                tensor=quantized_bytes,
                raw_dtype=q_type,
            )
            quantized_count += 1
        else:
            # Standard F32 for 1D tensors
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(tensor_name, tensor_np)

        tensor_count += 1
        if tensor_count % 50 == 0:
            print(f"Processed {tensor_count} tensors...")

    print(f"Writing {tensor_count} tensors to disk...")
    writer_gguf.write_header_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_kv_data_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_tensors_to_file()
    writer_gguf.close()

    print(f"Successfully converted to GGUF at {path_output}.")
    print(f"Total: {tensor_count} | Quantized (Q8_0): {quantized_count}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Repack VibeVoice to GGUF with Q8_0 Fix.")
    parser.add_argument("--input", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    vibevoice_repack_with_padding(args.input, args.output)
```

Hope this helps anyone trying to get the file size down while we wait for native C++ support!

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4 + HiCache write_through: TP ranks deadlock under concurrent long prefills (scheduler and detokenizer go silent, /health 503)
items.author: divyvasal
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

DeepSeek-V4 with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-write-policy write_through` deadlocks across TP ranks under a burst of long one-shot prompts. The same config without HiCache does not.

When it hangs:
- The scheduler stops and the detokenizer heartbeat goes quiet.
- `/health` returns 503 (`Server couldn't get a response from detokenizer`) indefinitely.
- All 4 GPUs of the replica sit at **100% utilization at ~260 W**, which on B300 means spin-waiting.
- Nothing is logged: no traceback, no watchdog fire within 5+ minutes.

It reproduced 3 times out of 3 on two replicas:
- 48 concurrent prompts of ~540K tokens: hung after ~14 min in the first run and ~1 min in the second.
- 8 concurrent: hung after ~1.5 min.

The same burst with the same flags minus `--enable-hierarchical-cache` processed 5.9M (48 in flight) and 8.3M (8 in flight) input tokens, about 11 and 15 completed ~540K prompts, with no stall.

In all three hangs, the last prefill batch logged before the stall is one in which **a long prompt finishes prefill while the next begins** (`#new-seq: 2`, `swa token usage` jumps from 0.00 to 0.09). In the two short runs it was the first such batch. Example from the 48-concurrent run that hung after ~1 min:

```
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 8192, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.00, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 15, #pending-token: 7978739
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 2, #new-token: 8107, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.09, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 14, #pending-token: 7970632
<no further batches; health 503 from 06:36 on; last_heartbeat 06:35:54>
```

That is the point where the first ~540K-token prefix is inserted and written through to host while other long prefills are still being chunked.

py-spy, taken 3 times over 3 minutes, is identical each time. The TP ranks are one step apart:

```
TP0, TP1, TP2  MainThread:
    _prepare_engram_history (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:203)   # torch.tensor(..., device=cuda) H2D copy = stream sync
    prepare_for_forward (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:117)
    get_next_batch_to_run (scheduler.py:3759)
    event_loop_overlap (scheduler.py:1970)
TP3  MainThread:
    forward (engram.py:312)
    _forward_layers_hc_pre_from_prev (deepseek_v4.py:4424)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:4755)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:5110)
    _execute_extend (runner/eager_runner.py:372)
detokenizer: idle in recv_pyobj
```

TP3 has launched the next forward, presumably waiting in a collective, while TP0-2 are blocked on a stream sync before theirs. This looks like the ranks scheduled different batches at that step. One guess is that the write-through backup's completion, or the prefix-match state it changes, is observed at different times on different ranks. We haven't confirmed which state diverges.

### Reproduction

- **sglang:** nightly at `4cbf290f`
- **Model:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4), 4x B300 per replica
- **Flags:** `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4 --mem-fraction-static 0.60 --context-length 1048576 --max-running-requests 128 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --max-prefill-tokens 8192 --schedule-policy shortest-prefill-first --prefill-decode-interval 4 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-write-policy write_through`

Steps:
1. Send N unique prompts of ~540K tokens each (random words and numbers) at the same time, `max_tokens 4`, with N = 8 or 48.
2. Within ~1-1.5 min the replica stops; it hangs every time.
3. The identical burst without `--enable-hierarchical-cache` completes.

An earlier load did not hang in two 15-18 minute runs: 48 threads of growing ~540K-token multi-turn conversations, started 6 s apart.

### Environment

8x B300 (2 replicas of TP4/EP4 on one node), CUDA image from the nightly above. Happy to collect more: py-spy `--native`, NCCL debug, or a run with `--disable-overlap-schedule`.

items.title: [Performance][ROCm][gfx1100] compressed-tensors silently enables fp8 KV cache, which is far slower than bf16 for paged decode attention on RDNA3
items.author: youyoulyz
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On a Radeon RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100, RDNA3), a compressed-tensors checkpoint that carries a `kv_cache_scheme` gets its KV cache silently switched to `fp8`, even though `--kv-cache-dtype` is left at its default `auto`. In this configuration decode attention is substantially **slower** than with bf16 KV — the halved KV traffic does not pay for the fp8→fp16 conversion, because gfx11 has no native FP8.

This also has a knock-on effect: **it blocks the split-KV decode fix in #45916**, whose kernel explicitly requires non-fp8 KV.

I could not find an existing report of this magnitude. The closest are #45038 (the override mechanism itself, but the guard proposed there is NVIDIA capability-based and does not cover RDNA) and a gfx1100 fork A/B that measured fp8 KV decode attention as a wash.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), 24 GiB |
| vLLM | `0.27.1.dev5+rocm10.0.0.gf46a9dfe2` |
| torch | `2.12.0+rocm10.0.0`, ROCm 10.0 |
| Model | Qwen3.8-27B-INT4, compressed-tensors W4A16 |
| Architecture | hybrid: 48 gated-DeltaNet layers + 16 full-attention layers |
| Attention shape | `head_dim=256`, `num_kv_heads=4`, `num_attention_heads=24` |
| Forced block size | **1568** (derived from mamba page alignment, `platforms/interface.py:904`) |

Launch flags: CUDA graph enabled (`--cudagraph-capture-sizes 1 2 4 8 16 32 --max-num-seqs 32`), `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`, plus the standard ROCm setup (`FLASH_ATTENTION_TRITON_AMD_ENABLE=TRUE`).

### The silent override

The checkpoint's `quantization_config` contains:

```json
"kv_cache_scheme": {
  "num_bits": 8, "type": "float", "strategy": "tensor",
  "symmetric": true, "observer": "static_minmax", "dynamic": false
}
```

vLLM resolves the attention KV dtype from this and ends up with `fp8`. The startup log is misleading here — the engine config dump prints `kv_cache_dtype=auto`, while the value reaching the attention op is `fp8`. I only found this by logging the value at the gate in `chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py`.

### A/B measurement

Identical server config **except** the KV cache dtype. Critically, **both arms run the same attention kernel** — the Triton `kernel_paged_attention_2d` fallback (the custom HIP kernel is gated off for this shape, see #50264). The only intended difference is the KV dtype.

Workload: 8 sequences, single wave (`num-prompts == max-concurrency`), 64 output tokens, `--ignore-eos`.

| KV dtype | TPOT @1k ctx | TPOT @2k ctx | decode slope |
|---|---|---|---|
| **fp8** (as shipped) | 93.2 ms | 159.9 ms | 65.1 µs / ctx-token |
| **bf16** | 73.7 ms | 104.6 ms | 30.2 µs / ctx-token |

**The per-token cost of context is 2.2× higher with fp8 KV.** End-to-end decode throughput at 2k context goes 21.6 → 29.1 tok/s.

Note: the bf16 arm requires a lower `--max-model-len`, since bf16 doubles the KV footprint (47,786 → 24,576 tokens available on this card).

### Kernel-level evidence

`rocprofv3` kernel traces, batch 8 / seq 1024, same `kernel_paged_attention_2d` kernel:

- **fp8 KV: 1653 µs per dispatch** (from a server profile)
- **bf16 KV: 597 µs per dispatch** (isolated microbenchmark)

fp8 reads **half the bytes** and is **2.8× slower**. That is consistent with gfx11 having no native FP8: the Triton path upcasts fp8→fp16 in software, and at this parallelism (4 KV heads, batch 8) the kernel is instruction/latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound, so the extra conversion work dominates.

*Caveat: those two numbers come from different harnesses (in-server profile vs. standalone microbenchmark). The A/B table above is from a single harness and is the primary evidence.*

### Why this matters beyond the raw number

The split-KV kernel added in #45916 requires `"fp8" not in kv_cache_dtype`. So any compressed-tensors checkpoint with a `kv_cache_scheme` — which silently becomes fp8 — **cannot use that fix at all**. In our case the gate logs:

```
head_size=256 alibi=False sw=0 sinks=False out_scale=False kv_dtype=fp8 => use=False
```

Every other condition for the split-KV path is satisfied. Switching KV to bf16 flips this to `use=True` and gives a further 19% on the decode slope (30.2 → 24.4 µs/ctx-token) on top of the bf16 gain.

### Ask

1. The `kv_cache_scheme` auto-override probably should not fire on gfx11 (analogous to the pre-SM90 guard proposed in #45038), or at minimum should warn that the resulting dtype is known to perform worse than bf16 on RDNA3.
2. It would be worth looking at the fp8 path in the ROCm Triton paged attention kernel — on this hardware the conversion cost appears to exceed the bandwidth saving.

Happy to provide full traces, the exact server command lines, and the microbenchmark script if useful.

```
I think the problem is that each DP worker finds/assigns free ports dynamically/independently.. so there is a race condtion. We'll have to look at how to catch and re-find a port if possible (though I have a memory this might be nontrivial).
```


I'm looking at the code and I see that all code paths for getting ports eventually to go to _get_open_port, and that in _get_open_port there is basically no defence against choosing the same port twice. Can you please confirm my understanding?

_get_open_port in main is here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/utils/network_utils.py#L177

UPD: I imagine the assumption here is that once a code path gets a port, that code path will use it immediately, and thus the port will be come busy. It doesn't seem to hold though.


Even where all sockets that vLLM chose for itself are unique, I get the stack trace below.
I have the following explanation in mind:

- vLLM chooses zmq ports before launching the engines
- launching the engines takes ~5 mins
- by the time the engines are launched, something can listen on this port, like for example Ray
- **It looks the right solution is to hold on to then chosen ports immediately are they are chosen.**

items.title: [P2P] Stress test and performance characterization for P2P KV cache sharing
items.author: Liusixuuu
items.body_excerpt:
Summary

The v1 P2P KV cache sharing path (P2PL2Adapter + P2PController + NIXL transfer channel) is functionally complete but has no load testing or performance characterization. This issue proposes a scoped set of tests plus one small config change and a benchmark to close the biggest gaps.

Details

Current test coverage is limited to unit tests with mocked MQ/transfer channel (test_p2p_l2_adapter.py), a single-peer/3-key loopback integration test (test_p2p_l2_adapter_integration.py), mocked reconcile/handler logic (test_p2p_controller.py), and a skipped old-arch flow test (test_p2p_backend_with_controller.py, disabled because it "may hang in CI/CD").

Key gaps:

  1. No concurrent lookup stress test. P2PL2Adapter tracks in-flight tasks (_lookup_tasks, _load_tasks) with no locks, on the assumption that the two code paths run on separate threads. Nothing floods the adapter with concurrent lookups from the controller thread while store tasks are submitted — the exact high-cache-hit-rate production scenario.

  2. No multi-peer test. P2PController._reconcile (p2p_controller.py:458) creates one P2PL2Adapter per discovered peer, but no test verifies multiple adapters working together (e.g. two peers each holding different halves of a key set, with lookups routed across both).

  3. Uncharacterized hot-path constants. Three constants have never been measured: _PERIODIC_NOTIFIER_INTERVAL_MS (5 ms, p2p_l2_adapter.py:46) sets the poll rate for every lookup + load completion and adds directly to TTFT; _LOOKUP_RPC_TIMEOUT_S (3.0 s, p2p_l2_adapter.py:47) is the internal MQ RPC timeout per submit_lookup_and_lock_task and blocks the prefetch loop thread on a hit; _MAX_MISSES (consecutive coordinator poll misses before removing a peer adapter) is not in P2PConfig. Worst-case added latency per lookup is one polling interval (5 ms), which at high RDMA bandwidth can dominate the actual transfer for small KV objects.

  4. No end-to-end RDMA throughput benchmark. A transfer-channel benchmark exists, but nothing measures bytes/sec and tail latency through the full stack (submit_lookup_and_lock_task → query_lookup_and_lock_result → submit_load_task → query_load_result).

  5. No peer churn resilience test. _reconcile has no test for a peer disappearing mid-lookup (adapter removed while a load task is in flight).

Steps / Reproduction (if applicable)

Not a bug — this is a testing/characterization gap. Current state can be observed by:

  1. Reviewing the P2P test files above and noting all real-I/O coverage is single-peer, 3-key, loopback.
  2. Grepping the hot-path constants in p2p_l2_adapter.py and confirming none have associated benchmarks or config knobs.
  3. Confirming _MAX_MISSES is a module constant, not a P2PConfig field.

Expected Outcome / Goal

A scoped set of deliverables: - **A. Multi-peer concurrent stress test** (new file `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_stress.py`): stand up N peers (≥3), each with context + MQ server (reusing the `test_p2p_l2_adapter_integration.py` pattern); drive concurrent lookups across all peers from multiple workers; verify every transferred key matches the peer's source bytes. Ensure the test actually runs in our unit test environment rather than being skipped — confirm `nixl` is available there (or provide/install it) so the `pytest.importorskip("nixl")` guard doesn't silently skip the test. - **B. Peer churn test** (same file): simulate a peer disappearing mid-lookup (close its MQ server before `query_lookup_and_lock_result` resolves); verify the adapter times out cleanly (all-zero bitmap) without hanging or leaking tasks in `_lookup_tasks`. - **C. Benchmark script** (new file under `lmcache/tools/p2p_benchmark/`, extending the existing transfer-channel benchmark): measure end-to-end P2P lookup+load across payload sizes (1, 16, 128 chunks); report P50/P99 latency and aggregate throughput; sweep `_PERIODIC_NOTIFIER_INTERVAL_MS` (1/5/10 ms) to find the optimal value and whether it should become configurable.

Actual Outcome (if applicable)

No stress, multi-peer, churn, or end-to-end throughput coverage exists. The three hot-path constants are unmeasured, and _MAX_MISSES is hard-coded outside of config.

Additional Context

File | Change -- | -- tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_stress.py | Multi-peer concurrent stress test tests/v1/multiprocess/test_p2p_controller.py | Peer churn / mid-lookup disappear test lmcache/v1/multiprocess/config.py:136 | Add max_peer_misses to P2PConfig lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/p2p_controller.py:46 | Replace _MAX_MISSES constant with config lmcache/tools/p2p_benchmark/ | New end-to-end benchmark script

items.title: [Bug] Shutdown and L1 TTL expiry can reclaim a buffer an L2 adapter is still loading into
items.author: JulianZJN
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`L2AdapterInterface` makes the *caller* responsible for keeping a load buffer
valid "until the load task is completed", but gives the caller no way to find out
that a load it is no longer waiting for has stopped touching that buffer.
`PrefetchController.stop()` therefore frees L1 write reservations that an adapter
still owns, and, independently, the L1 write lock guarding such a reservation
is a TTL lock that expires after 600 s by default, after which the object becomes
readable by other requests and evictable by the eviction controller.

Both are reproducible on `dev` with in-tree components only.

## Affected version

`dev` at `dd35168c801fec49889b34b083a12204d3c02a2a` (reproduced there).

## Background: the contract gap

`lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/base.py:321-328` (`submit_load_task`):

> The caller is responsible for managing the lifecycle of the memory objects, and
> should make sure that the memory buffer is valid until the load task is
> completed.

`base.py:93-96`: *"The L2 adapter is not supposed to manage the lifecycle of the
memory objects."* But "completed" is defined only as `query_load_result`
returning non-`None` (`base.py:335-353`), and `close()`, `base.py:587-593`, says
nothing at all about in-flight loads. There is no `drain`, `join`, `quiesce`,
`wait_for_idle` or `num_inflight` anywhere in `L2AdapterInterface`.

From reading each adapter's `close()`, they do not agree on this. Some wait for their workers (`dax`, `raw_block`, `valkey`), several cancel their tasks and tear down, and at least two do neither for work that is already running:

* `p2p` (`p2p_l2_adapter.py:353-368`) unregisters its fds and removes the transfer-channel client without cancelling or joining posted reads.
* `fs` cancels a coroutine whose actual read runs on the default executor (`run_in_executor(None, self._read_with_odirect, ...)`, `fs_l2_adapter.py:707-718`), which cancellation cannot stop and `close()` never shuts down.

`serde_wrapper.py:350-355` already documents the hazard and asserts the guarantee
it needs, *"Both close() calls block until their in-flight reads / writes against
the temp MemoryObjs finish"*, which does not hold for the second and third
groups above.

## Repro 1, shutdown frees a buffer a pending load still owns

The test below (drop it in as `tests/v1/distributed/test_shutdown_ownership_repro.py`) drives the real `PrefetchController` and
`L1Manager` with a mock adapter whose gate sits before the copy into the
caller's buffers, so at the moment of shutdown the adapter has written nothing
and still holds the `MemoryObj`s it was handed. It asserts the safety contract
and is therefore RED:

```
E  AssertionError: shutdown reclaimed 4 of 4 L1 buffers that a pending L2 load
   still owns and has not written; PrefetchController.stop() joins only its own
   loop thread and no in-tree L2 adapter exposes a quiescence guarantee for
   in-flight loads (L2AdapterInterface.close() says nothing about them)
```

Mechanism, `storage_manager.py:1113-1127`:

```
    self._prefetch_controller.stop()     # joins its own thread, then frees
    ...
    for adapter in self._l2_adapters.values():
        adapter.close()                  # adapters consulted only afterwards
    self._l1_manager.close()
```

`PrefetchController.stop()` (`prefetch_controller.py:600-611` on dev) calls
`_cleanup_in_flight_requests()` (`prefetch_controller.py:1474-1491` on dev),
which does

```
    if request.phase == PrefetchPhase.PLAN_AND_LOAD:
        if request.write_reserved_keys:
            l1_mgr.finish_write_and_delete(request.write_reserved_keys)
```

`L1Manager.close()` (`l1_manager.py:902-909`) then frees everything else
unconditionally, with no lock check, so any adapter in the "cancel" or "neither"
group that returned from `close()` with work still in flight lands on freed
memory.

Swapping the two `close()` calls is not a fix by itself, since not every adapter's `close()` waits for in-flight loads.

## Repro 2, L1 write-lock TTL expiry, with `write_ttl_seconds=1`

The L1 read/write locks are `TTLLock` (`csrc/lmcache_native/ttl_lock.{h,cpp}`)
and the entire rule is `ttl_lock.cpp:74`:

```cpp
  return (counter_ > 0) && (current_time < expiration);
```

No TTL is ever refreshed for the duration of an operation: `write_lock.lock()` is
called once at `reserve_write` (`l1_manager.py:486`, `:522`), and neither
`unsafe_read` (`l1_manager.py:306-310`) nor `touch_keys`
(`l1_manager.py:782-796`) touches it. So the default 600 s
(`config.py:213-217`) is a hard wall-clock cap on how long an L2 load may hold a
reserved L1 buffer, unrelated to any L2 timeout.

Against the real `L1Manager` with `write_ttl_seconds=1` and `finish_write` never
called, exactly the state of a buffer a stalled load still owns:

```python
m.reserve_write([k], [False], layout)                     # SUCCESS
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # False, KEY_NOT_READABLE
time.sleep(1.6)                                            # TTL expires
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # True,  SUCCESS  <-- hands out the MemoryObj
m.delete([k])                                              # SUCCESS         <-- buffer returned to the allocator
m.finish_write([k])                                        # KEY_IN_WRONG_STATE
# WARNING L1Manager: finish write on non-write-locked key ...,
#         potential inconsistent data might be written
```

Consequences:

1. A second request reads a half-written buffer. `reserve_read` passes
   `available_for_read()` (`l1_manager.py:53-59`, "not write-locked") and returns
   `entry.memory_obj` (`l1_manager.py:288`).
2. Eviction frees it. `is_key_evictable` (`l1_manager.py:867-884`) returns
   True; the eviction controller passes it as the filter and calls plain
   `delete()` (`eviction_controller.py:184-198`); `delete`'s own "check again"
   safety net (`l1_manager.py:728-736`) uses the same expired `is_locked()`, so
   it does not help. The buffer goes back

items.title: [RFC][MP][L2] End-to-end integrity check for the fs L2 adapter (CRC32 trailer, verify on load)
items.author: malikoyv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The MP `fs` L2 adapter checks only a file's **length** when it loads a KV chunk. A file of the right size but with wrong bytes is served to the engine as a cache hit. The model then produces fluent garbage, and users debug the model rather than the cache.

This RFC proposes an **opt-in** integrity check:
- On store, write a small trailer (magic + CRC32) after the payload.
- On load, verify it; a mismatch becomes a cache miss and the file is deleted.

A draft implementation with tests is ready. I'd like agreement on the on-disk format and the failure semantics before opening the PR.

## Motivation

Silent-corruption reports keep reaching the tracker, and each was found by a person reading bad output rather than by LMCache:

- **#4991:** `fs_native` failed stores stay visible and cache hits produce gibberish. The analysis there found two concurrent writers of one key sharing a staging file, which leaves a torn file in place.
- **#5263:** a buffer is reclaimed while an L2 load is still writing into it.

A checksum does not fix any of these root causes. It turns an L2 content error into a detected miss, so the engine recomputes instead of silently serving wrong KV. Some related reports are not L2 content errors and a checksum would **not** catch them: #5344 (a tensor-parallel shard never written to L1) and #4247 (layout/view mismatch). This RFC is scoped to the L2 bytes.

Ways the same-size wrong bytes can reach `fs` today:
1. **Torn concurrent writes.** Writers of the same key share one temp path. The Python `fs` adapter uses the same `<name>.tmp` pattern as `fs_native`.
2. **Files from another writer or version** in a shared or reused directory.
3. **Media or firmware errors** (silent data corruption): rare per drive, but non-zero at fleet scale.
4. **Power loss or crash.** There is no `fsync` before rename, so after a crash a renamed file can contain stale or zeroed blocks.

What exists today:

| Mechanism | Covers |
|---|---|
| `fs` load length check | Truncated files only |
| AES-GCM serde | Tampering, but only when encryption with key management is enabled |
| `POST /cache/checksums` | Manual GPU-block debugging, not the load path |

## Proposal

**Config.** A new `fs` adapter field, a string rather than a boolean so it can gain algorithms later:

```json
{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/data/lmcache/l2", "checksum": "crc32"}
```

`"none"` is the default and keeps today's on-disk format byte for byte.

**On-disk format** (with `crc32`):

```
<payload bytes> | trailer: magic "LMC1" (4 B) | zlib.crc32(payload) (4 B, little-endian)
```

- Under `use_odirect`, the trailer is padded to one filesystem block so all writes stay aligned. Readers only look at the first 8 bytes after the payload, so buffered and O_DIRECT files are readable by either mode.
- The magic carries a format version (`LMC1`), so the layout can change later without misreading old files.

**Load semantics.**
- The payload is re-hashed off the adapter's event loop (`run_in_executor`; `zlib.crc32` releases the GIL on large buffers).
- A mismatch, missing trailer or unknown magic becomes a **miss** for that key. The prefetch controller already treats it as a gap, and the engine recomputes.
- The file is **deleted**, and listeners get `on_l2_keys_deleted`. Otherwise the key would miss forever: `_execute_store` skips existing files, and `fs` never evicts.

**Accounting.** Store reports the full file length, so usage stays consistent with `delete()`, which subtracts `st_size`.

**Related fix.** On the O_DIRECT path, check the byte count `os.write` returns. Today a short write is renamed into place as if complete.

## Cost

A typical chunk: Llama-3-8B, bf16, 256 tokens, about 32 MiB.

| | Overhead |
|---|---|
| Space | 8 B per file (one extra 4 KiB block allocated; 4 KiB under O_DIRECT), about 0.01% |
| Extra read bandwidth | 8 B per load (at most one extra 4 KiB page) |
| CPU per store and per load | One CRC32 pass. Measured on one host with zlib-ng 1.3.1: about 48 GB/s per core, about 0.7 ms per 32 MiB. Classic zlib is several times slower. |

Space and bandwidth are negligible; the real cost is **latency**. `_execute_load` handles keys sequentially, so each CRC adds directly to that chunk's load time. That's why this is opt-in. Hashing chunk N while reading chunk N+1 is the obvious follow-up. I'll post a `none` vs `crc32` load-throughput table on NVMe with the PR.

## Compatibility

- **Default `"none"`:** no behaviour or format change.
- **Enabling `"crc32"` on an existing directory:** old files have no trailer, so each is discarded on first access, a one-time miss.
- **A `"none"` reader on files written with `"crc32"`:** reads the payload length and ignores the trailer, so it works.
- **Shared directories:** all writers sharing a directory should use the same setting. It's documented.
- **Shared directories with `fs_native`:** it uses the same filenames, so the same rule applies. This RFC changes only the Python `fs` adapter.

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Why not (for now) |
|---|---|
| A checksum serde type (runs through the existing `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`) | Covers every backend, but an adapter takes only one serde today, so it can't combine with fp8/turboquant; it also adds a temp-buffer copy. It's a good follow-up once serdes can chain. |
| xattr for the CRC | Not available on every filesystem (some NFS/FUSE setups); lost when files are copied. |
| A separate checksum file per object | Two files per object, and no atomic publish of both. |
| XOR / parity | No faster in practice (numpy XOR fold about 42 GB/s vs zlib-ng CRC32 about 48 GB/s on the same host), and it misses word reordering and paired bit flips. |
| crc32c (`google-crc32c`) / xxh3 | Faster on some CPUs but adds a dependency. The `checksum` string leaves room to add them. |
| Verifying at lookup | Would need a full read per lookup; load time is the natural point. |

## Open questions for maintainers

1. **Delete on mismatch:** is deleting t

items.title: [Bug][MP] AffinityThreadPool retains stale ZMQ client bindings after instance reaping, so live clients can end up sharing a worker slot
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`AffinityThreadPool` binds each new affinity key to a worker slot on first use,
but there is no lifecycle path that retires that binding.

With the ZMQ transport, the affinity key is derived from the ZMQ client
identity. When an engine process restarts, the new connection can get a new
identity/key. The old key remains in the pool and `_next_slot` continues to
advance as new identities arrive.

The server does independently detect dead workers: after
`--worker-reap-timeout-seconds`, the reaper removes stale GPU instance state.
However, liveness is tracked by `instance_id`, while the affinity pool is keyed
by transport identity. The transport affinity binding associated with the old
connection is not retired when the instance is reaped.

Consequences:

- With `--max-gpu-workers N` and N live engine clients, repeated reconnects can
  eventually route two live clients to the same worker thread while another
  worker thread has no live client.
- The overflow warning can tell the operator to "Increase the worker count"
  even when the configured worker count is sufficient for the number of
  currently live clients.
- Historical client bindings accumulate for the lifetime of the LMCache
  server.

This is a performance / observability issue, not a KV correctness issue:
clients that share a worker thread have their GPU-transfer tasks serialized on
that thread.

---

**To Reproduce**

Environment:

- LMCache dev @ `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
- vLLM `0.30.0`
- MP mode
- ZMQ transport
- `lmcache_driven` transfer
- default `--max-gpu-workers` (1)
- 1x A100

### A. Real deployment

1. Start the LMCache MP server and one vLLM instance using
   `LMCacheMPConnector`.
2. Send a request so the vLLM client gets an affinity binding.
3. `kill -9` the vLLM process group.
4. Wait for the worker reaper (default 120 s).
5. Start a fresh vLLM process and send a request.

Server log:

```text
[01:56:06,701] INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-1652852005048858395 assigned to worker slot 0 of 1 (thread affinity-pool-0-0); 1 distinct key(s) now bound

=== kill -9 vLLM at 02:12:21 UTC ===

[02:14:17,484] WARNING: Reaped GPU instance 1656016543341237076: silent for 120.7s (pinged=True)

=== new vLLM process, first request ===

[02:16:04,742] INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=582847870371926892 assigned to worker slot 0 of 1 (thread affinity-pool-0-0); 2 distinct key(s) now bound
[02:16:04,742] WARNING: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=582847870371926892 wrapped onto worker slot 0 (only 1 workers), so it shares a thread with an earlier key and their tasks are serialized. Increase the worker count to give each client its own thread.
[02:16:04,744] INFO: Retrieved 96 tokens in 0.001 seconds
```

The old GPU instance was reaped at 02:14:17.

At 02:16:04, the affinity pool still reports `2 distinct key(s) now bound` and
emits an overflow warning, although only one vLLM client is alive.

### B. Standalone behavior with multiple worker slots

The following demonstrates the worker-assignment consequence without requiring
a GPU:

```python
import threading

from lmcache.v1.multiprocess.affinity_pool import AffinityThreadPool

pool = AffinityThreadPool(max_workers=2)

def thread_for(key):
    return pool.submit(
        lambda: threading.current_thread().name,
        affinity_key=key,
    ).result()

print("A   ->", thread_for(1001))
print("B   ->", thread_for(1002))

# Simulate A reconnecting with a new transport identity.
print("A'  ->", thread_for(1003))

# Simulate A reconnecting again.
print("A'' ->", thread_for(1004), "  B ->", thread_for(1002))

pool.shutdown()
```

Output:

```text
INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=1001 assigned to worker slot 0 of 2 (thread affinity-0); 1 distinct key(s) now bound
INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=1002 assigned to worker slot 1 of 2 (thread affinity-1); 2 distinct key(s) now bound
INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=1003 assigned to worker slot 0 of 2 (thread affinity-0); 3 distinct key(s) now bound
WARNING: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=1003 wrapped onto worker slot 0 (only 2 workers), ...
INFO: AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=1004 assigned to worker slot 1 of 2 (thread affinity-1); 4 distinct key(s) now bound

A   -> affinity-0
B   -> affinity-1
A'  -> affinity-0
A'' -> affinity-1   B -> affinity-1
```

At the end, the two conceptual live clients (`A''` and `B`) are both routed to
`affinity-1`, while `affinity-0` has no live client.

Relevant code at `1ca53a8a`:

- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/affinity_pool.py:103-106`

  `_slot_for_key()` assigns a newly observed key using
  `_next_slot % _num_workers`, stores the binding, and increments
  `_next_slot`. There is no corresponding lifecycle operation to retire an
  affinity key.

- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/transport/zmq_impl/mq.py:589`

  ZMQ derives the affinity key from the transport identity:

  ```python
  affinity_key = hash(prefix_frames[0])
  ```

- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/management.py:119,134`

  PING refreshes liveness using `instance_id`, and the reaper calls
  `reap_stale_instances()` for stale instance state. The transport-derived
  affinity binding is not part of that cleanup path.

---

**Expected behavior**

When an engine instance is no longer live, stale affinity state associated
with its old connection should not continue to affect worker-slot assignment
for future clients.

After restart/reaping, the configured GPU worker count should still be enough
to provide distinct worker threads for the currently live vLLM instances, as
described in the deployment guide.

`docs/source/mp/deployment.rst` recommends setting `--max-gpu-workers` to at
least the number of vLLM instances sharing the cache server so each instance
gets its own dedicated thread. That property can stop holding after client
restarts while the LMCache server remains alive.

---

**Screenshots**

Not required for reproduction. The relevant server logs and standalone output
are included above.

---

*

items.title: Unauthenticated cross-tenant KV cache read, write, and unbounded storage on LMCache server
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

The LMCache server (`lmcached`, `python -m lmcache.v1.server`) is a raw TCP KV-cache store with no authentication, no per-caller identity, and no eviction. Any host that can reach its port reads another tenant's cached KV data (GET), overwrites it (PUT), enumerates keys (EXIST), and grows the server's memory without bound (the storage dict has no evictor and no quota). Runtime-confirmed on lmcache 0.5.5 (latest PyPI release). Suggested severity: Critical, CVSS 9.1.

### Details

`lmcache.v1.server.__main__` binds the operator-supplied host/port (documented deployments use 0.0.0.0) and serves one thread per connection with a fixed 186-byte request header (9 int32 fields + 150-byte key string; commands PUT=1, GET=2, EXIST=3, LIST=4, HEALTH=5). Keys are parsed by `parse_cache_key` in `lmcache/utils.py` with the format `model@world@worker@chunk_hash@dtype` — every field is attacker-chosen, so a peer can address any model's and any worker's cache entries.

The backing store (`lmcache/v1/server/storage_backend/local_backend.py`) is an `OrderedDict[key] -> data` with the in-source comment `# TODO(Jiayi): please add evictor`: entries are never evicted, there is no size cap per entry or per store, and no caller identity is recorded or checked anywhere in the server.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, `pip install lmcache==0.5.5`, `python -m lmcache.v1.server 0.0.0.0 8900 cpu`. Victim and attacker are plain sockets from separate processes (no LMCache client library needed). Frame helper:

```python
import socket, struct
def hdr(cmd, length, key):  # fmt=4(BINARY), dtype=6(uint8)
    return struct.pack(f"<9i150s", cmd, length, 4, 6, 0, length,0,0,0,
                       key.encode().ljust(150))
KEY = b"victim-model@1@0@aaaabbbbcccc0001@uint8"
# victim: PUT 64 KiB canary
s = socket.create_connection(("192.168.105.123", 8900))
s.sendall(hdr(1, 65536, KEY) + b"L1CANARY_1_" + b"X"*65525)
# attacker (different process): GET the same key
a = socket.create_connection(("192.168.105.123", 8900))
a.sendall(hdr(2, 0, KEY))
meta = a.recv(36)   # code=200, length=65536 ...
data = b""
while len(data) < 65536: data += a.recv(65536 - len(data))
assert data.startswith(b"L1CANARY_1_")   # victim's bytes returned
# overwrite: attacker PUTs the same key
a.sendall(hdr(1, 65536, KEY) + b"ATTACKER_POISON" + b"P"*65522)
# victim's next GET now returns the attacker payload
# control: GET a non-existent key -> code=400, length=0
```

Observed on 0.5.5: GET of a victim key returned the exact 64 KiB canary (code 200); the attacker's PUT replaced it and the victim's poll loop read back the attacker payload; EXIST answered 200 for present and 400 for absent keys; and a PUT loop of unique keys (1 MiB each) raised the server RSS from 608 MB to 3.27 GB with 2600 entries and no reclaim after 3 idle minutes. Expected secure behavior: the server authenticates callers, scopes keys per client/tenant, and bounds storage.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the lmcached port, with no credentials, gets: confidentiality — cached KV bytes of every tenant/model served on demand (KV cache is derived from user prompts); integrity — silent poisoning of other tenants' cache entries, which inference engines then feed into generation; availability — unbounded, never-evicted storage growth kills the server process with OOM and takes the shared cache tier down until restart. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (9.1), CWE-306. Affected: lmcache <= 0.5.5 (latest release at time of report), deployments using the TCP lmcached backend; no patched version yet.

items.title: bug: a client-set `X-Conversation-Id` disables disconnect-cancellation and accumulates uncapped resumable-stream sessions, can cause memory DoS
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

`llama-server`, git `4b1a27f` (`version: 0.5.0-dev (build 1)`), CPU build, Linux x86_64, `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf`. No special launch flag (the resumable-stream manager starts unconditionally at boot).


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8137 -c 2048 -np 1 --no-webui python3 repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos.py --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8137
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Repro script: [repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/f99b245d040ac2604178c1bef9541d6b#file-repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos-py)

The resumable-stream session manager keys a per-request session on the **client-controlled** `X-Conversation-Id` header. When that header is present, two things go wrong, both exploitable by an unauthenticated client:

**(A) A socket disconnect no longer cancels the generation.** With `X-Conversation-Id`, `server_res_spipe::should_stop()` (`tools/server/server-stream.cpp:622-628`) returns `spipe->is_cancelled()`, which is set only by an explicit `DELETE /v1/stream` — instead of `!conn_alive()`. So a streaming request whose client hangs up keeps the inference slot busy generating to its natural stop. An attacker fires `stream:true` requests with a large `max_tokens` and drops each connection immediately; every abandoned request still consumes a full generation and pins a slot. 

Measured on a single-slot server (`-np 1`): after abandoning one stream, a normal follow-up request was blocked **36.9 s** (the whole generation) with the header, versus **0.07 s** without it (disconnect cancels normally).

**(B) Sessions accumulate with no cap and a 300 s post-completion TTL.** Each session buffers up to `STREAM_SESSION_MAX_BYTES = 4 MiB` of SSE output (`server-stream.cpp:18`) and is retained for `STREAM_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS = 300 s` **after** the generation completes before the GC removes it (`gc_loop`, `server-stream.cpp:356`). `create_or_replace` (`:235`) just `emplace`s into an `unordered_map,  **there is no cap on the number of sessions**. A client that sends streaming requests with a fresh `X Conversation-Id` each time and never issues `DELETE /v1/stream` accumulates ~`rate × 300 s` sessions, each holding up to 4 MiB, eventually will cause memory exhaustion.

Ablation confirms the header is the cause: 150 streaming requests **without** the header grow `VmHWM` by ~0 MB (sessions are evicted on completion — `on_complete` at `server-stream.cpp:638`), while 150 **with** unique headers retain their sessions (monotonic growth; at large `max_tokens` each retains up to 4 MiB).

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->

```console

```
</details>

<!-- Long logs that you upload as files go here, outside the "console" area -->

comments.author: benthecarman
comments.body:
A related problem: sessions live in one global map (`g_stream_sessions`, `server-stream.cpp:65`), keyed only by the client-supplied `X-Conversation-Id`. Nothing ties a session to the caller's API key. So anyone who knows or guesses another client's ID can:

- read that client's buffered output: `GET /v1/stream` (`:454`)
- cancel their generation: `DELETE /v1/stream` (`:561`)
- replace their session by sending their own request with the same ID; `create_or_replace` cancels the existing session (`:235-255`)

Also, a `DELETE` with an unknown ID writes every live conversation ID to the log at WARN (`:297-304`).

This only matters when several clients share one server and IDs aren't random (the web UI uses UUIDs). One possible fix is to scope sessions to the API key that created them, and to stop logging live IDs.

items.title: [RFC] Align KV cache events with vLLM's schema so shared consumers have a standard format
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

# Motivation

## Summary

#37482 switched KV cache events to tagged msgpack maps, the same encoding vLLM moved to in vllm-project/vllm#42892. The fields both engines have use the same names. A consumer however can't treat events from both engines in a standard fashion because of the following:

1. Replay responses are missing the topic frame vLLM added in vllm-project/vllm#45177.
2. There's no `lora_name` in SGLang events. vLLM always sends it and its msgspec types reject events without it.
3. The salt is in a `cache_salt` field in SGLang. vLLM puts it in `extra_keys` on block 0 which is where a consumer like llm-d looks for it.
4. Event hashes leave out `extra_key` in SGLang, so LoRA and base model blocks with the same tokens share a hash.

This RFC proposes fixing those four in SGLang's native format in three phases to align with vLLM for standardization. It doesn't propose a vLLM hash mode or a format flag. Consumers like llm-d don't need vLLM's hash recipe and the in-repo router depends on SGLang's.

## Background

### What already matches

| Area | SGLang and vLLM |
|---|---|
| Event encoding | Tagged maps, class name under `type`, `None` optionals omitted |
| Batch | Positional `[ts, events, dp_rank]` |
| Live frames | `(topic, seq, payload)` |
| `BlockStored` fields | `block_hashes`, `parent_block_hash`, `token_ids`, `block_size`, `lora_id`, `medium`, `session_id` |
| `BlockRemoved`, `AllBlocksCleared` | Same, apart from vLLM's optional `group_idx` |

### Consumers checked

| Consumer | How it reads SGLang events |
|---|---|
| llm-d `engineType: sglang` | Positional arrays only. It can't read anything since #37482. That's llm-d's to fix |
| llm-d `engineType: vllm` | Reads SGLang's maps today. Derives its own block keys from `token_ids`, `lora_name` and `extra_keys` and uses engine hashes only as opaque keys |
| `experimental/sgl-router` | Decodes SGLang maps and ignores unknown keys. Recomputes SGLang's hash recipe on the request side (`kv_events/hash.rs`). Decodes hashes as `i64`. Maps `medium` strings to tiers |
| sgl-router replay client (#32729, open) | Parses today's two frame replay reply |
| vLLM's msgspec types | Fail on SGLang events (see below) |

Dynamo wasn't checked.

## Gaps

### 1. Replay replies have no topic frame

| | Replayed batch | End marker |
|---|---|---|
| vLLM | `(client_id, b"", topic, seq, payload)` | `(client_id, b"", b"", END_SEQ, b"")` |
| SGLang (`kv_events.py:541,546`) | `(client_id, b"", seq, payload)` | `(client_id, b"", END_SEQ, b"")` |

llm-d's replay client requires three frames after the delimiter (`parseEventFrame` in `pkg/kvevents/zmq_subscriber.go`). From reading that code: with `replaySocketPort` set for an SGLang pool, every replay
is rejected as malformed and the pod's index entries are cleared. Live batches that arrive before a successful replay are dropped and the retry 30 seconds later fails the same way, so the pod never gets indexed.

### 2. No `lora_name`

vLLM declares `lora_id`, `medium` and `lora_name` without defaults, so all three are always on the wire. Decoding a SGLang batch with vLLM's struct definitions (copied from `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py` at `de24e51908`) fails:

```
msgspec.ValidationError: Object missing required field `lora_name` - at `$[1][0]`
```

The reverse direction works. llm-d also uses `lora_name` as the model name when it derives keys, so SGLang LoRA blocks are indexed as base model blocks.

### 3. The salt isn't in `extra_keys`

vLLM sends one `extra_keys` entry per block: LoRA name, multimodal identifiers, then `cache_salt` only on the block starting at token 0. llm-d reads the salt only from there. Its precise prefix cache README says salted SGLang requests "are precise-cache misses until SGLang emits `extra_keys`". Unsalted requests can also score hits against salted only copies. SGLang still isolates the cache, so this costs routing quality, not safety.

A side note that corrects the earlier #27682 discussion: vLLM's hashes are salt namespaced too because the salt in block 0's extra keys is part of the hash. Neither engine has `BlockRemoved` ambiguity across salts.

### 4. Event hashes leave out `extra_key`

`compute_node_event_hash_values` (`mem_cache/utils.py:178`) seeds the chain with the salt only. `Req` folds the LoRA uuid into `extra_key` (`schedule_batch.py:1096-1099`). So from reading the code, a LoRA block and a base model block with the same tokens emit the same hash and a `BlockRemoved` for one looks like a removal of both. Storage hashes already include the namespace (`storage_namespace_seed`, `utils.py:125`). vLLM includes the LoRA name in its block hash.

## Proposal

### Phase 1: additive fields, no consumer breaks

**1a. `lora_name`, with `medium` required.** Use vLLM's field order:

```python
class BlockStored(KVCacheEvent):
    block_hashes: list[int]
    parent_block_hash: Optional[int]
    token_ids: list[int]
    block_size: int
    lora_id: Optional[int]
    medium: Optional[str]
    lora_name: Optional[str]
    extra_keys: Optional[list[Optional[tuple]]] = None
    cache_salt: Optional[str] = None
    session_id: Optional[str] = None


class BlockRemoved(KVCacheEvent):
    block_hashes: list[int]
    medium: Optional[str]
```

msgspec needs `medium` to lose its default so that `lora_name` is always sent. Every constructor already passes `medium`. `lora_name` stays `null` until phase 3. `lora_id` stays `null` because vLLM's is a deprecated int and SGLang's is a uuid string.

**1b. `extra_keys` with the salt.** When a node's parent is the root (its first page starts at token 0) and `cache_salt` is set, send `extra_keys=[(salt,), None, ...]` lined up with `block_hashes`. `KVCacheEventRecorder.enqueue` merges parent linked stores and w

items.title: [Bug] HiCache + hybrid (SSM/Mamba): failed cudaHostRegister on a secondary host pool aborts the whole instance, and the error path throws TypeError thereby hiding the real rc
items.author: flymysql
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On sglang `0.5.19` (torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, H20), starting a **hybrid SSM/Mamba** model
with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend dynamic` fails during
`attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache` and **kills the entire instance**.

Two coupled defects:

1. **`cudaHostRegister` failure is treated as fatal.** `alloc_with_host_register` raises, which
   aborts scheduler init for all TP ranks. But the failure only means "this host pool is not
   zero-copy registered" — and sglang's own non-zero-copy path (`_generic_page_get/_set`) is
   fully functional without registration. A missing acceleration is escalated into a full outage.
2. **The error path destroys its own diagnostic.** Inside the `raise`, `cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)`
   is called with a **plain `int`**, which raises `TypeError` on this torch build — so the real
   `rc`/`offset`/`size` are swallowed. Operators only see a bare `TypeError`.

Additionally, the failure **leaves a sticky CUDA error**, which then surfaces later at an unrelated
call site (`_create_sync_groups` → `all_gather_object` → `torch.zeros`), which made this
considerably harder to root-cause.

### Environment

- sglang `0.5.19`
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- 8 × H20 (96 GiB) / 8 × H20-3e (141 GiB), driver `535.161.08`
- Model: `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, pool stack **KV + MAMBA**)
- Backend: `--hicache-storage-backend dynamic` with `interface_v1: 1` in the extra config
  (this selects the zero-copy page functions; the crash itself is in host-pool allocation and is
  not specific to any particular dynamic backend)
- Relevant flags: `--mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
  --hicache-io-backend direct --tp 8`

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <hybrid SSM/Mamba model, e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 1.0 \
  --hicache-storage-backend dynamic \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct \
  --hicache-io-backend direct \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"backend_name":"...","module_path":"...","class_name":"...","interface_v1":1,...}'
```

Failures are **not deterministic per machine** — we observed the same config **succeed on a 96 GiB
box and fail on a 141 GiB box**, consistent with a pool-geometry / allocation-order dependence.

### Observed failure trace (verbatim)

```
[TP5] attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1759, in attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache
    result = strategy.build(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1329, in build
    host_pool_group, cache_controller = build_hybrid_mamba_stack(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 735, in build_hybrid_mamba_stack
    kv_host_pool = build_kv_host_pool(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 160, in build_kv_host_pool
    return kv_host_pool_cls(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 89, in __init__
    super().__init__(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/base.py", line 205, in __init__
    self.kv_buffer = self.init_kv_buffer()
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 191, in init_kv_buffer
    buffer = alloc_func(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 235, in alloc_with_host_register
    _cuda_host_register(buffer, registration_granularity_bytes)
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 163, in _cuda_host_register
    f"{cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)}) at offset={offset} size={size} "
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: cudaGetErrorString(): incompatible function arguments. The following argument types are supported:
    1. (arg0: torch._C._cudart.cudaError) -> str
Invoked with: 1                      <-- the real rc is only visible here, by accident
```

A second, later-surfacing variant of the same root cause (sticky CUDA error), reached when the
first pool *does* register successfully:

```
[TP6] Scheduler hit an exception: ...
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_cache_controller.py", line 161, in attach_storage_backend
    super().attach_storage_backend(
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 590, in attach_storage_backend
    self.prefetch_hits_sync_groups = self._create_sync_groups()
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 415, in _create_sync_groups
    create_custom_parallel_group(
  File ".../distributed/parallel_state.py", line 2762, in create_custom_parallel_group
    torch.distributed.all_gather_object(gathered_configs, local_config)
```

Instrumenting `_cuda_host_register` on the failing box (141 GiB) shows the KV pool registers fine

`offset=0`, the size is page aligned, and `chunk_limit=256 GiB` (i.e. a single call) — so this is

items.title: [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via /dev/shm
items.author: VNG-VMONITOR
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via `/dev/shm`

## Motivation

In deployments running multiple DP ranks on a **single node** (e.g. one host with 8 GPUs and `--dp-size 8`), each rank maintains a fully private L2 host KV cache. When two ranks receive requests with the same prefix — a common pattern for system prompts, few-shot examples, or shared document context — Rank B cannot see the KV pages that Rank A already produced, and must recompute the prefix from scratch.

Existing HiCache L3 backends (Mooncake, NIXL, AIBrix, 3FS, LMCache) do solve cross-instance sharing, but they all go through a networked / service-mediated data path. For **same-node** sharing that is common in single-box multi-DP deployments, the network round-trip is pure overhead — the ranks are all local processes with access to the same physical DRAM.

## Proposed design: `shm_peer_l2` HiCache storage backend

Two DP ranks on the same node map the same L2 host pool via named shared memory (`/dev/shm` tmpfs). Metadata (key → owner rank + slot address) is exchanged through a small direct-mapped index (also in `/dev/shm`). When Rank B misses in its own L1/L2, it looks up the index; on a hit, it performs one `memcpy` within the shared SHM to bring the peer's page into its own slot, then DMAs to GPU — no recompute.

Compared to a hypothetical "share via existing L3 file" approach (see `shm_cross_dp` below), the peer variant eliminates the L3 data copy: only a 288-byte pointer per page is written, giving:

- **Storage overhead**: ~55 MB total for a 475 GB L2 (vs. ~L2_size for a full mirror)
- **Read path**: 1 index lookup + 1 SHM memcpy + 1 DMA (vs. L3→CPU_buf→L2 + memcpy + DMA)
- **Write path**: 1 GPU→shared_L2 DMA + 1 index write (vs. + 1 memcpy to L3 file)

### Correctness

A per-page **generation counter** in shared memory prevents stale reads: when Rank A evicts and reallocates a slot, its generation counter increments. Rank B compares the stored generation against the current one; a mismatch is treated as a miss instead of copying whatever bytes now occupy the slot. The check is best-effort (no full memory barrier) — the tiny TOCTOU window between the generation read and the memcpy is accepted as per the "stale reads may be silently accepted" contract already present in HiCache read paths.

### Operational envelope

- `--dp-size >= 2`
- All DP ranks on the **same node** (`/dev/shm` is node-local tmpfs)
- `--hicache-write-policy write_through` required (`write_back` only flushes on eviction, so Rank B would not see data timely)
- Optionally with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first`/`page_first_direct` layouts

Auto-computed capacity (`page_num × 4`, 25% load factor) at startup; explicit override via `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"peer_l2_capacity": N}'`.

Collision rate emitted every 10,000 writes; WARNING once it exceeds 10% (actionable — increase capacity).

## Existing prototype

A working implementation exists in a downstream fork. It shipped as two related backends registered through `backend_factory.py`:

- `shm_cross_dp` — shared L2 pool + full SHM L3 data file (simpler, more memory, extra copy)
- `shm_peer_l2` — shared L2 pool + tiny SHM index only (optimized; strict improvement)

Both reuse a common `ShmHostTensorAllocator` and named-SHM helpers added to `pool_host/common.py` and `storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`. Tests included: `test/registered/mem_cache/test_shared_l2_hicache.py` (CPU-only, `register_cpu_ci`), covering allocator wiring, slot partitioning, index CRUD, generation-counter stale-slot behavior, collision detection, auto-capacity, and a cross-process shared-L2 round-trip via subprocess.

The prototype hooks into:
- `HiRadixCache` — for `shm_name` derivation, `dp_rank/dp_size` forwarding to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost`
- `HostKVCache` (`pool_host/base.py`) — `clear()` partitions `free_slots` to `[slot_start, slot_start+local_size)`; `alloc()` fires registered callbacks; `slot_used` spans the full pool for cross-DP double-free detection
- `cache_controller` — `shm_peer_l2` added to the V1 interface allow-list

## The upstreaming question

We noticed [#40787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40787) (merged 2026-09-22) removed `HiRadixCache` since [#35081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35081) migrated HiCache to `UnifiedRadixCache`. The prototype above was written against `HiRadixCache` and does **not** apply cleanly to current `main`.

Before we invest in porting to `UnifiedRadixCache`, we would like guidance from HiCache maintainers on a few design points:

1. **Integration point in UnifiedRadixCache** — where is the equivalent of `HiRadixCache.write_backup`, `_inc_hit_count`, and `prefetch_from_storage` in the unified architecture? Is there a documented extension surface for backends that need per-page alloc callbacks and slot-partitioned allocators?

2. **Shared L2 pool ownership** — is there interest in a first-class "shared host pool" concept inside `MHATokenToKVPoolHost` (dp_rank / dp_size / shm_name parameters)? The prototype adds them minimally, but a maintainer-blessed shape would be preferable.

3. **Scope split** — would you prefer:
   - (a) A single PR introducing the shared L2 pool infrastructure + one backend using it (either `shm_cross_dp` or `shm_peer_l2`), then a follow-up for the other, or

4. **Naming / positioning** — `shm_peer_l2` vs `shm_cross_dp` overlap significantly; would maintainers prefer we upstream only `shm_peer_l2` (the optimized variant) and drop `shm_cross_dp`, or keep both as complementary options?

5. **Alternative direction** — is there an existing or planned effort (Mooncake local mode, an internal HiCache broadcast, etc.) that already covers the same-node peer sharing use case and would make this redundant? We searched issues/PRs and did not find one but want to double-check.

items.title: [Bug] `/hicache/storage-backend/clear` returns "Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared." with a 400 when it did not clear anything
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Simply purely a reporting defect. 

Both the current endpoint and its deprecated alias build a **fixed** response body and vary only the status code, so the failure path returns a message that affirmatively claims the operation succeeded, and the reason it actually failed, which the handler is holding in `ret`, is discarded.

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1072
@app.api_route("/hicache/storage-backend/clear", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
async def clear_hicache_storage_backend():
    ret = await _global_state.tokenizer_manager.clear_hicache_storage()
    return Response(
        content="Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.\n",     # <- always this
        status_code=200 if ret.success else HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
    )
```

The deprecated `/clear_hicache_storage_backend` (line ~1059) has the same shape, with the deprecation notice prepended to the same unconditional "cleared" sentence.

The body is `text/plain`, not JSON, so a client that reads the message, which is the natural thing to do for a plain-text endpoint, is told the cache was cleared when it was not.



### Reproduction

On a server with no hierarchical cache configured:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --port 30000
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/hicache/storage-backend/clear
```

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
...
Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.
```

## Expected

The body should reflect the outcome and carry the reason the handler already has, e.g.

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
{"success": false, "message": "<whatever ret carries, e.g. no hierarchical cache storage backend is configured>"}
```

Status says the request failed; body says the work was done; neither says why.

items.title: [Bug] Anthropic /v1/messages: inline system messages are still merged into the top system block on system-first templates (Qwen), so the prefix cache misses every turn
items.author: rgrashel
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Follow-up to #28883 / #28906. Inline `role: "system"` messages now stay in place on templates that can render a non-leading system role. On templates that cannot (Qwen's `System message must be at the beginning.` guard; Qwen3.8-27B here), `AnthropicServing._convert_to_chat_completion_request` still folds every one into the leading system block (`_merge_inline_system`), so the same prefix-cache fork remains.

Claude Code 2.1.x sends a `role: "system"` message after every user turn and tool result (an environment block, then `<total_tokens>...</total_tokens>` reminders). Each request has one more than the last, so the leading system block grows every turn and the rendered prompt changes right after the base system text. The radix cache matches only up to there, and the rest of the conversation is prefilled again on every turn.

Observed (1x RTX PRO 6000, Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4, Claude Code on `/v1/messages`, with and without `CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0`):

- `#cached-token` in the Prefill log stays at 19-22K (tools + base system) however long the conversation is. A session at 75-109K context prefilled 75-109K new tokens on every turn.
- 5-turn task with the attribution header off: every turn reused exactly 19,304 tokens.

With the fix below, same setup: an 11-turn task reused 20,800 -> 22,976 tokens and read 228-596 new tokens per turn; a 42-step agent run at ~94K context averaged ~6 s per step; over 69 requests 96% of prompt tokens were cached and mean TTFT was 0.5 s (8.3 s and 32% over the 167 requests before).

The same code is on `main` as of 2026-10-02 (`self._merge_inline_system = not openai_serving_chat.supports_inline_system`); I compared the file but have not run `main`.

**Proposed fix.** On the merge path, keep each inline system message where it arrived: append its text (wrapped, e.g. ``) to the preceding user/tool message, or emit it as a user message when there is none. Only the top-level `system` field goes in the leading block. Earlier turns then render identically from request to request. It is about 25 lines in `_convert_to_chat_completion_request`. I run it in production with 5 unit tests; the 3 existing tests that assert the merge need new expectations. Happy to open a PR.

**Patch** (against 8874c51a; the same hunks apply to `main` as of 2026-10-02):

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py
@@ -419,13 +419,11 @@
                     if block.type == "text" and block.text:
                         system_parts.append(block.text)
 
-        if self._merge_inline_system:
-            for msg in anthropic_request.messages:
-                if msg.role != "system":
-                    continue
-                text = _extract_system_text(msg.content)
-                if text:
-                    system_parts.append(text)
+        # Mid-conversation system messages are not hoisted into this leading block on
+        # the merge path. Hoisting rewrites the start of the prompt every time a client
+        # adds one (Claude Code adds one per turn), so the prefix cache stops matching
+        # near the top and each turn re-reads the whole conversation. They are attached
+        # in place instead; see ``_attach_inline_system`` below.
 
         if system_parts:
             openai_messages.append(
@@ -448,9 +446,32 @@
                 openai_messages.append({"role": "user", "content": list(parts)})
             parts.clear()
 
+        def _attach_inline_system(text: Optional[str]) -> None:
+            """Keep a mid-conversation system message at the position it arrived.
+
+            The chat template cannot render a system role here (that is why
+            this is the merge path), so the text is appended to the preceding
+            user or tool message, or sent as its own user message when there is
+            none. Earlier turns then render identically from request to request.
+            """
+            if not text:
+                return
+            note = f""
+            prev = openai_messages[-1] if openai_messages else None
+            if prev is not None and prev.get("role") in ("user", "tool"):
+                content = prev.get("content")
+                if isinstance(content, str):
+                    prev["content"] = f"{content}\n\n{note}" if content else note
+                    return
+                if isinstance(content, list):
+                    content.append({"type": "text", "text": note})
+                    return
+            openai_messages.append({"role": "user", "content": note})
+
         # Convert messages
         for msg in anthropic_request.messages:
             if msg.role == "system" and self._merge_inline_system:
+                _attach_inline_system(_extract_system_text(msg.content))
                 continue
             if isinstance(msg.content, str):
                 openai_messages.append({"role": msg.role, "content": msg.content})
```

**Tests.** With the patch, `test/registered/unit/entrypoints/anthropic/test_serving.py` runs 61 tests with 3 failures, all of them tests that assert the old merge: `test_in_messages_system_merged_when_template_requires_first`, `test_in_messages_system_merged_with_top_level_when_merge` and `test_constructed_message_objects_merged_on_merge_path`. Five new tests pass: the text is attached to the preceding user message, the top-level `system` is left alone, it is attached to a preceding tool result, a leading inline system beco
