items.title: Unauthenticated fleet control plane on LMCache MP Coordinator (default 0.0.0.0:9300)
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

The LMCache MP Coordinator — the fleet-level cache control plane — starts by default on 0.0.0.0:9300 with no authentication on any endpoint. A network peer registers fake cache instances, deregisters real ones (removing them from scheduling), rewrites tenant quotas, injects fabricated cache events, and enumerates the fleet's key directory. Runtime-confirmed on lmcache 0.5.5 (latest PyPI release); the companion controller API server (`lmcache.v1.api_server`, default 0.0.0.0:9000) exposes the same unauthenticated /lookup, /clear and /pin surface. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator.config` hardcodes `host: str = "0.0.0.0", port: int = 9300`. The coordinator's FastAPI app (`lmcache/v1/mp_coordinator/app.py`) mounts routers with no authentication middleware anywhere in the package (a full-source scan for api_key/auth/token primitives returns zero hits):

- `POST /instances` / `PUT /instances/{id}/heartbeat` / `DELETE /instances/{id}` — anyone registers, keeps alive, or removes fleet instances; deletion removes the instance's reported placements from scheduling.
- `PUT /quota/config` and `PUT /quota/{cache_salt}` — fleet and per-tenant quota tampering.
- `POST /cache/pins`, `DELETE /cache/pins`, `POST /events` — pin manipulation and fabricated cache events that feed the coordinator's placement/eviction views.
- `GET /directory/keys` (paged), `POST /directory/lookup`, `POST /directory/blend-lookup` — full key directory with token-id lists and per-instance placements.

The controller API server (`lmcache/v1/api_server/__main__.py`, `--host` default 0.0.0.0, port 9000) adds `POST /lookup` (token-to-placement layout), `POST /clear` and `POST /pin` for any instance_id, likewise with no authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, `pip install lmcache==0.5.5`, `python -m lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9300` (`ss -ltnp` confirms 0.0.0.0:9300). From any peer:

```bash
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/healthz                       # 200
# register a fake instance (schemas read from the installed package's pydantic models)
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @fake_instance.json   # 200/201
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances                      # fake instance listed
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-aaa/heartbeat -d @hb.json      # 200
# remove an instance from the fleet
curl -s -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-bbb                          # 200
# quota tampering and event injection
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/config -d @quota.json                           # 200
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/default -d '{"...": 0}'                         # 200
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/events -d @fake_events.json                          # 200
# fleet key directory
curl -s "http://192.168.105.123:9300/directory/keys?limit=100"                                   # keys+placements
```

Observed on 0.5.5: every call above succeeded without any credential; the fake instance appeared in `GET /instances`, the DELETE removed an instance, quota writes were accepted, `/events` accepted a fabricated batch, and `/directory/keys` returned the directory enumeration surface. The api_server on 0.0.0.0:9000 likewise answered unauthenticated `/lookup` (200 with layout structure) and accepted `/clear` and `/pin` requests. Expected secure behavior: a fleet control plane authenticates callers and authorizes instance/quota mutations.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the coordinator port (fixed, documented default 9300, bound on all interfaces) corrupts the fleet's shared cache state: deregistered workers disappear from placement (requests lose their cache or fail over), fake instances redirect placement decisions, quota tampering starves or floods tenants, injected events poison placement and eviction views, and the key directory discloses which prefixes (token id lists) are cached where across the fleet. Confidentiality (directory/placement disclosure), integrity (fleet membership, quotas, events), availability (instance removal, quota starvation). Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:H (8.8), CWE-306. Affected: lmcache <= 0.5.5 (latest release), deployments running the MP coordinator / controller API server; no patched version yet.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Eval bug: SM_60 Quality Loss, FP32 math silently done in FP16, fix merged in two forks.
items.author: apollo-mg
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 9967 (4f37f5197)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Linux / CUDA / 4× Tesla P100-PCIE-16GB (sm_60), dual Xeon, driver 580.159.03, CUDA 12.4. Tested on Ubuntu Server 26.04.

### Models

Qwen3.6-27B Q6_K (22,523,238,624 bytes) for the quality panel; Qwen3.6-4B dense and Darwin-36B-A3B (Qwen3.5-MoE arch) Q6_K for the speed legs.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

SM_60 currently gets put into a hardware accelerated fast-path by default, which uses a FP16 hardware accelerator. The problem is that some FP32 math is silently getting truncated to FP16 that shouldn't be, causing significant accuracy deviations from baseline (0.002298 median KL divergence vs FP32 reference/1-in-29 flipped top tokens).

The fix for this is to carve out SM_60 the same way SM_61 already is, bypassing the Fast Path gate, and keeping FP32 math at 32 bits as it should be.

## How to Fix

261- #if defined(FP16_AVAILABLE) && __CUDA_ARCH__ != 610
261+ #if defined(FP16_AVAILABLE) && __CUDA_ARCH__ != 610 && __CUDA_ARCH__ != 600

305-        (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc) && fp16_available(cc) && ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc) != 610) ||
305+        (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc) && fp16_available(cc) && ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc) != 610 && ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc) != 600) ||

311-    return (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc) && cc >= GGML_CUDA_CC_PASCAL && cc != 610) || GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_AMD(cc) ||
311+    return (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc) && cc >= GGML_CUDA_CC_PASCAL && cc != 610 && cc != 600) || GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_AMD(cc) ||

TheTom (Tom Turney) has shipped: https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/releases/tag/tqp-v0.3.0 
https://github.com/TheTom/llama-cpp-turboquant/pull/212 
spiritbuun has merged: https://github.com/spiritbuun/buun-llama-cpp/pull/80


## Steps to Reproduce:

1. Build stock llama.cpp using  `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=60`.
2. Generate the truth base, run `llama-perplexity --kl-divergence-base out.kld` with fp32 KV, FA off,
   on a patched build (fp32 arithmetic) — this is the step everyone skips.
3. Compare the stock vs patched runs against that base with `--kl-divergence`, 2048 ctx, 32 chunks.
4. Speed: `llama-bench` pp8192/tg32 @ d8192, patched vs unpatched, same host, nothing else
   on the GPUs.



### First Bad Commit

We followed the 610-only exemptions in their present form back through the 2024-era commits dc685be46 (#7188, FP32 FA vec kernel), 9b596417a (#7527, quantized KV for FA vec), and a818f3028 (#8075, MMQ-by-default) — sm_60 has been on the fast path the whole time,  no bisect needed.

### Relevant log output

items.title: [RFC]: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference（CCF 赛题四）
items.author: Pinoeer-kingxi
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

<!-- GitHub-safe plain Markdown. Copy from the raw .md text, not from Word or a rich-text preview. -->

# RFC: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| RFC | RFC-EPD-Agent-Multimodal-2026 |
| Status | Draft |
| Date | 2026-07-05 |
| Target Project | Mooncake / Mooncake Transfer Engine / MooncakeStore |
| Target Integrations | vLLM, SGLang, Qwen-VL/Qwen3-VL-style multimodal models |
| Scope | Encoder-Prefill-Decode disaggregation, Agent state cloning, cross-step KV reuse, evaluation protocol |
| Primary Audience | Mooncake maintainers, serving-system contributors, vLLM/SGLang integration reviewers |
| Implementation Horizon | One-month prototype milestone, followed by staged hardening |
| Compatibility Target | Preserve existing PD and colocated serving paths; new features must be gated by configuration |

---

## Summary

This RFC proposes an extension to Mooncake for **agentic multimodal inference**. The core idea is to generalize Mooncake's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving capability from a two-stage Prefill-Decode model into a broader **Encoder-Prefill-Decode (EPD)** architecture, while also supporting:

- **Agent state cloning** for multi-branch reasoning;
- **visual feature caching** for repeated image/document contexts;
- **cross-step KV reuse** for repeated workflow prefixes;
- **tool-call offload/restore** to release GPU memory during blocking I/O;
- **A2A handoff** for state transfer among planner, executor, verifier, and domain agents;
- **coordinated scheduling** across Encoder, Prefill, Decode, and storage resources.

The proposal introduces a unified `MultimodalState` abstraction that represents visual feature bundles, textual/multimodal KV pages, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, TTL, and ownership.

The design intentionally avoids a single global strongly-consistent KV registry. Instead, it uses:

1. **KV Directory** for eventually consistent metadata lookup;
2. **Workflow Shards** for per-workflow strong consistency, refcount, CAS, fork, release, and CoW;
3. **Decentralized Scheduler** for admission control, priority scheduling, offload/restore, and A2A-aware routing.

For KV reuse correctness, the RFC uses a conservative default:

> **Exact Prefix Reuse by default; Approximate Reuse only behind validation gates and feature flags.**

Approximate reuse is never required for correctness. If any validation step fails, the system falls back to exact prefix reuse or full Prefill.

---

## Motivation

### Multimodal inference is naturally EPD-shaped

Multimodal inference contains three computationally different stages:

1. **Encoder**: image/video/audio features are produced by a modality encoder.
2. **Prefill**: the language model processes the full multimodal prompt and builds KV cache.
3. **Decode**: autoregressive generation produces output tokens.

Traditional PD disaggregation couples Encoder with Prefill. This becomes inefficient when the same multimodal context appears repeatedly across turns, agent steps, or branch candidates. Separating Encoder from Prefill enables:

- independent scaling of visual encoder workers;
- reuse of visual features across turns and workflows;
- lower repeated prefill cost for multimodal prompts;
- more flexible routing for prefill-heavy versus decode-heavy workloads.

### Agent workflows require persistent state

Agent workloads are not simple one-shot requests. They involve:

- multi-turn conversations;
- external tool calls and long I/O waits;
- multi-branch reasoning such as Tree-of-Thought, beam search, and verifier branches;
- A2A handoff between planner, executor, retriever, tool agent, and verifier;
- repeated prefixes across workflow steps.

These patterns make KV state a first-class runtime object rather than a temporary per-request artifact.

### Mooncake is well positioned for this extension

Mooncake already focuses on disaggregated KVCache management and high-performance transfer. Extending it to EPD and agentic workflows is a natural next step because the same core primitives are needed:

- cross-node tensor transfer;
- distributed KVCache pooling;
- offload and restore;
- memory ownership;
- scheduling across heterogeneous workers;
- efficient movement of large intermediate states.

This RFC defines a practical architecture that can be implemented incrementally and reviewed in stages.

---

## Goals

This RFC has the following goals.

### G1. Support EPD disaggregation

- Separate Vision Encoder, Prefill, and Decode into independently schedulable workers.
- Transfer Encoder outputs to Prefill and Prefill KV pages to Decode through Mooncake Transfer Engine.
- Preserve fallback paths to normal colocated or PD-only execution.

### G2. Introduce a unified multimodal state abstraction

- Represent FeatureBundle, KVPage, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, leases, and TTL.
- Support snapshot-based state reads, page-level refcount, and Copy-on-Write.
- Provide clear lifecycle transitions for active, shared, offloaded, restored, released, and aborted states.

### G3. Support Agent State Cloning

- Enable low-cost fork for multi-branch reasoning.
- Avoid deep-copying full KV state for each branch.
- Make branch writes safe through page-level CoW.
- Make refcount correctness testable and observable.

### G4. Support cross-step KV reuse

- Use exact prefix reuse as the safe default.
- Add approximate or non-contiguous reuse behind validation gates and feature flags.
- Always preserve fallback to full Prefill.

### G5. Reduce control-plane bottlenecks

- Avoid a globally locked GDKR-style metadata service.
- Move refcount and CAS to workflow-local shards.
- Keep cross-workflow metadata eventually consistent with bounded staleness.
- Prevent a single hot workflow or global registry from throttling unrelated workflows.

### G6. Provide a reproducible evaluation protocol

- Define datasets, workload construction, ba

- Error counts covering submission and completion failures.

items.title: GSP: grammar-conditioned sparse LM-head projection - replication and SGLang integration feedback wanted
items.author: StealthEyeLLC
items.body_excerpt:
I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback
- datacenter GPU replication
- heterogeneous-batch measurements
- negative results / dense-winning crossover cases

Release, verified preprint, source, raw evidence:
https://github.com/StealthEyeLLC/grammar-sparse-projection/releases/tag/v0.1.1

items.title: [Bug] parse_arguments turns comma-containing values into Python tuples
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


`parse_arguments`' Strategy 3 calls `ast.literal_eval`, which parses a bare comma-separated
expression as a **Python tuple**. A scalar argument such as `1,000` (a thousands separator) or
`"a","b"` is therefore returned as a tuple and serialised into the tool arguments as a JSON array:
`parse_arguments("1,000", "number")` returns `((1, 0), True)` and the tool receives `[1, 0]`.


### Reproduction


```python
import json

from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import Function, Tool
from sglang.srt.function_call.glm4_moe_detector import Glm4MoeDetector, parse_arguments

print(parse_arguments("1,000", "number"))
print(parse_arguments('"a","b"', "number"))

tools = [
    Tool(
        type="function",
        function=Function(
            name="book",
            description="Book seats",
            parameters={"type": "object", "properties": {"n": {"type": "number"}}},
        ),
    )
]
text = "<tool_call>book\n<arg_key>n</arg_key>\n<arg_value>1,000</arg_value>\n</tool_call>"
print(Glm4MoeDetector().detect_and_parse(text, tools).calls[0].parameters)
```

Output:

```
((1, 0), True)
(('a', 'b'), True)
{"n": [1, 0]}
```

### Expected behavior and impact

`1,000` is a plain, common way for a model to write a number, and `"1,000"` is exactly the kind of
value the surrounding fallback chain exists to salvage. Turning it into the two-element array
`[1, 0]` is silent data corruption in two directions at once: the magnitude is wrong (1 instead of
1000) and the JSON type is wrong (array where the schema declares a number). The tool is invoked
with plausible-looking but incorrect arguments, and nothing downstream can detect it.

Note the `1,000` → `(1, 0)` result also depends on Python's octal-literal rules (`000` → `0`),
which have no relationship to the tool-call format being parsed. `ast.literal_eval` is meant here
as a lenient JSON-ish fallback for scalars, not as a Python expression evaluator.

### Suggested fix

Reject tuple results from `literal_eval` so the value falls through to Strategy 4 (treat as
string).

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/function_call/glm4_moe_detector.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/function_call/glm4_moe_detector.py
@@ -132,9 +132,12 @@ def parse_arguments(
     # Strategy 3: ast.literal_eval
     try:
         parsed_value = safe_literal_eval(json_value)
-        return parsed_value, True
+        # A bare comma makes literal_eval build a Python tuple ("1,000" ->
+        # (1, 0)); that is a Python-expression artefact, not the value the
+        # model wrote, so fall through and treat it as a string instead.
+        if not isinstance(parsed_value, tuple):
+            return parsed_value, True
     except (ValueError, SyntaxError):
         pass
```


### Environment


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.18 and 0.5.20 (latest release tested), Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: [Bug] sglang.srt.parser.conversation LLAMA2 style derives role tags from message index parity instead of the message's own role
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


`Conversation.get_prompt()` is the only separator style that ignores the role stored on each
message and instead computes it as `self.roles[i % 2]`. For any chat request that is valid per
the OpenAI schema but not strictly user/assistant-alternating (e.g. two consecutive `user`
messages), the `llama-2`, `mistral` and `devstral` templates silently mislabel turns and, worse,
terminate the prompt with the *user* tag `[INST]` instead of the assistant tag `[/INST]` — so the
model is prompted to write the user's next turn rather than to answer.


### Reproduction


```python
from sglang.srt.entrypoints.openai.protocol import (
    ChatCompletionMessageUserParam,
    ChatCompletionRequest,
)
from sglang.srt.parser.conversation import generate_chat_conv

request = ChatCompletionRequest(
    model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct",
    messages=[
        ChatCompletionMessageUserParam(role="user", content="Here is my code."),
        ChatCompletionMessageUserParam(role="user", content="Please review it."),
    ],
)

conv = generate_chat_conv(request, "llama-2")
print(conv.messages)
print(repr(conv.get_prompt()))

assert conv.messages == [
    ["[INST]", "Here is my code."],
    ["[INST]", "Please review it."],
    ["[/INST]", None],
]
assert conv.get_prompt().endswith("[/INST]"), conv.get_prompt()
```

Output:

```
[['[INST]', 'Here is my code.'], ['[INST]', 'Please review it.'], ['[/INST]', None]]
'[INST] Here is my code. [/INST] Please review it. </s><s>[INST]'
AssertionError: [INST] Here is my code. [/INST] Please review it. </s><s>[INST]
```

### Expected behavior and impact

* `generate_chat_conv` records the correct role on every message — `conv.messages` is
  `[['[INST]', ...], ['[INST]', ...], ['[/INST]', None]]` — and then `get_prompt()` throws that
  information away in favour of `self.roles[i % 2]` (conversation.py:219). The second user turn
  is rendered as `[/INST] Please review it.`, i.e. attributed to the assistant.
* `generate_chat_conv` explicitly appends a blank assistant turn (`# Add a blank message for the
  assistant`, conversation.py:711-712) whose sole purpose is to open the generation slot. Because
  the tag is taken from parity, that slot is emitted as `[INST]`, so the model continues the
  conversation as the *user*. The output is silently wrong with no error raised.
* Consecutive user messages (and requests beginning with an assistant message) are accepted by
  `ChatCompletionRequest`; neither the protocol layer nor
  `OpenAIServingChat._apply_conversation_template` validates alternation, so this reaches users
  of the HTTP API directly.
* Every other separator style in the module (`ADD_COLON_SINGLE`, `CHATML`, `GEMMA3`, `MPT`, …)
  uses the stored per-message role and renders the same request correctly:
  `chatml` → `…<|im_start|>user\nHere is my code.<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user\nPlease review it.<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n`.

### Suggested fix

Use the role recorded on the message. This leaves strictly-alternating conversations
byte-for-byte identical (verified for `[user, assistant, user]`) and fixes the tag for
non-alternating ones:

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/parser/conversation.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/parser/conversation.py
@@ -216,7 +216,7 @@ class Conversation:
                 ret = "[INST] "
             for i, (role, message) in enumerate(self.messages):
-                tag = self.roles[i % 2]
+                tag = role
                 if message:
                     if i == 0:
                         ret += message + " "
```

Note that the separator is likewise chosen by parity (`seps[i % 2]`), so a fully correct
rendering of non-alternating history would also need to pick `sep`/`sep2` from the role
(`seps[0]` for user turns, `seps[1]` to close an assistant turn). The one-line change above
fixes the role mislabeling and the wrong trailing tag, which are the parts that change what the
model is asked to do.


### Environment


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.18 and 0.5.20 (latest release tested), Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: [Bug] get_hf_text_config` erases the text sub-config's `dtype` on the `thinker_config` path
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug


For configs that carry a `thinker_config` (Qwen2.5-Omni / Qwen3-Omni), `get_hf_text_config` unconditionally overwrites `thinker_config.text_config.dtype` with `thinker_config.dtype`. When the thinker has no `dtype` (which is the transformers-v5 default), a valid dtype already present on the text sub-config is replaced with `None`.


### Reproduction


```python
import torch
from transformers import PretrainedConfig

from sglang.srt.utils.hf_transformers.common import get_hf_text_config

config = PretrainedConfig()
config.architectures = ["Qwen2_5OmniForConditionalGeneration"]
config.thinker_config = PretrainedConfig()
config.thinker_config.text_config = PretrainedConfig(
    num_attention_heads=8, dtype=torch.bfloat16
)

print(get_hf_text_config(config).dtype)
```

Prints `None`, not `torch.bfloat16`.

The same happens through a real checkpoint load — a `config.json` that declares the dtype only on `thinker_config.text_config`:

```python
import json, os, tempfile
import transformers
from transformers import AutoConfig
from sglang.srt.utils.hf_transformers.common import get_hf_text_config

d = transformers.Qwen2_5OmniConfig().to_dict()
d["thinker_config"]["text_config"]["dtype"] = "bfloat16"
d.pop("dtype", None)
d["thinker_config"].pop("dtype", None)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
    with open(os.path.join(td, "config.json"), "w") as f:
        json.dump(d, f)
    cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(td)

print(cfg.thinker_config.text_config.dtype)   # torch.bfloat16
print(get_hf_text_config(cfg).dtype)          # None
```

### Expected behavior and impact

Only ~20 lines above, the same function goes out of its way to *preserve* an existing sub-config dtype, propagating the parent's value only when the sub-config's is missing:

```python
if getattr(_sub, "dtype", None) is None:
    _sub.dtype = parent_dtype
```

and the comment there spells out the consequence of losing it: "Without this, `_get_and_verify_dtype` falls back to float32 and then `auto` downcasts to float16, which overflows the Pixtral vision tower on real images and produces NaN features."

The `thinker_config` branch then does the opposite with a plain `setattr`, destroying the very attribute the earlier loop was written to protect. The returned object *is* `thinker_config.text_config`, so the damage is also persisted on the caller's config object, not just the return value.

### Suggested fix

Apply the same guard the surrounding code already uses — fill in only when the target dtype is missing.

```diff
--- a/python/sglang/srt/utils/hf_transformers/common.py
+++ b/python/sglang/srt/utils/hf_transformers/common.py
@@ -436,13 +436,10 @@ def get_hf_text_config(config: PretrainedConfig):
     if hasattr(config, "thinker_config"):
         # qwen2.5 omni
         thinker_config = config.thinker_config
         if hasattr(thinker_config, "text_config"):
-            setattr(
-                thinker_config.text_config,
-                "dtype",
-                getattr(thinker_config, "dtype", None),
-            )
+            if getattr(thinker_config.text_config, "dtype", None) is None:
+                thinker_config.text_config.dtype = getattr(
+                    thinker_config, "dtype", None
+                )
             text_config = thinker_config.text_config
         else:
             text_config = thinker_config
```


### Environment


### Environment

SGLang 0.5.18 and 0.5.20 (latest release tested), Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64.

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

comments.author: Arthur031221
comments.body:
Some of this is in the tutorials, though spread out: [01 vector add](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/01-vector-add.html) explains the `meta` grid, and [08 grouped GEMM](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/08-grouped-gemm.html) and [09 persistent matmul](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/09-persistent-matmul.html) between them use both kinds of tensor descriptor (08 builds them in the kernel, 09 uses both). I checked each answer below with triton 3.8.0 and torch 2.14 on an RTX 5090 (compute capability 12.0). The script and its output are at the bottom.

**What can be passed to a kernel?** torch tensors, ints, floats, bools, `None`, tuples (I tried `(2, 3.0)`), and `TensorDescriptor` objects. A `str`, `list`, `dict` or `torch.float32` passed as a normal argument fails with `TypeError: failed to specialize argument of type: ...`. A `tl.constexpr` parameter is more permissive: it took `tl.float32` and the string `"double"`.

**What is `meta`?** A dict of the launch arguments keyed by parameter name, constexprs included. For `add[grid](x, y, o, x.numel(), BLOCK=256)` its keys were `BLOCK, n, out, x, y`. That lets the grid depend on a constexpr such as the block size: `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(meta["n"], meta["BLOCK"]),)`.

**How do I get one element?** Inside the kernel, a tensor argument is a pointer, and `tl.load` gives you a block. Blocks have no element indexing at all: `av[i]` with a runtime `i` fails with a confusing message (`Did you forget to add @triton.jit ?`), and `av[I]` with a constexpr `I` fails with `unsupported tensor index: constexpr[5]`. Load the element from the pointer instead:

```python
s = tl.load(a + i)
tl.store(out + offs, s * tl.load(b + offs))
```

If the values are already in a block, `tl.sum(tl.where(offs == i, av, 0.0), axis=0)` pulls out one element. Both give `a[i] * b` in the script.

**`tensor_descriptor` vs `TensorDescriptor`?** Both describe an array by base pointer, shape, strides and a block shape, and both are used through `desc.load([row, col])` and `desc.store([row, col], value)`. The difference is where they are made. `triton.tools.tensor_descriptor.TensorDescriptor` is built on the host, e.g. `TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(x, [BM, BN])`, and passed in as a kernel argument; inside the kernel it has the type `tl.tensor_descriptor`. `tl.make_tensor_descriptor(ptr, shape=..., strides=..., block_shape=...)` builds one inside the kernel, which is what you want when the pointer or shape is only known inside the kernel, as in the grouped GEMM tutorial. On my card the in-kernel version needed `triton.set_allocator(...)` first; without it the launch failed with `Kernel requires a runtime memory allocation, but no allocator was set`. On GPUs older than Hopper (compute capability below 9) the NVIDIA backend rewrites descriptor loads and stores into ordinary pointer loads (`make_ttir` in `backends/nvidia/compiler.py`).

**`tl.constexpr`?** The value is baked into the compiled kernel, and yes, each new value compiles a new variant: `K = 1, 2, 2, 3` gave 3 variants. Some things require a constexpr: `tl.arange(0, B)` with a plain int `B` fails with `arange's arguments must be of type tl.constexpr`, and `tl.static_range` bounds have the same requirement. Plain int arguments are specialized too, on whether the value is 1 and whether it is divisible by 16: in the script 7, 9 and 13 shared one variant, 16 added a second (32 and 48 reused it), and 1 added a third. `@triton.jit(do_not_specialize=[...])` turns that off for the arguments you list.

**`tl.const`?** In 3.8.0 it is a compile-time check. Storing through a `tl.const` pointer fails with `Cannot store to a constant pointer`, and on this NVIDIA card a small kernel compiled with and without `tl.const` on its input gave the same PTX once the kernel name and debug lines were removed. On main it does more on AMD: #11294 (merged 2026-08-21) puts `tl.const` pointer arguments in the AMDGPU constant

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: [RFC]: Agent-Aware KV Cache Affinity Scheduling and Lifecycle Management
items.author: daisyEliot
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix has established a production-grade distributed KV cache architecture with L1 DRAM offloading, L2 shared cache clusters, prefix-aware routing, and P&D (Prefill/Decode) disaggregation, delivering significant efficiency gains for general inference workloads. As agent-based traffic becomes dominant in production clusters, the current cache stack lacks semantic awareness of agent task properties, leading to suboptimal cache reuse, avoidable eviction of high-value prefixes, and misalignment between cache lifetime and agent execution cycles.

This RFC proposes extending the AIBrix stack with agent-native cache management capabilities built on top of standard `agent_hints` fields. The changes span the API gateway routing layer, KV cache runtime, event synchronization protocol, and P&D scheduler — all while preserving full backward compatibility with existing engines, cache backends, and routing policies. The proposal introduces program-level cache affinity, context-weighted eviction, session-aligned cache pinning, and intent-driven speculative prefill, optimized specifically for AIBrix's layered cache and disaggregated architecture.

### Motivation

Agent workloads now account for 40%–60% of production inference traffic in AIBrix deployments, and exhibit fundamentally different cache behavior compared to one-shot requests. The current AIBrix cache stack was designed for generic prompt-based traffic and faces four structural gaps when handling agent workloads:

### 1. Prefix routing lacks program-level semantic affinity

AIBrix's existing `prefix-cache` routing plugin matches requests purely by recursive token block hashes, with no awareness of agent program identity. Requests from different sessions of the same agent program — which share identical system prompts, tool definitions, and role instructions that can span thousands of tokens — are treated as unrelated prefixes. This results in:

- Redundant prefills of the same program prefix across multiple Serving Units
- Wasted L2 cache capacity from duplicate copies of identical program-level prefix blocks
- No ability to intentionally colocate same-program workloads for maximum cache sharing

In multi-tenant agent clusters, this limits global prefix cache reuse rate to roughly 30%, even when most workloads share common agent program templates.

### 2. Cache eviction is blind to context value and task priority

AIBrix's current scan-resistant eviction policy ranks KV blocks only by access frequency and recency, uniformly across all block types. In agent scenarios, cache value varies by orders of magnitude:

- `system_prompt` and `tool_def` blocks are reused across the entire session and have the highest durable value
- `conversation` history blocks accumulate incrementally and have moderate value
- `reasoning` intermediate blocks are single-use and have near-zero reuse value

Without semantic differentiation, high-value permanent prefixes are frequently evicted to make room for low-value temporary reasoning state. Additionally, there is no priority differentiation between production-critical agent tasks and background batch workloads, so low-priority traffic can evict high-priority session cache and cause SLA violations.

### 3. Cache lifetime is decoupled from agent task execution cycles

Agent workloads alternate between inference generation and external tool/API calls, with idle windows ranging from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds. Under AIBrix's default LRU-based eviction, session cache becomes eligible for eviction during tool call idle periods. When the agent resumes execution:

- The full context must be re-prefilled, increasing end-to-end latency by 2–5x
- GPU cycles are wasted recomputing previously computed cache
- In P&D disaggregation mode, the session must be re-mapped to a Prefill GPU, adding scheduling overhead

The existing `session-affinity` routing only maintains pod stickiness but does not protect cache from eviction during idle periods.

### 4. KV event protocol carries no agent semantic metadata

The AIBrix KVCache v1 Connector and event synchronization protocol only transmits block-level physical attributes (block hashes, token IDs, size, medium) to the L2 cache cluster and gateway. Without agent semantic fields in events:

- The L2 cache cannot implement tiered storage policies based on priority or context type
- The gateway cannot make routing decisions informed by agent program identity
- Observability stacks cannot break down cache metrics by agent program or priority tier

### 5. No proactive prefill orchestration for multi-turn agent conversations

AIBrix's P&D disaggregation architecture separates compute-heavy prefills from decode-heavy generation, but prefill operations are still triggered only by incoming requests. For multi-turn agent dialogues, the next turn's prefix (conversation history + latest assistant reply) is highly predictable. Without an intent-driven prefill mechanism, every agent turn incurs full cold-start prefill latency, leaving first-token latency suboptimal for interactive agent use cases.

### Proposed Change

All proposed changes are additive and backward-compatible. Existing workloads without `agent_hints` continue to behave exactly as today. The proposal is structured around five targeted extensions to the AIBrix stack:

### 1. Standardized `agent_hints` Field and End-to-End Propagation

Define a standard set of agent semantic fields propagated from the API gateway through to the KV cache runtime and event protocol:

- `program_id`: string identifier for the agent program, used for affinity scheduling
- `priority`: integer task priority level, used for tiered eviction and storage
- `context_type`: enumerated value (`system_prompt`, `tool_def`, `conversation`, `reasoning`)
- `speculative_prefill`: boolean flag enabling proactive next-turn prefill
- `session_ttl_hint`: suggested cache lifetime for the session

comments.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed RFC. A few questions, mostly on the routing / P&D parts:

1. **Program affinity vs. existing prefix routing.** The gateway already builds the prefix-match text as system prompt + canonicalized `tools` JSON + messages (`combinePrefixText` / `canonicalToolsText`, `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_INCLUDE_TOOLS` defaults to on), and hashes it as chained content blocks from the start. So requests from different sessions that share an identical system prompt and tool definitions already produce the same leading block hashes and are routed toward the same pods. Is the gap that prompts/templates differ across sessions of the same program, or the affinity-vs-load trade-off? Some data on this would help scope Part 2.
2. **Overlap with #2742.** `x-aibrix-session-key` (set by the caller from the first request, Redis-backed across gateway replicas) already covers part of Parts 2 and 4. Would `program_id` / session pinning build on that key rather than add a parallel mechanism?
3. **KV event fields.** `BlockStored` / `BlockRemoved` are emitted by the engine (AIBrix decodes vLLM's msgpack format), so the new fields would need engine-side changes. How would `context_type` / `priority` be defined for a block that spans a boundary (e.g. end of system prompt, start of conversation), or for a prefix block shared by requests with different hints?
4. **Speculative prefill.** In P&D, the decode pod already holds the KV for history + reply when decode finishes. Would offloading that KV to L2 be cheaper than recomputing it on a prefill GPU? Also, the 5s default TTL seems short given the tool-call idle windows (up to tens of seconds) in the motivation.

Given the scope, splitting this into phases (e.g. gateway-side affinity first, evaluated with the agent session workload generator from #2483) might make it easier to review.

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

### Proposed Change.

items.title: [Usage]: Recommended way to serve multiple models (e.g. embedding) on a single GPU
items.author: mfournioux
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

**Description:**

### Context
We run vLLM to serve a small embedding model on a dedicated GPU. The model uses only a fraction of the GPU's memory and compute. We would like to co-locate several models on the same GPU to improve utilization.

### What we found
- A single vLLM process serves a single model.
- The docs say `gpu_memory_utilization` is a per-instance limit, so several instances can share a GPU (e.g. 0.5 each).
- Community answers say this works in online (server) mode, but not in offline mode with several `LLM` objects in one process (#6155).

### What we could not find
There is no official guidance on the recommended way to do this in production, in particular:
1. Is running several vLLM server instances on one GPU with split `--gpu-memory-utilization` values the officially recommended approach? Are there known limitations (e.g. memory profiling when instances start at the same time, CUDA graph memory, interference between workloads)?
2. Is there any plan for native multi-model serving in a single vLLM process or a built-in model router, or is this out of scope?
3. For small embedding models, are there recommended settings (e.g. `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, `--max-num-seqs`) to keep their footprint minimal?

### Request
Could you point us to the recommended approach ?

### How would you like to use vllm




### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: Feature Request: MoE expert cache with GPU-resident LRU - cache decisions and copies run on the GPU inside the compute graph
items.author: lich-77
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

1. Cache MoE experts on the GPU with an LRU, so that MoE models can run on GPUs with limited VRAM.
2. Everything runs on the GPU - there is no host/GPU switching: no per-step readback of expert ids, no 3. synchronization.
3. Works with MTP speculative decoding, on both HIP and CUDA, including dual-GPU setups.

A working implementation is complete: measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload. Code: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57)

### Motivation

GPU-side caching of host-offloaded MoE experts is well proven by now, but none has progressed toward merge
-  #20757 was closed as completed, it confirmed strong temporal locality
-  the RFC in #28248 has received no maintainer response
-  #27861 has seen no author updates for weeks 
- the earlier PRs (#21609, #21614, #21620, #24524) were closed
-  #29887, opened yesterday, implements this differently. In same-machine, same-prompt tests, my implementation measured about 1.5x faster (details in the results section).

### Possible Implementation

A working implementation is complete: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57) (branch `lru-upstream-v3`, rebased on current master). Measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload.

Each layer whose expert weights are on the host gets a fixed-size pool of N slots (`--moe-lru-slots N`). Two new graph ops do all the work inside the compute graph:

- `LRU_DECIDE` - a single-thread deterministic kernel (CUDA-graph replay safe) that reads the router's expert ids, updates the LRU state, and returns one flat output: remapped slot ids plus a fill list
- `LRU_FILL` - copies the experts named in the fill list from host memory into their pool slots, and returns a view of the pool that the existing `mul_mat_id` reads directly

The expert weights live in pinned host memory, so the fill kernel reads them directly over PCIe.

No scheduler, fusion, or CPU changes.

Correctness was verified before performance:

- Perplexity is unchanged from the no-pool baseline across slot counts: 1.4290 (no pool) vs 1.4292 (s64 through s192) on the test model
- Greedy decoding is deterministic: 12/12 runs of the same command produce identical output - single text hash, single cache counter set, single hit rate
- Generated text was inspected for every benchmark configuration (English, Chinese, and code-generation prompts)

### Local results (7900 XTX, 24GB, single GPU)

*UD-IQ3_XXS, all 48 layers pooled (`-ncmoe 48`), greedy, natural end-of-sequence, English prompt:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| no pool, plain | 9.7 | - |
| no pool + MTP-Q8 | 11.3 | - |
| 160 slots, plain | 37.2 | 89.4% |
| 160 slots + MTP-Q8 | 44.8 | 90.1% |

*UD-IQ4_XS, reverse placement (8 layers with native GPU experts + 40 pooled): pinning all 48
layers would need ~57 GB of locked host memory, above the Windows pinned-memory limit on this
64 GB machine (RAM - 16 GB); 40 layers (~47 GB) fits.*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| 72 slots, plain (6.4 GiB pool) | 31.2 | 77.9% |
| 40 slots, plain (3.6 GiB pool) | 28.8 | 66.9% |
| 40 slots + MTP-Q4 | 30.5 | 73.3% |

### Remote results (2x RTX 3090, 48GB total)

*UD-IQ4_XS, 48 layers pooled, 320 slots (34.7 GiB pool), MTP-Q8 draft:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| EN, plain | 47.6 | 93.6% |
| EN + MTP-Q8 | 59.6 | 96.0% |

Note: MTP gains depend on the workload - about +20% on English prose, but +37-40% on
code-generation prompts (the IQ3 row above reaches 50.0 t/s and the 40-slot IQ4 row 38.5 t/s).

For reference, I also measured #29887 (applied on the same base commit) on the same machine,
same prompt, and equal cache budget (~6.5 GiB, reverse placement):

| implementation | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| #29887 | 20.1 | 75.0% |
| this implementation | 31.2 | 77.9% |

Would this direction be welcome? I can open a PR right away if there is interest.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (7900 XTX, single GPU)</summary>

Model: [unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (UD-IQ3_XXS),
draft: [ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (mtp-Q8_0).

```bash
llama-cli -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -ngl 99 -ncmoe 48 -c 4096 --moe-lru-slots 160 \
  --load-mode none --poll 0 -st --temp 0 -n 2048 \
  -p "The history of artificial intelligence began in antiquity"
```

items.title: Eval bug: Nondeterministic FA prefill with Qwen 3.5 9B on RDNA3 (ROCm/HIP) on multimodal requests since b10905
items.author: Googulator
items.body_excerpt: ### Name and Version $ ./llama-cli --version version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10905, commit 16378d93f) built with GNU 15.2.0 for Linux x86_64 ### Operating systems Linux ### GGML backends HIP ### Hardware - AMD Ryzen 5 4500 + AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT (issue present) - AMD Ryzen 5 4500 + AMD Radeon RX 7800 XT (issue present) - AMD Ryzen 5 4500 + AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT (issue NOT present) ### Models Qwen 3.5 9B Q8_0 (quantized locally from the official HuggingFace release) ### Problem description & steps to reproduce We are using llama-server to process scanned documents (passed as images) via Qwen 3.5's multimodal capabilities on RDNA3 and RDNA4 hardware, using the ROCm/HIP backend. Recently, we upgraded llama.cpp from v0.3.0 to v0.5.0. Subsequently, we noticed nondeterministic output from requests that would previously show perfectly reproducible behavior. The nondeterminism persisted even after setting a fixed seed and zero temperature. Further investigation showed that the issue first appeared in build b10905, and would affect RDNA3, but not RDNA4. On RDNA3, the issue could be reproduced with ROCm versions as old as 6.3.3, and as new as 10.0.0. On ROCm 10.0.0, restarting the llama-server process caused it to generate the same sequence of outputs when repeatedly called after each restart; with ROCm 6.3, we were never able to get the same output twice, even after restarting llama-server or rebooting the machine. Using Qwen 3.8 (running on unaffected llama.cpp 0.3.0), we found the following simple reproducer: [repro-minimal.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33217907/repro-minimal.json) The embedded image is shown below: Repeatedly sending this request to llama-server running Qwen 3.5 9B @ Q8_0 quantization gave a different response to each request on all builds tested, starting with b10905. On earlier builds, the output is unchanged between requests; likewise, on an RDNA4 box, we also received reproducible (although different) output, even with builds after b10905. Qwen 3.8 also identified the following possible fixes: - Disabling 256-wide kernels on RDNA3 (losing the performance advantage from the FA tuning commit): ```patch diff --git a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh index 7d14ce906..259f1df3c 100644 --- a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh +++ b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh @@ -351,6 +351,14 @@ static bool amd_wmma_available(const int cc) { return (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA4(cc) || GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA3(cc)); } +// The flash attention kernel configs and grid heuristics that go beyond the head sizes supported by RDNA3 +// (wide tiles with DKQ > 128, the whole-tile grids instead of stream-k, the GQA column switching) were tuned +// on RDNA4. RDNA3 has the same WMMA instructions but a very different memory subsystem, and it is moreover not +// bit-reproducible with the DKQ > 128 WMMA kernel instances, so those changes are limited to RDNA4. +static bool amd_wmma_fattn_tuned(const int cc) { + return GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_RDNA4(cc); +} + static bool volta_mma_available(const int cc) { return GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc) && ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc) == GGML_CUDA_CC_VOLTA; } diff --git a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn.cu b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn.cu index ceb472793..3e361e4e0 100644 --- a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn.cu +++ b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn.cu @@ -665,7 +665,9 @@ static best_fattn_kernel ggml_cuda_get_best_fattn_kernel(const int device, const } // AMD WMMA is faster than the tile kernel if the wide tiles with high arithmetic intensity can be utilized. - if ((amd_wmma_available(cc) && gqa_opt_applies && Q->ne[0] <= 256) && Q->ne[0] != 40 && Q->ne[0] != 72 && + // The DKQ > 128 configs are only used on RDNA4, see amd_wmma_fattn_tuned(). + const int max_dkq_amd_wmma = amd_wmma_fattn_tuned(cc) ? 256 : 128; + if ((amd_wmma_available(cc) && gqa_opt_applies && Q->ne[0] <= max_dkq_amd_wmma) && Q->ne[0] != 40 && Q->ne[0] != 72 && Q->ne[1] * gqa_ratio_eff > (Q->ne[0] <= 128 ? 8 : 16)) { return BEST_FATTN_KERNEL_MMA_F16; } ``` - Zero-initializing fully masked KV cache rows (much smaller performance hit, but not a fully generic fix): ```patch diff --git a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh index 48b631e60..d35c60f3e 100644 --- a/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh +++ b/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/fattn-common.cuh @@ -718,6 +718,71 @@ static __global__ void flash_attn_mask_to_KV_max( KV_max[sequence*ne31 + jt] = KV_max_sj; } +// The sparse / compact-mask path, which does not load KV columns that the mask closes, is NVIDIA +// only (ggml_cuda_flash_attn_ext_mma_f16_shall_use_sparse), and even there only for DKQ == 512 +// and 576. Everywhere else - and in particular on the DKQ == 256 WMMA tiles that AMD uses for +// large head sizes - the dense kernel loads every KV column of the view and relies on the mask to +// cancel the ones past the end of the sequence. Those columns are KV cells that the current +// request never wrote, and the result of the dense DKQ == 256 kernel has been measured to depend +// on their exact bytes even though the mask is -inf there: with temperature=0 and a fixed seed the +// answer changed between identical requests in the same process, and only stopped changing once +// the memory around the cache was reproducible. +// +// Zeroing the rows whose mask column is -inf for every query row makes the input of the kernel a +// function of the sequence again. It does not avoid the loads the way the sparse index list would, +// but it does remove the dependence on memory the request never wrote, for ~1 % of prefill time +// (measured on gfx1100 / RDNA3, DKQ = DV = 256, GQA 4:1, a 46640 token request). +// +// SAFETY: a column that is masked in this graph can still hold the KV of *another* sequence when +// the ba

items.title: [Bug] HiCache: prefill forward stalls behind the entire host-to-device load burst because round-head H2D copies are issued after the burst hand-over
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--enable-hierarchical-cache`, a prefill forward whose requests hit the host cache can stall for the whole duration of the HiCache load burst, even though the per-layer load waits (`layer_done_counter`) are correct and the layer-by-layer overlap works in the other rounds.

**Mechanism.** In `Scheduler.get_new_batch_prefill` the load burst is handed over *before* the batch is prepared:

```python
if self.enable_hierarchical_cache or self.enable_unified_cache_external_linker:
    new_batch.hicache_consumer_index = self.tree_cache.ready_to_load_host_cache()

new_batch.prepare_for_extend()
```

`HiCacheController.start_loading` records `producer_event.start_event` on the schedule stream and the load stream waits on it, then submits the whole burst (one H2D copy per layer per pool, hundreds of copies for a multi-GiB burst). Every H2D copy the scheduler issues *after* that record is queued behind the burst on the copy engine:

- `prepare_for_extend`: `seq_lens`, `orig_seq_lens` (pinned H2D),
- `resolve_forward_inputs` at forward entry: the deferred `input_ids` upload (#25945),
- `ForwardBatch.init_new`: `extend_seq_lens`, `extend_prefix_lens`, and with DP attention `global_num_tokens` / `global_num_tokens_for_logprob`.

The forward's first kernels depend on those tensors, so the whole forward on the compute stream waits until the copy engine has drained the entire burst, not just layer 0's load. Under TP the stalled rank then delays all its peers through the first all-reduce.

**Observed.** On an 8 x H100 TP=8 deployment with hierarchical cache and multi-GiB load bursts, an nsys trace of ~80 prefill rounds showed:

| | before |
| --- | --- |
| rounds whose first attention kernel starts only after the last burst copy | 27 / 80 |
| launch-to-execution gap of the round's first small H2D copy, max | 373.8 ms |
| direct stall per gated round per rank | ~42-49 ms |

In the remaining rounds the first small copies were served before the burst and the forward overlapped the loads layer by layer as designed, i.e. the outcome depends on copy-engine arbitration, not on the stream contract.

**Expected.** The round-head H2D copies should be ordered ahead of the burst by construction: issue them on the schedule stream *before* `start_loading` records its `start_event`. That requires handing the burst over after the batch is final (after `mix_with_running` and the DP mlp-sync gather), i.e. in `run_batch` instead of at batch formation, and uploading the extend / mlp-sync metadata there so `init_new` does not issue them on the forward stream.

### Reproduction

Timing-dependent; needs a GPU with hierarchical cache and enough host-cache hits to produce a large burst.

1. Start a server with `--enable-hierarchical-cache` (large `--hicache-ratio` so many-GiB prefixes live on host), optionally `--enable-dp-attention` to also exercise the `global_num_tokens` uploads.
2. Warm up with long shared-prefix prompts, evict them from device (e.g. by running unrelated traffic until they are written back to host), then send them again so each prefill round pulls several GiB from host.
3. Profile with `nsys` / torch profiler and, for each prefill round, compare the timestamp of the last HiCache `Memcpy HtoD` on the load stream with (a) the first small HtoD on the forward stream (`input_ids`, `extend_seq_lens`) and (b) the first attention kernel. In the affected rounds (a) and (b) both land within a few ms after the last burst copy, while in the others (a) precedes the burst.

A CPU unit test that pins the required ordering (`pre_upload_forward_inputs` runs before `ready_to_load_host_cache`, `init_new` consumes the staged tensors exactly once) is included in the fix PR.

### Environment

Observation: NVIDIA H100 x 8, TP=8, hierarchical cache enabled, CUDA graphs on, overlap scheduling on.

The code paths quoted above are from `main` @ 2358916d5a; the observation was made on an earlier snapshot with the same hand-over order in `get_new_batch_prefill`.

`python3 -m sglang.check_env` fails on the CPU-only host used to prepare the fix (`NameError: name 'env' is not defined`), so the versions were collected manually:

```
sglang: main @ 2358916d5a (editable install from source)
python: 3.12.13
torch: 2.13.0+cpu (CPU host used for the unit tests)
OS: Ubuntu 24.04
```

items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

`HiCacheController.start_loading` submits the whole host->device load-back burst inline on the scheduler thread: `L2TransferEngine.submit_host_to_device` loops over every layer and calls `load_to_device_per_layer`, recording one event per layer so the forward can wait layer by layer.

The per-layer submission is pure CPU work on the scheduler thread. With `--hicache-io-backend direct` and the `page_first_direct` layout each layer builds a batched-copy descriptor (`cudaMemcpyBatchAsync`) before anything is issued to the GPU. On a deep model with two host pools per layer that is on the order of a few milliseconds per layer, i.e. several hundred milliseconds per burst during which the scheduler thread does nothing else.

The consequence is that the layer-wise pipeline (`LayerDoneCounter` / `wait_until` in the attention layers) almost never overlaps anything: by the time `start_loading` returns and the batch is built and launched, every copy has already landed. Profiling a prefill-only H100 TP=8 deployment with hierarchical cache and `io_backend=direct` showed:

| | value |
|---|---|
| per-layer `load_to_device_per_layer` submission (CPU) | ~2.4 ms |
| `start_loading` per burst (78 layers x 2 pools) | ~375 ms |
| share of the H2D copy time that overlapped compute | 0.04 % |

So the scheduler thread stalls for the full enqueue duration, and the forward that should have hidden the H2D copies only starts once they are essentially complete.

**Proposal**: keep the producer-slot hand-out (`update_producer`, `start_event.record()`) on the scheduler thread, since the batch is created with that slot as `hicache_consumer_index`, and hand the rest of the burst (index move + per-layer enqueue + ack) to a single FIFO daemon thread. Gated behind a new env var `SGLANG_HICACHE_ASYNC_LOAD_ENQUEUE` (default off, existing path unchanged).

What has to change for that to be correct:

- Waiting on a device event that has not been recorded yet is a no-op, so a consumer could sail past a layer the loader thread has not submitted. Each `LayerLoadingEvent` gets a CPU-side per-layer "recorded" flag that `wait()` blocks on before touching the device event.
- `update_producer` reuses a slot after checking `finish_event.query()`. While a burst is still queued, that slot's `finish_event` is the *previous* rotation's (long since done), so the check would pass and hand the slot out twice. A per-slot "enqueue done" flag provides backpressure on the rotation.
- `op.device_indices` values are produced by the allocator on the compute stream. Inline, the D2H copy in `move_indices` is implicitly ordered behind them; on the loader thread it is not, so the index move has to run under the H2D stream after waiting `start_event`.
- The overlap-scheduling fence (`load_fence_stream`) must capture the forward stream at hand-over time, so the scheduler records a fence event and the loader waits on it.
- A failure on the loader thread must release every layer event and still publish an ack, or a forward already parked on `wait_until` and every later burst in `ack_load_queue` (popped in order by `loading_check`) would hang.
- `is_load_back_event_done` (disaggregation decode restore) must not trust a slot's `finish_event` while the burst is still queued.

A/B on the same deployment (500 requests, same prompt set, gate off vs on):

| metric | change |
|---|---|
| throughput | +8.8 % |
| wall time | -8.1 % |
| TTFT mean | -7.9 % |
| TTFT p50 | -10.0 % |
| TTFT p95 | 22.12 s -> 20.41 s |
| TTFT p99 | flat |

I have a PR ready that implements the above with a CPU unit test covering the inline path (call sequence unchanged), the async hand-over, the slot backpressure, the index-move ordering, the fence capture, the loader failure path and shutdown. Happy to adjust the design if maintainers prefer a different shape (for example moving the split into `L2TransferEngine`).

### Related resources

- `python/sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py` (`start_loading`, `LayerDoneCounter`, `LayerLoadingEvent`)
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/l2_transfer.py` (`L2TransferEngine.submit_host_to_device`)
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py` (`layer_transfer_counter.wait_until` in the attention layers)
- Related: #38448 (load burst ordering in overlap mode)

items.title: [Bug]: FP8 KV cache startup can OOM because CUDA graph memory is omitted from the cache budget
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.28.0 on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug On a 24 GiB GPU, `LLM(..., kv_cache_dtype="fp8")` is accepted but fails during startup with an out-of-memory error, while the identical engine using the default KV cache dtype answers successfully. ```python from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams llm = LLM( model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", kv_cache_dtype="fp8", ) print(llm.generate( ["Hello, my name is"], SamplingParams(max_tokens=8), )) ``` Observed failure: ```text torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 150.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 23.49 GiB of which 122.00 MiB is free. ... RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. ``` The startup accounting allocates about 19.93 GiB to the KV cache after subtracting a near-zero CUDA graph estimate. CUDA graph capture happens afterwards and consumes about 0.80 GiB in the FP8 case, pushing actual usage beyond the memory reserved by `gpu_memory_utilization`. Reducing `gpu_memory_utilization` avoids the failure. ### Expected behavior KV cache sizing should reserve the actual CUDA graph memory so an accepted configuration does not exceed its memory budget during graph capture or the first sampling allocation. If vLLM cannot fit the configuration, it should fail early with an actionable error. ### Suggested fix Make `profile_cudagraph_memory()` account for the actual graph capture cost, including its dependence on the number of KV blocks, or adjust the KV cache after graph capture when measured use exceeds the requested budget. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

comments.author: Aravind0403
comments.body:
Hi @the-Shallow  @michaelmanly ,

I investigated the root cause and submitted a fix in **#60673**.

### Root Cause
During memory profiling, `_extrapolate_full_graph_memory()` previously applied a uniform 1 MiB floor (`_MIN_PER_GRAPH_BYTES = 1 << 20`) per `FULL` CUDA graph. For quantized KV caches (`fp8`, `int8`), the halved element sizes double the number of blocks, while CUDA graph capture allocates auxiliary scale factor tensors and block table graph bindings (~16–30 MiB per graph). Across ~30 full graphs, this underestimated capture overhead by ~0.8 GiB, leading to startup OOMs on 24 GiB GPUs during `capture_model()`.

### Fix
PR #60673 introduces a 16 MiB floor (`_MIN_QUANTIZED_PER_GRAPH_BYTES = 16 << 20`) when `is_quantized_kv_cache(kv_cache_dtype)` is true, reserving the necessary headroom during initial cache sizing without impacting non-quantized cache budgets.

comments.author: michaelmanly
comments.body: Nice, looks like the upstream fix is moving. Curious from the user side: while something like this is still broken upstream, would a verified alternate execution route be useful enough for you to keep working, or is waiting for the upstream patch usually fine?

comments.author: Aravind0403
comments.body:
@michaelmanly  

In the interim, while the upstream patch is being finalized in #60673, there is an immediate zero-code workaround you can use to unblock your workload:

1. **Lower `gpu_memory_utilization`**: Setting `gpu_memory_utilization=0.85` (or `0.88` depending on your card) gives the allocator an extra ~1–1.5 GiB buffer, absorbing the unbudgeted CUDA graph capture memory and preventing the startup OOM.
2. **Alternative flag**: Setting `VLLM_MEMORY_PROFILER_ESTIMATE_CUDAGRAPHS=0` disables the cudagraph memory estimation and lets you manually tune the headroom.

The permanent fix (measuring all full graphs during profiling to budget exact memory automatically) is actively being reviewed in #60673!

items.title: [Feature][MP] Commit windowed KV to L2 on turn boundaries
items.author: okdshin
items.body_excerpt:
# Problem
Hybrid models (Gemma 3, gpt-oss, Command-A, Qwen3-Next, ...) have object groups that only need the last `w` chunks for a prefix hit (SWA, Mamba). Older windowed chunks are never read back, and they are the big ones. `default` writes them all to L2. But skipping them isn't enough: once L1 evicts the window, the next turn pays a full prefill. We should commit only the last w chunks, at the turn boundary.

# Proposal
Two pieces that work together: stop writing windowed KV to L2, and copy the live window to L2 at natural timing (turn boundaries) so cross-turn prefix reuse isn't lost.

## 1. defer_windowed store policy
A new store policy that writes full-attention object groups through to L2 (same as default) but keeps windowed groups L1-only, eliminating the dead-weight writes. This policy requires `--separate-object-groups`.

## 2. window commit on turn boundaries
When a chat turn ends (vLLM sends END_SESSION), copy the live windowed layer’s window from L1 to L2. This is a copy, not a move: the L1 window stays for immediate reuse.

## Key design points:

- `CommitPolicy` decides per-request whether to commit, based on how the request ended. The built-in `turn_end` policy commits when the generation ended on a turn-end token (configurable via `--turn-boundary-token–ids`) at generation_end, and for any finish reason other than abort / error at prompt_end, where the prompt is re-sent regardless.
- `--window-commit-anchor (generation_end | prompt_end)` controls where the window ends. Normally the next prompt re-sends the previous assistant turn verbatim, so `generation_end` (default) — right when generation stops — is the correct anchor. `prompt_end` covers cases where the client re-renders the assistant turn differently before resending it (e.g. Qwen3 drops `<think>` blocks).  It anchors the window at the end of the looked-up prompt.
- `StoreController.submit_copy` copies keys to L2 without consulting the store policy and without evicting them from L1.
Extensible: custom policies register with `register_commit_policy_factory`.

I will send the draft implementation PR later. I work for this issue with @nilpe and @Alnusjaponica .
