items.title: [Roadmap]Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon
items.author: liusy58
items.body_excerpt:
# [Roadmap] Fast Engine Recovery: Weight Cache Daemon 
@liusy58 @QiuMike @alexnails 
Phase 1 landed in #27139 — a per-rank daemon holds post-quantized weights and serves them over CUDA IPC; weight load drops from ~306–327s to <1s on Qwen3-235B FP8 ([blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-08-21-sglang-fast-recovery)). This issue tracks the next steps. Contributions and feedback are welcome.

Related: #27052 (Fast Recovery framework), #27310 (GPU Memory Service / VMM)

Goals: <10s cold restart and <1s warm standby switch; broaden model & quant coverage; make the cache outlive the daemon; make resident weights usable beyond the one GPU they sit on.

Where Phase 1 stands: TP + PP, single-node and multi-node launch (each node spawns its share of ranks and joins one dist group), zero-copy IPC per GPU, unquantized + block-wise FP8. Not yet: cross-node daemon coordination / failover, DP & EP shard keying, spec-decoding draft models, weight update / sleep-wake, cache surviving daemon death.

## Model & quantization coverage

- [ ] parity harness — disk-load vs daemon-load `state_dict` diff (names / shape / dtype / stride / byte hash) + short GSM8K gate; required evidence for every new allowlist entry
- [ ] carry post-processing metadata in the manifest (final shape/stride, layout tag, whitelisted module attrs) instead of reproducing `process_weights_after_loading` on a meta-init model — this is what blocks most quant methods today
- [ ] quant methods: per-tensor fp8 / w8a8 int8 / mxfp8 / nvfp4 / compressed-tensors / awq / gptq-marlin #32398 
- [ ] archs: MoE (DeepSeek V3/V4, Ling, Kimi K3) / hybrid linear attention / multimodal (vision tower + projector) / LoRA base weights https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33684
- [ ] MTP & EAGLE draft models (per-rank draft daemon), removing the `--speculative-algorithm` rejection in `server_args.py` #32744
- [ ] generic post-map rebuild hook to replace the hardcoded `_rebuild_stale_views`; make tied storages, param→buffer flips and non-persistent buffers explicit in the manifest
- [ ] publish the support matrix in docs; unsupported combinations keep hard-erroring (no silent wrong numerics)

## Transport: CUDA VMM shareable handles (#27310 §4.2)



- [ ] `vmm_fd` backend (skeleton already in `weight_cache/transport.py`): `cuMemCreate` + FD handles over `SCM_RIGHTS`, VA reservation on import, `torch_ipc` stays the fallback, `--weight-cache-transport {auto,torch_ipc,vmm_fd}` #33279
- [ ] `mooncake` backend https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36293


## Weight update without reload

- [ ] epoch handoff on stable VAs: readers unmap → writer commits → readers remap at the same VAs, so captured CUDA graphs stay valid
- [ ] daemon as the weight delivery agent for trainer pushes (NCCL/RDMA); un-gate the `update_weights_*` rejections in `weight_updater.py`
- [ ] colocated RL: engine itself takes the writer role, same protocol, no daemon in the loop

## Multi-instance & cross-GPU sharing

- [ ] key the cache by physical GPU UUID + config fingerprint (plus optional `--weight-cache-namespace`) under a configurable runtime dir. Today the socket is `/tmp/sglang_weight_cache_rank{global_rank}.sock`, so 2× tp=4 on one 8-GPU node collide and rank 0 of the second instance attaches to the GPU 0 daemon
- [ ] discovery: replace static socket paths with a lightweight registry (file-based dir, optionally etcd) so an engine rank selects a daemon by `CacheConfig` match rather than by process rank, and locates daemons across nodes without a manual `--weight-cache-socket`
- [ ] `--weight-cache-peer-copy` — when no daemon holds the shard on the local GPU, `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` it from a peer-GPU daemon (NVLink-domain check, chunked on a low-priority stream, bandwidth cap so a serving neighbour is not disturbed). 1× memory per instance, sub-second over NVLink vs ~300s from disk
- [ ] preference order local zero-copy > peer copy > disk, reported per rank
- [ ] fleet fill: a daemon fills itself from a peer daemon instead of disk (P2P on-node, NCCL/RDMA cross-node), so a fleet cold start pays one disk read per shard group — the real bottleneck for 1T+ models on shared FS; align with the checkpoint-engine broadcast path
- [ ] out of scope for now: resharding across TP/EP topologies (tp=4 daemon → tp=8 engine)

## Multi-node, DP & EP

- [ ] primary–secondary daemon coordination for multi-node TP (e.g. TP=16 = 2 nodes × 8 GPUs): primary orchestrates daemon startup, cross-node NCCL process-group formation and readiness signalling; secondaries load their local shards in parallel and serve IPC handles to engines on their own node. Basic multi-node launch already works via `--nnodes/--node-rank/--dist-init-method`; what is missing is the cluster state machine
- [ ] cross-node daemon lifecycle: primary tracks which secondaries are alive, triggers coordinated restarts, signals engines on a dead secondary's node to fall back to disk; promote a secondary when the primary dies
- [ ] DP support: every DP rank on a GPU maps the same daemon's handles, so a model is read from disk and quantized exactly once per GPU regardless of DP degree (today each DP rank disk-loads independently). This is about supporting SGLang's DP deployment model, not cross-GPU sharing
- [ ] EP support: expert shards differ per EP rank, so cache and key them by `ep_rank`; handle partial expert loading when a rank owns a subset of experts
- [ ] `CacheConfig`: add `ep_rank`, `dp_rank` and `node_rank` for correct shard identification under EP and multi-node (`dp_size`/`ep_size` are already there)

## Ops & reliability

- [ ] `daemon status` command + Prometheus metrics (resident bytes, attached clients, load time, hit / mismatch / fallback), and an engine endpoint reporting how each rank got its weights
- [ ] runtime dir with owner-only permissions + `SO_PEERCRED` check before handing out handles (no world-writable `/tmp` sockets)
- [ ] `protocol_version` in the handshake with a documented skew policy (the env stamp alrea

    - Added reusable `cute_ext` GEMM mainloop and TMA epilogue helpers.

This pipeline lets user mix `cute_ext` APIs directly into `@cute.jit` and `@cute.kernel` code and is required for kernels that mix the two API surfaces. You may test this feature with the following:
  `CUTE_DSL_USE_EXTENSION_COMPILER=1 python your_program.py`
The pipeline is expected to preserve program behavior and performance, but generated PTX/SASS may differ.  Note that this pipeline will become the default in the future, no earlier than 4.10.

items.title: flex_attention fwd+bwd faults with "misaligned address" at head_dim 512 on sm_103 with default block sizes
items.author: qgallouedec
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Founds while training Gemma 4 training with TRL / transformers (trl core maintainer here 👋)

`flex_attention` forward+backward at head_dim 512 (Gemma 4 global layers) crashes on B300 (sm_103) with the default kernel options; head_dim 256 works. Any `BLOCK_M >= 64` faults, `BLOCK_M=32` runs and is correct. 

(Same class as #198224 / #198228 (sm_12x, head_dim > 128) and #165760 (Blackwell configs), but a different arch and failure: here it's a misaligned address, not an out-of-resource error.)

```python
import sys, torch
from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import create_block_mask, flex_attention

D = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 512
gqa = len(sys.argv) > 2 and sys.argv[2] == "gqa"
H, KV, L = 32, (4 if gqa else 32), 4096
q = torch.randn(1, H, L, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
k = torch.randn(1, KV, L, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
v = torch.randn(1, KV, L, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
bm = create_block_mask(lambda b, h, qi, ki: qi >= ki, 1, 1, L, L, device="cuda")
out = torch.compile(flex_attention)(q, k, v, block_mask=bm, enable_gqa=gqa)
out.sum().backward()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"D={D} gqa={gqa}: OK", torch.__version__, torch.cuda.get_device_name())
```

```
$ python repro.py 512 gqa
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: AcceleratorError: CUDA error: misaligned address
$ python repro.py 256 gqa
D=256 gqa=True: OK 2.16.0.dev20261008+cu130 NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC
```

`kernel_options` sweep at H32 / KV4 / D512, L=8192, causal, fwd+bwd, each config in its own process (the fault poisons the context):

| kernel_options | B300 (sm_103) | H100 (sm_90) |
|---|---|---|
| default | misaligned address | 193.8 ms |
| `BLOCK_M=64, BLOCK_N=32` | misaligned address | 193.7 ms |
| `BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=32` | unspecified launch failure | not run |
| `BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=32, num_stages=2, num_warps=4` | 98.4 ms, max err 0.007 vs fp32 | 115.6 ms |

### Expected

The default config runs at head_dim 512. Using `BLOCK_M=32` above head_dim 256 would fix sm_103 and is also 1.7x faster on sm_90. On packed 16k-token batches it is 3.4x faster than dense eager attention on B300 (59.7 vs 205 ms), which doubles Gemma 4 SFT throughput.

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi Linear / Kimi K3 fail to load from the release container: No module named 'fla'
items.author: vsabavat
items.body_excerpt:
## System Info

- TensorRT-LLM release container `1.3.0rc28` (and any plain `pip install tensorrt_llm` from the wheel)
- Models: Kimi Linear, Kimi K3 (Kimi Delta Attention layers)

## Who can help?

@juney-nvidia

## Reproduction

Load Kimi Linear or Kimi K3 in the release container (or a fresh environment with only the wheel's runtime requirements):

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fla'
```

`tensorrt_llm/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/kimi_kda_mixer.py` imports `fla.modules.ShortConvolution` at load time (line 26 in 1.3.0rc28). Short prefill and the decode / verify fallbacks also call `fla.ops.kda.chunk_kda` and `fla.ops.kda.fused_recurrent_kda`.

## Expected behavior

Both models load from a standard install.

## Actual behavior

flash-linear-attention is listed only in `requirements-dev.txt`. CI installs that file in every test stage, so CI passes. The release container and `pip install` of the wheel install only `requirements.txt`, so the import fails.

## Additional notes

Fix proposed in #19837: add `fla-core==0.5.2` to `requirements.txt`. It is the same version `requirements-dev.txt` already installs (via `flash-linear-attention==0.5.2`) and is MIT-licensed. The new-dependency license/vulnerability scan still needs the maintainers' tooling.

items.title: How to make Tensor static and only call kernel by pointer?
items.author: peterbjorgensen
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to turn Python cute dsl kernels into TensorRT QDP Plugins. It restricts the kind of parameters the PTX can have to (input_pointers..., scalar_arguments..., output_pointers...). I have it working for a simple "add_one_kernel" (see the program listing below if interested).

Instead of writing the kernel with pointer arguments, I would like to write it with some StaticTensorPointer class that automatically turns the layout etc. into compile-time variables and only the pointer ends up as a PTX parameter. I guess it's possible with a custom `DynamicExpression`, but I find the documentation a bit vague on this. Any ideas how to achieve this?

Another question: Is it possible to get the shared memory needed for a compiled kernel? I need it for the kernel launch parameters of the kernel in the plugin.

```
import tensorrt as trt
import numpy as np
from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map
import tensorrt.plugin as trtp
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import cutlass.cute as cute

from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map

trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)

STATIC_SHAPE = (16, 16)
STATIC_STRIDE = (1, 16)

@cute.kernel
def add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    STATIC_LAYOUT = cute.make_layout(shape=STATIC_SHAPE, stride=STATIC_STRIDE)
    tensor_x = cute.make_tensor(x, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tensor_y = cute.make_tensor(y, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
    idx = bidx * cute.arch.block_dim()[0] + tidx
    if idx < cute.size(tensor_x):
        tensor_y[idx] = tensor_x[idx] + 1

@cute.jit
def apply_add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE

    add_one_kernel(x, y).launch(
        grid = [num_blocks, 1, 1],
        block = [BLOCK_SIZE, 1, 1],
    )


@torch.library.custom_op("my::add_one", mutates_args=())  # type: ignore[misc]
def add_one(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    assert x.is_cuda
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    input_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[x.dtype]
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, y.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, x.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")
    compiled(x_ptr, y_ptr)

    return y


@torch.library.register_fake("my::add_one")
def _(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return X

@trtp.register("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_desc(X: trtp.TensorDesc) -> tuple[trtp.TensorDesc]:
    # Output has the same shape and dtype as the input.
    return X.like()


@trtp.aot_impl("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_aot_impl(
    X: trtp.TensorDesc, outputs: tuple[trtp.TensorDesc], tactic: int
) -> tuple[
    str | bytes, str | bytes, trtp.KernelLaunchParams, trtp.SymExprs
]:
    # Choose the pointer type based on the input dtype.
    if X.dtype == trt.float32:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float32]
    elif X.dtype == trt.float16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float16]
    elif X.dtype == trt.bfloat16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.bfloat16]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected dtype")
    input_dtype = x_dtype
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 32, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 64, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled_kernel = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")


    # Build symbolic launch parameters.
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE
    launch_params = trtp.KernelLaunchParams()
    launch_params.grid_x = num_blocks  # number of thread blocks
    launch_params.block_x = BLOCK_SIZE  # threads per block
    launch_params.shared_mem = 0  # bytes of shared mem (I have no idea how to get this)

    # ``extra_args`` are scalar arguments appended to the kernel's argument list at
    # launch. Here ``n_elements`` is passed as a 32-bit symbolic integer so TRT
    # evaluates it from the actual tensor size at runtime.
    extra_args = trtp.SymIntExprs(0)

    kernel_name_ptx = list(compiled_kernel.kernel_info.keys())[0]
    return (
        kernel_name_ptx,  # kernel function name in PTX
        compiled_kernel.artifacts.PTX,  # PTX source — embedded in TRT engine
        launch_params,
        extra_args,
    )


torch_tensorrt.dynamo.conversion.plugins.generate_plugin_converter(
    "my::add_one",
    supports_dynamic_shapes=False,
    requires_output_allocator=False,
    use_aot_if_available=True,
)


class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        res = torch.ops.my.add_one.default(X)
        return res


if __name__ == "__main__":


    my_model = MyModel().to("cuda").eval()
    m = torch.full(STATIC_SHAPE, 2, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    assert my_model(m)[0][0] == 3.0
    assert my_model(m)[1][1] == 3.0

    with torch_tensorrt.logging.debug():
        trt_inputs = [m]
        model_trt = torch_tensorrt.compile(
            my_model,
            inputs=trt_inputs,
            min_block_size=1,
        )
        print("Model compiled successfully!")
        print("Running inference with compiled model...")
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(10):
                res = model_trt(m)
                assert torch.allclose(res, my_model(m)), "Results do not match!"

        program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(
            my_model,
            arg_inputs=trt_inputs,
        )
        engine_bytes: bytes = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.convert_exported_program_to_seri

items.title: Example 64 (Ada FP8 grouped GEMM) refuses capable GPUs via exact CC 8.9 gate
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

examples/64_ada_fp8_gemm_grouped/ada_fp8_gemm_grouped.cu (~line 1107) gates execution on exactly compute capability 8.9:

```cpp
if (!(properties.major == 8 && properties.minor == 9)) {
    std::cerr << "... requires a device of compute capability 89." ...
```

The grouped FP8 kernels here compile cleanly for newer architectures, and the sibling example 58_ada_fp8_gemm uses the inclusive form:

```cpp
if (properties.major < 8 || (properties.major == 8 && properties.minor < 9))
```

On an RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120a, CUDA 12.8.1) the stock binary exits immediately with the capability message; with the gate relaxed to the sibling's form the example builds and runs to completion including device-reference verification (`Passed`). Example 64 is therefore refusing capable hardware for no functional reason.

### Suggested fix

Use the same `major*10+minor < 89` / `major < 8 || (major == 8 && minor < 9)` inclusive check as example 58.

items.title: [BUG] [BUG] `cute.arch.store` doesn't work with fp8 vector
items.author: gau-nernst
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
A clear and concise description of what the bug is.

`cute.arch.store` documents `val` as "scalar Numeric or vector ir.Value". Storing a `TensorSSA` vector works for f32, bf16, f16, u8, i8 and i16, for example `cute.arch.store(ptr, x.load().to(BFloat16))`; each lowers to a single `st.global.v8.b32`. With an fp8 element type (`Float8E4M3FN` or `Float8E5M2`), the same call passes tracing, but backend compilation fails with an internal error:

```
error: NVVM backend compilation failed
error: libNVVM failed while compiling generated device IR.
       LLVM Translation failed for operation: builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast
       Failed creating the llvm::Module.
```

It is not about bit width: 8-bit integer vectors work, and so does the same fp8 vector after `.bitcast(Uint8)` (also a single `st.global.v8.b32`). It looks like a vector of fp8 has no type conversion in the LLVM lowering of the store. `Tensor.store()` of the same fp8 vector does work, but it emits extra byte shuffles (`PRMT`) compared with the bitcast path.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
Follow this guide http://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports to craft a minimal bug report. This helps us reproduce the issue you're having and resolve the issue more quickly.

Compile-only (no GPU run needed):

```python
# CuTeDSL MRE: cute.arch.store of an fp8 vector fails in the NVVM backend.
#
# cute.arch.store documents `val` as "scalar Numeric or vector ir.Value". An
# f32 / bf16 / u8 / i8 TensorSSA stores fine (one st.global.v8.b32), but an
# fp8 one (x.to(Float8E4M3FN) or Float8E5M2) traces and then fails while
# lowering:
#   LLVM Translation failed for operation: builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast
# Not a bit-width issue: the same fp8 vector bitcast to Uint8 stores fine.
#
# Compile-only; prints one line per variant.
#   python arch_store_fp8_vector.py
import importlib.metadata

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass import BFloat16, Float8E4M3FN, Float8E5M2, Float32, Int8, Uint8

N = 32  # elements per thread


def make(dtype, via_u8):
    @cute.kernel
    def kernel(out: cute.Tensor):
        tid, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
        x = cute.make_rmem_tensor(N, Float32)
        for i in cutlass.range_constexpr(N):
            x[i] = Float32(tid + i)
        v = x.load().to(dtype)
        dst = out[tid, None].iterator
        if cutlass.const_expr(via_u8):
            cute.arch.store(cute.recast_ptr(dst, dtype=Uint8), v.bitcast(Uint8))
        else:
            cute.arch.store(dst, v)

    @cute.jit
    def run(out: cute.Tensor):
        kernel(out).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1))

    return run


print("nvidia-cutlass-dsl", importlib.metadata.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"))
for dtype, via_u8 in (
    (Float32, False),
    (BFloat16, False),
    (Uint8, False),
    (Int8, False),
    (Float8E4M3FN, False),
    (Float8E5M2, False),
    (Float8E4M3FN, True),
):
    t = cute.runtime.make_fake_tensor(dtype, (32, N), stride=(N, 1), assumed_align=32)
    name = f"{dtype.__name__:13s} {'bitcast->u8' if via_u8 else 'direct'}"
    try:
        cute.compile(make(dtype, via_u8), t)
        print(f"  {name}: ok")
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        msg = " ".join(str(e).split())
        key = "unrealized_conversion_cast"
        print(f"  {name}: FAILED ({key if key in msg else msg[:200]})")
```

Output on 4.8.0:

```
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0
  Float32       direct: ok
  BFloat16      direct: ok
  Uint8         direct: ok
  Int8          direct: ok
  Float8E4M3FN  direct: FAILED (unrealized_conversion_cast)
  Float8E5M2    direct: FAILED (unrealized_conversion_cast)
  Float8E4M3FN  bitcast->u8: ok
```

**Expected behavior**
A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen.

`cute.arch.store(ptr, fp8_vector)` lowers to a vector store of the packed bytes, the same as the `Uint8` bitcast path. If fp8 vectors are intentionally unsupported, the DSL should raise a clear error at trace time, not an ICE in libNVVM.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: [Bare-metal, Docker, Cloud(specify cloud provider)] 

 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (sm_103a), driver 610.43.02
 - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (aarch64), Python 3.12.13
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl: 4.8.0

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

items.title: [dynamo] Meta-issue: torch.compile gaps found via the CPython test suite
items.author: guilhermeleobas
items.body_excerpt:
I asked an agent to look at the graph break messages from the CPython test suite and
summarize the missing features in Dynamo. This is not an exhaustive list of all missing
features, but it contains some of the gaps that we want to close in the near term.

Some items are harder than they look (`functools.lru_cache` is the usual example).

## Disclaimer

I really appreciate anyone who tries to contribute to the project, but please avoid creating LLM generated code without really understand what the AI is doing. This just burns resources and human review time.

## How to run

```bash
# one module
PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_iter.py -v

# one test
PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_DYNAMO=1 python test/cpython/v3_13/test_iter.py -v -k test_countOf
```

PyTorch must be built against Python 3.13. A known-failing test reports as `skipped` with
the graph-break reason attached, because it has a file under
`test/dynamo_expected_failures/CPython313-<module>-<Class>.<test>`. **Deleting that file is
part of your fix** - CI fails the test as an unexpected success otherwise.

---

## Shared root causes

The six items below each account for several failures across unrelated modules. Fixing one
unlocks every test listed under it, which makes these the highest-leverage work in this
issue.

### 1. `type.__new__` on a C-implemented type

`Unsupported method call: type.__new__`. This is the general "constructing any
non-allowlisted C-implemented type" gap, confirmed at four unrelated call sites. Probably
the single highest-leverage fix here.

- [ ] `test_functools.py::TestLRUPy::test_lru_no_args` and `TestLRUC::test_lru_no_args` - `@lru_cache` decoration
- [x] `test_set.py::TestSetSubclass::test_keywords_in_subclass` - `set`/`frozenset` subclassing (#196425)
- [ ] `test_sys.py::ExceptHookTest::test_excepthook` - `io.StringIO()` construction
- [ ] `test_contextlib.py::TestRedirectStdout::test_enter_result_is_target` - `io.StringIO()` construction

### 2. `Read uninitialized cell` (gb0091)

One root cause, eight tests, four unrelated modules - containers, exceptions, iterators.

- [ ] `test_list.py::ListTest::test_repr_mutate`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_getitem`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_reentrant_insertion`
- [ ] `test_dict.py::DictTest::test_str_nonstr`
- [ ] `test_set.py::_TestJointOps::test_deepcopy`
- [ ] `test_exceptions.py::NameErrorTests::test_gh_111654`
- [ ] `test_iter.py::TestCase::test_3720`
- [ ] `test_iter.py::TestCase::test_free_after_iterating`

### 3. Detected user errors don't surface as the real exception

Dynamo already knows the call is invalid, but instead of raising the `TypeError` CPython
would raise, it produces a generic wrapper, an internal crash, or an
`InternalTorchDynamoError`. Three severities, same underlying gap: user errors detected
during tracing need a path to "raise the real exception."

items.title: [NJT] SDPA math fallback graph-breaks under torch.compile (builds a strided NestedTensor)
items.author: roydonsequeira
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I ran into this while working on the `MultiheadAttention` PR (#200297). `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` works correctly with jagged NestedTensors, but on CPU, `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` fails because Dynamo cannot trace `aten._nested_tensor_from_tensor_list`; without `fullgraph=True`, it graph-breaks and executes that part eagerly. The issue comes from the math fallback in `torch/nested/_internal/sdpa.py`, which converts jagged inputs to the legacy strided NestedTensor layout, so the goal is to make jagged SDPA traceable without falling back to an unsupported layout.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

nt = torch.nested.nested_tensor(
    [torch.randn(3, 8), torch.randn(5, 8)], layout=torch.jagged
)


def attend(x):
    h = x.unflatten(-1, (2, 4)).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, heads, j, head_dim)
    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(h, h, h)


attend(nt)  # eager works
torch.compile(attend, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(nt)
```

#### Agent details

The notes below were drafted with an AI coding assistant; I've reviewed them.

> Ablation on CPU: with `fullgraph=True`, both `backend="eager"` and `backend="aot_eager"` raise
> `Unsupported: Operator does not support running with fake tensors` for `aten._nested_tensor_from_tensor_list`.
> With `fullgraph=False` the call graph-breaks, runs eagerly, and matches the eager output.
>
> Cause: on CPU the fused jagged backends aren't available, so SDPA takes the `SDPBackend.MATH` branch of
> `jagged_scaled_dot_product_attention` (`torch/nested/_internal/sdpa.py`). That branch converts each input to a
> strided-layout NestedTensor (`get_strided_layout_nested_tensor` calls `torch.nested.as_nested_tensor`), and
> FakeTensor rejects strided NestedTensor construction by design (`nested_tensors_unsupported` in
> `torch/_subclasses/fake_impls.py`). The conversion even emits the prototype warning that recommends
> `layout=torch.jagged` because that layout works with torch.compile.
>
> From the code, any input that falls back to MATH should hit this, including CUDA inputs the fused kernels reject;
> only CPU was tested. The compiled jagged SDPA test (`test_sdpa_compile` in `test/test_nestedtensor.py`) is
> `@onlyCUDA`, so this path isn't covered.
>
> A possible direction is to compute the math path on padded dense tensors (`_jagged_to_padded_dense_forward` with a
> key padding mask, then `_padded_dense_to_jagged_forward`), as the jagged softmax over the ragged dim already does.
> `to_padded_tensor` compiles with `fullgraph=True` on CPU.

> Related but different: #126472 (graph breaks when an NJT is built in-graph before SDPA). Found while adding jagged

items.title: When should a new accelerator target an existing kernel DSL?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. I’m researching the smallest useful programming boundary a new accelerator should expose to external kernel developers.

Targeting an existing DSL can accelerate adoption, but doing it before execution, layout and debugging semantics are stable may freeze the wrong abstraction. What evidence should decide whether an architecture targets Triton compatibility, extends an existing path, or begins with a narrower interface?

What must exist between ISA and usable kernel development besides code generation—numerical regression, profiling, layout visibility, or reproducible diagnostics? @ptillet @ThomasRaoux

— Rui, Psync.labs

items.title: Runtime and metadata-service nightly images are unexpectedly large (~970 MB)
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

The current ARM64 nightly images for `aibrix/runtime` and `aibrix/metadata-service` are both approximately 970 MB unpacked:

```text
aibrix/runtime:nightly           970MB
aibrix/metadata-service:nightly  970MB
```

This appears unusually large for the runtime and metadata-service processes and is worth investigating.

Both images are built from `build/container/Dockerfile.python`, which installs the dependencies declared by the AIBrix Python wheel. The largest image layer is the `pip install` layer at approximately 814 MB.

## Measurements

| Component | Approximate size |
|---|---:|
| Debian + Python base layers | 156 MB |
| Final `pip install` layer | 814 MB |
| `site-packages` | 844 MiB |

The largest installed distributions are:

| Distribution | Size |
|---|---:|
| scipy | 142 MiB |
| pandas | 74 MiB |
| numpy | 59 MiB |
| plotly | 58 MiB |
| scikit-learn | 55 MiB |
| PuLP | 38 MiB |
| matplotlib | 37 MiB |
| dash | 32 MiB |
| kubernetes | 30 MiB |

Most of the scientific-computing and visualization imports appear under `aibrix.gpu_optimizer`, rather than the runtime or metadata-service entry points. Their installed dependency closure accounts for approximately 584 MiB.

There is also a mismatch between the Dockerfile comment and the package metadata: the Dockerfile says the profiling group is excluded to avoid packages such as pandas and matplotlib, but those packages are currently declared as main dependencies in `python/aibrix/pyproject.toml`. Therefore, `--without profiling` does not exclude them.

The two image names are also built independently from the same Dockerfile. In the inspected nightly builds, their large dependency layers have different digests, so those layers are not shared even though their installed contents and sizes are nearly identical.

## Impact

- Longer image pull and node startup times
- More registry and node storage usage
- Slower scale-out and cold starts for runtime workers
- Longer CI image builds and duplicate uploads
- Larger dependency and vulnerability-scanning surface

## Possible Changes

The exact implementation should be decided after confirming the dependency requirements of every published entry point. Possible changes include:

- Audit direct and transitive dependencies for `aibrix_runtime`, `aibrix_metadata`, `aibrix_batch_worker`, downloader, and GPU Optimizer.
- Adjust Python package metadata and container build targets so each published image installs only the dependencies required by the processes it runs.
- Preserve the storage backends and Kubernetes integrations currently supported by each entry point.
- If two published images remain identical, build the image once and apply both tags so their layers have the same digest.
- Correct the stale Dockerfile comment about excluded dependencies.
- Add image-size reporting or a regression threshold to CI, together with container smoke tests for the affected entry points.

The GPU Optimizer currently runs from `aibrix/metadata-service:nightly`, so any dependency changes must also update or preserve that deployment path.

## Environment

- Architecture: ARM64
- Tags: `nightly`
- Observed image sizes: approximately 970 MB each

`NewLRUStore` always starts a goroutine that calls `time.NewTicker`. items.title: [RFC]: Normalize the token_load decode score by each pod's KV capacity
items.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The `token_load` decode score (#2842, with output growth from #2852 and the cross-replica ledger from #2868) counts the tokens each decode pod holds. It compares those counts across pods as if every decode pod had the same KV capacity. When capacities differ, for example in a heterogeneous GPU deployment (`docs/source/features/heterogeneous-gpu.rst`), the smaller pods fill up first and overflow. In simulation, `token_load` then does worse than the default `load_balancing` on long-output workloads. This RFC proposes dividing each pod's `token_load` score by its KV capacity in tokens, read from metrics the engines already expose (`vllm:cache_config_info`). With equal capacities the ranking is unchanged.

## Motivation

`load_balancing` reads `KVCacheUsagePerc`, which is already relative to each pod's capacity. `token_load` replaced that stale signal with an exact ledger, but in absolute tokens: 60k tokens on a 100k-token pod is 60% full, and on a 200k-token pod 30% full, yet both score the same.

Decode pods with different KV capacities are a supported setup, not an edge case:

- **Heterogeneous GPUs.** The same model deployed on several GPU types (one Deployment per type, sharing `model.aibrix.ai/name`) gives decode pods different KV capacities.
- **Different engine settings** on pods of the same model: vLLM sizes its KV cache from `gpu_memory_utilization` unless `kv_cache_memory_bytes` or `num_gpu_blocks_override` sets it directly.
- **Per-engine KV limits** set by ModelClaim on shared cards (#2795) are another source, discussed under open questions.

In the simulation below, with four 200k-token and four 100k-token decode pods, `token_load` has 65× the excess KV it has with equal capacities on steady chat traffic. On long-output workloads it is worse than `load_balancing`.

## Proposed Change

**Capacity per decode pod.** Read each pod's KV capacity in tokens during the regular metric scrape:

- vLLM: `vllm:cache_config_info`, an info gauge whose `num_gpu_blocks` and `block_size` labels give `capacity = num_gpu_blocks × block_size`. AIBrix already reads label values this way (`QueryLabel`, as for `max_lora` from `vllm:lora_requests_info`).
- SGLang: `sglang:max_total_num_tokens`, a gauge of the KV pool size in tokens that the engine sets once at startup.
- The capacity is fixed for an engine process, so a missing or unparsable value just leaves the pod without one.

**Score.** Under `token_load`, a decode pod's score becomes the fraction of its capacity in use:

```
decode_score = (local tokens + local growth + remote tokens + remote growth) / capacity
```

The ledger, growth and cross-replica sharing are unchanged; only the final division is new. `finalPDScore` already normalizes decode scores by the maximum in the run, so the unit change doesn't affect how prefill and decode scores combine.

**Missing capacities.** A pod without a known capacity uses the mean capacity of the candidates that have one. If none has one, the score stays in absolute tokens, which is today's behavior. With equal capacities, dividing by a constant doesn't change the ranking.

**Switch.** `AIBRIX_DECODE_TOKEN_LOAD_CAPACITY_AWARE`, default `true`, since it changes nothing for pools with equal capacities. Only the `token_load` decode policy reads it.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Fall back to `load_balancing` when capacities differ.** It is capacity-relative, but brings back the stale-scrape herding that `token_load` removed (chat, bursty: 69.40 vs 4.17 excess KV below).
- **A configured capacity per pod or per GPU type.** It drifts from the engine's actual configuration, and operators would have to keep it in sync. The engines already report it.
- **Normalize by the scraped `KVCacheUsagePerc` instead** (combine the ledger with the scraped fraction). It reintroduces the 1 s staleness for the part of the signal that matters during bursts, and needs capacity in tokens anyway to combine the two.

## Evidence (simulation, not engine measurements)

The same simulation as #2849 and #2867: it drives the real `filterPrefillDecodePods` (fast paths, scoring, ledger with growth) against a per-pod KV model with load-dependent decode speed and a 1 s metric scrape. Eight decode pods: four with 200k tokens of KV and four with 100k. A prototype passes each pod's capacity to the router. The metric is excess KV: time-averaged demand above each pod's capacity, summed, as % of the mean pod capacity (lower is better). Spread is the time-averaged max − min utilization across pods.

| workload | load | seeds | `load_balancing` | `token_load` | `token_load` / capacity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chat (outputs 256) | steady | 10 | 27.74 (±5.10) | 16.99 (±5.24) | **0.82** (±0.56) |
| chat | bursty | 10 | 69.40 (±11.82) | 36.68 (±7.34) | **4.17** (±2.38) |
| long outputs (40% generate 2k–16k) | steady | 30 | 0.83 (±1.37) | 4.66 (±4.54) | **0.50** (±0.88) |
| long outputs | bursty | 30 | 7.65 (±5.34) | 16.01 (±9.65) | **1.85** (±1.89) |

- Spread on chat, steady: 88.8% / 66.4% / 28.6%.
- **Control:** with eight 150k-token pods (same total capacity), `token_load` and `token_load` / capacity give identical results in all four rows (for example 0.26 and 2.50 on chat, steady and bursty), as expected from dividing by a constant.
- On long outputs, steady, the capacity-aware score and `load_balancing` are within noise of each other. The clear results are that today's `token_load` is worse than `load_balancing` there, and that the capacity-aware score is better under bursts.

Limitations: this is a model (no engine preemption or queueing, assumed step times), and capacities are given to the router exactly. Two capacity tiers are one example; the effect grows with the ratio between them.

## Open Questions

1. Should the switch default to `true`? It changes nothing with equal capacities, but it is a new input to the score.
2. With ModelClaim on shared cards, an engine's effective KV limit can be lower than `num_gpu_blocks × block

items.title: [PyTorch backend][encoder-decoder] KvCacheConfig(dtype="fp8") overruns the cross-attention KV pool: illegal memory access or silently wrong output unless the pool is 2x the required size
items.author: lminer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With an encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend, setting the KV cache dtype to `fp8` makes
the cross-attention cache access memory beyond its pool. A request only succeeds when the
cross-attention pool holds at least **twice** the blocks the in-flight requests need. Below that
the process either dies with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` or, when the
stray access lands in other mapped memory, returns wrong tokens with no error. The same pool
sizes work with the default cache dtype.

## Environment

- Images: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29` and
  `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.4.0rc0.dev202610040000` (both reproduce)
- GPU: NVIDIA L4 (24 GB), driver 595.91.07; AWS g6.2xlarge
- Model: `google/flan-t5-base`, weights loaded as bf16
- `LLM(backend="pytorch", ...)`, block reuse off, no CUDA graphs

## Reproduction

The prompt is 483 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool. With
`cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5`, `max_tokens=768` gives a 24-block pool and `max_tokens=1024` a
32-block pool (the log line `Max KV cache blocks per sequence: 16 [window size=512], tokens per
block=32, primary blocks=24` confirms the sizes).

```bash
docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host -v $PWD:/w nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29 \
  python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 768     # crashes on the first request
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 1024    # decodes
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py auto 768    # decodes (default cache dtype, same pool)
```

| KV dtype | `max_tokens` | cross pool blocks | blocks needed | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp8 | 768 | 24 | 16 | `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` |
| fp8 | 1024 | 32 | 16 | OK |
| auto | 768 | 24 | 16 | OK |

After the error the process does not exit by itself; it has to be killed.

`fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py`:

```python
"""Encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend: an FP8 KV cache overruns the cross-attention pool.

    python3 fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py <kv dtype: fp8|auto> <kv max_tokens>

The prompt is ~480 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

from tensorrt_llm import LLM, SamplingParams
from tensorrt_llm.llmapi import KvCacheConfig


def main():
    kv_dtype, kv_tokens = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
    # The backend takes the weight dtype from the checkpoint's config.json, so write a bf16 copy.
    src = snapshot_download("google/flan-t5-base", allow_patterns=["*.json", "*.model", "model.safetensors"])
    ckpt = "/tmp/flan-t5-base-bf16"
    os.makedirs(ckpt, exist_ok=True)
    for name in os.listdir(src):
        if name != "config.json" and not os.path.exists(f"{ckpt}/{name}"):
            os.symlink(os.path.realpath(f"{src}/{name}"), f"{ckpt}/{name}")
    config = json.load(open(f"{src}/config.json"))
    config["torch_dtype"] = config["dtype"] = "bfloat16"
    json.dump(config, open(f"{ckpt}/config.json", "w"))

    llm = LLM(
        model=ckpt,
        backend="pytorch",
        max_batch_size=1,
        max_beam_width=1,
        max_input_len=512,
        max_seq_len=2048,
        kv_cache_config=KvCacheConfig(
            enable_block_reuse=False, max_tokens=kv_tokens, cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5, dtype=kv_dtype
        ),
        cuda_graph_config=None,
    )
    prompt = "summarize: " + "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank. " * 30
    print("prompt tokens:", len(llm.tokenizer.encode(prompt)), flush=True)
    params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=32)
    for i in range(3):
        out = llm.generate(prompt, params)
        print(f"request {i}: {list(out.outputs[0].token_ids)[:12]} {out.outputs[0].text[:60]!r}", flush=True)
    print("OK", kv_dtype, kv_tokens)
    llm.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## More than one request in flight

The same rule holds with several requests submitted together. Measured on rc29 with a second,
larger encoder-decoder model, a batch of requests that needs 752 blocks in total:

| cross pool blocks | result |
|---|---|
| 768 | illegal memory access (also on the 1.4.0 nightly) |
| 896 | illegal memory access |
| 1,024 | **no error, wrong output**: every request runs to `max_tokens`, none matches the same request decoded alone |
| 1,280 | illegal memory access |
| 1,536 | OK |

So the threshold is 2 x 752 = 1,504 blocks. With the default cache dtype, 768 blocks are enough.
Admitting the requests one at a time only helps because fewer are then in flight together.

With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` that run reports the failure in the cross-attention context pass:

```
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/cross_attention.py", line 268, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/trtllm.py", line 2330, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/fmha/fallback.py", line 122, in forward
    thop.attention(
RuntimeError: [TensorRT-LLM][ERROR] CUDA runtime error in cudaStreamIsCapturing(stream, &status): an illegal memory access was encountered (../include/tensorrt_llm/common/cudaUtils.h:157)
  tensorrt_llm::common::op::AttentionOp::enqueueContext<__half, tensorrt_llm::kernels::KVBlockArray>(...)
```

## Expected

Either the FP8 cross-attention cache stays inside a pool sized for the requests (as the default
dtype does), or the configuration is rejected for encoder-decoder models. An out-of-range access
should not be able to return wrong tokens silently.

## Guess at the cause

The 2x factor suggests the cross-attention pool is allocated at one byte per element (FP8) while
the cross-attention kernel addresses it with a two-byte element size. Not verified in the source.

## Also seen

With the FP8 cache and a large enough pool, on the larger model the first request after start-up
returns different tokens from the identical request sent again (every run). This does not happen
wit

If I can reproduce or confirm the root cause, I’ll work on a regression test and a focused fix.

items.title: [BUG | QST] CPU overhead regression with TVM-FFI
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
In v4.6 update, the following is changed in `python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/cutlass_dsl/cutlass.py`:
```
-                if kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults:
+                # Route through the kwargs-capable compiled class whenever
+                # the signature has kwonly/defaults OR any positional arg
+                # carries a dataclass instance (detected by the spec
+                # converter, including Union[...] over dataclasses). The
+                # kwargs wrapper is the only place tvm-ffi's
+                # ``map_dataclass_to_tuple`` unpack hook fires.
+                if (
+                    kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_names
+                    or map_dataclass_to_tuple
+                ):
```
So basically if a @cute.jit function satisfies one of the following:
- `kwonly_names`: have keyword only arguments (indicated by *)
- `arg_defaults`: have default arguments
- `arg_names`: have any argument that is not a keyword only argument
- `map_dataclass_to_tuple`: have dataclass arguments

With these restrictions (especially `kwonly_names` and `arg_names`), basically only a CuTeDSL function with no arguments can go to the else branch and become a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` which is a subclass of `tvm_ffi.Function` so they get to be called in C++ and bypass python completely. For CuTeDSL functions with arguments, they now have to go through the `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs` path.

This will slightly slow down calling a CuTeDSL function from python due to extra python layers from in `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs`, which isn't a big deal since python is slow anyway. However, if you register the CuTeDSL function via tvm-ffi and call it from C++, the overhead becomes obvious because you will leave C++ and enter python (`TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs.__call__`) and then enter the compiled CuTeDSL function. This makes the CPU overhead regress compared to pre-4.6 version since there wasn't going through python with GIL and argument wrapper stuff.

I also wonder what's the motivation behind this. My guess is this makes a @cute.jit function behave more like a python function where it can use kwargs instead of can only be called using positional args, but meanwhile when we do want to call it with positional args (in C++) this only makes it slower.

Currently there is a hack to fix this, which is instead of registering the compiled CuTeDSL function, we can register its `__tvm_ffi_object__` which would be a `tvm_ffi.Function` object, and we need to guarantee the args order is exactly the same in C++. I feel it's a bit hacky and fragile as cutlass evolves. 

Another proposition of mine is we can tell users (probably in docs) that if they define CuTeDSL functions in this format: `def func(a, b, c, /)` with nothing after / and no default values, then we can optimize this case into a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` because we know nobody will use kwargs in this case. I think if this fix is OK I can open a PR on it.

Not sure what's the opinion of the CUTLASS people?

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
I think my explanation should be clear enough so I don't think I need an example to reproduce.
You can just follow the example in https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3289 and measure the CPU time to notice the difference.

**Expected behavior**
Should be faster?

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
This regressed after v4.6 update

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

But per our benchmark, the overhead it introduces is < 1us, while the overall launch overhead is typically <10 us. We think it is fine to keep this overhead for compatibility of diversed inputs. And we agree to have more documents here. Any PR is appreciated.

items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |

items.title: [Bug] mm_mxfp8 silently writes wrong results for a non-contiguous out (cutlass, cute-dsl, auto)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`mm_mxfp8` silently returns wrong results when `out` is not contiguous, for the `cutlass`, `cute-dsl` and default `auto` backends. The kernels write a compact row-major `M x N` block starting at `out`'s data pointer and ignore its real strides. The result in `out` is garbage, and the write also overwrites memory just outside it (for example, the neighbouring columns of a larger buffer that `out` was sliced from). Nothing in `mm_mxfp8` checks the layout of `out`.

### Measured behavior

`M, N, K = 256, 1536, 1024`, bf16 output, inputs quantized with `mxfp8_quantize(..., sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)`. "Correct" means cosine similarity 0.9993 against a bf16 `torch.mm` reference; "wrong" means about 0.001.

| `out` layout | `cute-dsl` | `cutlass` | `auto` | `cudnn` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| row-major, strides `(N, 1)` | correct | correct | correct | correct |
| row slice of a taller buffer, `buf[:M]` (still contiguous) | correct | correct | correct | correct |
| column slice of a wider buffer, `buf[:, :N]` (row stride > N) | **wrong**, neighbouring columns overwritten | **wrong**, neighbouring columns overwritten | **wrong** | correct |
| column-major view, `buf.T` (strides `(1, M)`) | raises `ValueError: Mismatched mC.strides[1] ...` from the compiled kernel | **wrong** | **wrong** | correct |

`cudnn` honors arbitrary output strides. `auto` resolves to `cutlass` here, so the default path is affected. Not tested: `trtllm`, `cutedsl_low_latency`, `b12x`.

### Reproduction

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from flashinfer import SfLayout, mm_mxfp8
from flashinfer.fp8_quantization import mxfp8_quantize

m, n, k = 256, 1536, 1024
a = torch.randn(m, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
w = torch.randn(n, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
a8, a_sf = mxfp8_quantize(a, sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)
w8, w_sf = mxfp8_quantize(w, sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)

buf = torch.full((m, n + 64), 7.0, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
out = buf[:, :n]  # non-contiguous: row stride n + 64
mm_mxfp8(a8, w8.T, a_sf, w_sf, out=out, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16, backend="cutlass")

ref = a @ w.T
print(F.cosine_similarity(out.float().flatten(), ref.float().flatten(), dim=0))  # ~0.001
print((buf[:, n:] == 7.0).all())  # False: columns outside `out` were overwritten
```

### Expected

Either honor `out`'s strides, as `cudnn` does, or reject a non-contiguous `out` with a clear error. Silently writing a wrong result, and writing outside the given view, should not happen.

### Notes

- **Checks:** no check on `out`'s layout exists in `mm_mxfp8`, `_check_mm_mxfp8_problem_size`, or the `cutlass` / `cute-dsl` backend requirement functions. The only stride check on this path, in the `cutedsl_low_latency` requirement, covers the inputs `a` and `b`. The docstring does not state a layout requirement for `out`.
- **`cute-dsl` error:** its error for the column-major case is incidental. It comes from the compiled kernel's stride check on the last dimension, which does not catch a padded row stride.
- **Possible fixes:** raise `ValueError` for a non-contiguous `out` in the affected backends, or compute into a temporary contiguous buffer and copy into `out`.

### Environment

- FlashInfer main `125c989e0` (2026-10-05)
- Measured on SM107 (cc 10.7), nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8. The affected code paths are not architecture-specific, but other architectures were not measured.

items.title: [SM121 / GB10] cutlass_fused_moe: GEMM2 FINALIZE tactics 32 and 33 fail to initialise at every M (follow-up to #4847)
items.author: Col-5555
items.body_excerpt:
This follows up a note in #4847. That PR says gemm2 tactics {32, 33} on SM120 still fail at cutlass `initialize` with real problem shapes, and leaves them as profiling-time skips. We see the same pair fail the same way on **SM121 (GB10, DGX Spark)**, with a different model shape and at every M we tried. That suggests they may never be runnable on SM12x, in which case they could be removed from the candidate list instead of being tried and skipped on every tuning pass. We have not found the root cause.

**Setup.** 2× GB10 (sm_121), TP=2. FlashInfer 0.7.0 built from source (AOT, `sm121a`), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.178.04, torch 2.13.0+cu130. Model `RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` (288 experts, top-8, NVFP4 weights and activations).

**What we ran.** `flashinfer.fused_moe.cutlass_fused_moe` on synthetic NVFP4 inputs with our per-rank layer shapes (hidden 4096, intermediate 1024, bf16 output). We forced each autotuner candidate through `profile_ids` with GEMM1 fixed at tactic 18, and made 20 calls at each of M = 1, 24 and 256. The IDs are as numbered on our build. GEMM2 offered 32 candidates: 20–23, 26–33, 36–43, 46–53 and 56–59. The 8 IDs that #4847 reports as dispatch-rejected on SM120 (24, 25, 34, 35, 44, 45, 54, 55) were not offered.

**Result.** Tactics 32 and 33 failed at all three M with:

```
RuntimeError: [TensorRT-LLM][ERROR] Assertion failed: Failed to initialize cutlass TMA WS grouped gemm. Error: Error Internal (/workspace/build/aot-providers/sm121a/generated/cutlass_instantiations/12…
```

Our log kept only the first 200 characters, so the file and line were cut off. We can re-run to capture the full message and stack. Every other GEMM2 tactic ran at every M. In normal serving the autotuner skips 32 and 33 and carries on, so the impact is wasted tuning time and log noise, not a crash.

**Context.** 32 and 33 are in the FINALIZE (fused finalize epilogue) family. The other 14 FINALIZE tactics run but are non-deterministic run to run on our build, which is what vllm#54945 / vllm#54948 address with `use_fused_finalize=False`. With that switch, neither 32 nor 33 is offered.

**Suggestion.** If the failure is architectural, filtering these configs on SM12x in `get_valid_tactics` (or in the candidate config list) would save the tuning attempts. One guess is a shared-memory limit, given that SM12x has 99 KB per block and FINALIZE adds epilogue storage, but we have not checked that against the configs. If the cause depends on the shape after all, remembering an init failure per (tactic, problem shape) would at least stop it being retried.

We can test a candidate fix on 2× GB10 in a maintenance window if that helps. Related: #4847, #2077, vllm#54948.

items.title: [RFC]: Mooncake Data Plane Model Distribution, Phase 1
items.author: XucSh
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed ## Summary This RFC proposes a Phase 1 model distribution capability inside Mooncake's data plane. In this design: - Mooncake Store is the storage and transfer substrate for model weights. - `mooncake_master` exposes HTTP APIs for model distribution orchestration. - node-side `mooncake_client` executes data movement tasks. - initial external acquisition is handled by a new `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` task. - follower replication continues to use Mooncake's existing object copy path. Phase 1 ends when a model is `Staged` on the requested nodes. It does not include runtime model loading, warmup, or serving readiness. ## Motivation Mooncake already has the right primitives for model distribution: - object-based storage - replica-aware transfer - task orchestration - node-side execution What is missing is a model-aware orchestration path that can do two things in sequence: 1. download model data from an external source onto one seed node and publish it into Mooncake Store 2. fan out the same data to follower nodes through Mooncake's internal replication path This should be solved inside Mooncake's data plane, not by introducing a new node-level service. ## Goals Phase 1 must provide the following: 1. `mooncake_master` accepts a model distribution job over HTTP. 2. Mooncake can determine whether a seed node already has the required objects. 3. If not, Mooncake can issue a `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` task to the seed node. 4. The seed node can download model files from a given source and write chunked objects into Mooncake Store. 5. After seed data is available, Mooncake can issue copy tasks to follower nodes. 6. Mooncake can return aggregated job and placement state over HTTP. 7. The terminal success state for Phase 1 is `Staged`. ## Non-Goals Phase 1 does not attempt to solve: - runtime model load into serving engines - runtime warmup - serving readiness - scheduler integration - artifact deletion and GC workflows - complex multi-source fallback - cross-cluster distribution ## Scope Boundary This RFC is intentionally about Mooncake only. It defines: - Mooncake's HTTP contract for model distribution - Mooncake's internal task model - Mooncake's data movement behavior - Mooncake's job and placement state model It does not define the external control plane in detail. An external control plane, such as `smg`, may call Mooncake's HTTP APIs, track its own higher-level lifecycle state, and present operator-facing workflows. That integration is an example, not the subject of this RFC. ## Terminology ### Model Manifest An immutable description of one model version, keyed by: `model_id + revision + format + provider` The manifest uses file-level semantics, while Mooncake stores the payload as chunked objects. ### Distribution Job A Mooncake-managed request to stage one model version on a set of target nodes. ### Placement The per-node staged state of one model version. ### Seed Node The node responsible for initial external acquisition when the requested objects are not already present. ### Follower Node A target node that receives the model through Mooncake's internal replication path after seed data becomes available. ## Architecture Overview ```mermaid flowchart LR CP[External Control Plane
example: SMG] MM[mooncake_master
distribution orchestrator] S[Seed mooncake_client] F[Follower mooncake_client] MS[(Mooncake Store objects)] NV1[(Seed local NVMe)] NV2[(Follower local NVMe)] CP -->|Create / Query distribution job| MM MM -->|MODEL_DOWNLOAD task| S S -->|publish chunked objects| MS MM -->|copy tasks| F MS -->|replicate objects| F S --> NV1 F --> NV2 ``` ## Component Responsibilities ### `mooncake_master` `mooncake_master` is the data plane orchestration entrypoint. It is responsible for: - exposing model distribution HTTP APIs - validating create/query job requests - checking whether the seed node already has all required objects - issuing `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` tasks when seed acquisition is needed - issuing copy tasks to follower nodes after seed data is available - computing aggregate job and placement state ### node-side `mooncake_client` The existing Mooncake client process is responsible for execution. It is responsible for: - executing `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` - reading the source file or URL - writing chunked objects into Mooncake Store - executing existing copy tasks - materializing staged model data on local storage ### External Control Plane An external control plane is out of scope for this RFC, but a typical caller is expected to: - build or store the model manifest - select target nodes - choose the seed node - create a distribution job in Mooncake - poll Mooncake for job state `smg` is one example of such a caller. ## Why There Is No Standalone Model Agent We explicitly reject a separate node-level model agent for Phase 1. Reasons: - it adds one more process and deployment artifact on every node - it duplicates logic that already belongs in Mooncake's task execution path - it creates another operational boundary for storage and transfer behavior The simpler model is: - `mooncake_master` orchestrates - `mooncake_client` executes ## End-to-End Workflow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CP as External Control Plane participant MM as mooncake_master participant Seed as Seed mooncake_client participant Store as Mooncake Store participant Follower as Follower mooncake_client CP->>MM: POST /api/v1/model-distribution/jobs MM->>MM: Check if seed already has all objects alt Seed already has objects MM->>MM: Skip initial download else Seed missing objects MM->>Seed: Submit MODEL_DOWNLOAD task Seed->>Seed: Download source file Seed->>Store: Publish chunked objects end MM->>Follower: Submit copy tasks Follower->>Store: Pull / materialize objects CP->>MM: GET /api/v1/model-distribution/jobs?job_id=.

items.title: [RFC]: TENT Local Transfer Admission Queue
items.author: zbchi
items.body_excerpt: ### Changes proposed ## Summary This RFC proposes a local transfer admission queue inside `TransferEngineImpl`. The queue orders logical transfers and applies backpressure before work is handed to `Transport::submitTransferTasks()` or `ProxyManager::submit()`. This covers the local-runtime part of the Transfer Queue roadmap item in #1883, before adding distributed pressure signals or receiver credits. It does not replace transport or ProxyManager execution. RDMA slice scheduling, CQ/QP handling, staging state machines, retries, and KVCache placement remain owned by their existing layers. Phase 1 keeps the normal submit path direct and adds a private queue model plus compatibility tests. Distributed pressure and receiver credits can be added later as inputs to local admission; this RFC does not propose a cluster-wide per-transfer executor. ## Motivation The current path is optimized for direct submission: ```text submitTransfer() -> merge requests -> resolve transport or staging -> allocate SubBatch -> assign sub_task_id -> Transport::submitTransferTasks() or ProxyManager::submit() ``` This is fast when the process is not overloaded. Under heavy load, background prefetch or migration traffic and foreground Store `get` traffic can enter transport queues through the same direct path. By the time foreground work is visible to the runtime, transport-side queues may already contain background work. Transport execution and ProxyManager staging remain owned by their existing layers. This RFC adds an earlier runtime admission point in `TransferEngineImpl::submitTransfer()`, so accepted work can be capped and latency-sensitive requests can be ordered before handoff. ## Current Code Shape The queue would be inserted into the current `submitTransfer()` path: ```text Current direct-submit shape Application / Store | | allocateBatch(batch_size) v TransferEngineImpl::submitTransfer(batch_id, requests) | | merge requests | append public TaskInfo entries to Batch::task_list | allocate SubBatch state and assign sub_task_id | +-- direct path --> Transport::submitTransferTasks() | -> RDMA / TCP / SHM / NVLink / GDS execution queues | +-- staged path --> ProxyManager::submit() -> shard queue with TaskInfo* -> stage buffers / internal batches / engine callbacks Status and lifetime side paths getTransferStatus() -> expects valid transport state for non-staging tasks -> treats UNSPEC as retry/fallback, not as "queued" freeBatch() -> currently recycles through caller-thread-local state -> async queueing needs explicit engine-owned lifetime ``` In the direct path, public task state is published before any queue admission point. The queued path must therefore: - Introduce explicit queue metadata instead of overloading `UNSPEC`, `TaskInfo::xport_priority`, or transport `sub_task_id`. - Admission capacity is charged by public request/task ids. Merged or derived task ids resolve through an owner map instead of becoming independent queue items. - Production async dispatch needs the engine to own batch lifetime and pin local buffers such as `Request::source`. `BatchID` is effectively a `Batch*`, and `SegmentTracker::ref_count` is not a transfer pin. - Transport and ProxyManager keep execution ownership; the queue only controls admission and scheduling before handoff. Production staged queueing also needs stable task addresses because `ProxyManager::submit()` stores `TaskInfo*`. ## Architecture The queue sits between caller submit and transport/proxy execution. L2 signals are inputs to the queue, not executors: In Phase 1, the normal submit path stays direct; the new code only exercises the queue model, side-table state, and owner mapping to ensure direct-path compatibility. ## Runtime Queue Design ### Data Model A queue item represents one logical transfer owner. It is not an RDMA slice and does not copy payload data. The first implementation can keep this as a private model, but the model should already reflect production boundaries such as batch ownership, derived-task mapping, byte charge, priority class, route plan, queue state, and reserved internal work. The logical owner is the single queued task for a merged request. Derived public task ids resolve to that owner and are not independently queued, dispatched, retried, or charged. An implementation can start with a private shape like this: ```cpp struct QueueOwner { QueueOwnerId id; BatchRef batch; // model id first; engine-owned ref later size_t owner_task_id; std::vector derived_task_ids; Request request; // metadata only, no payload copy size_t task_charge; size_t byte_charge; PriorityClass priority; RoutePlan route; // transport or staging decision QueueState state; uint64_t attempt_generation; TimePoint enqueue_time; CreditReservation credits; bool internal_staging_work; }; ``` The key point is to keep queue state in this private model instead of encoding it in `TaskInfo` fields. ### Admission For the production queued path, queue admission for one `submitTransfer(batch_id, request_list)` call is all-or-nothing. If every logical owner derived from the call can be admitted, it returns `Status::OK`. If admission would exceed hard limits, it returns `Status::TooManyRequests` and leaves no partial submission behind. Transport execution can still fail later and report failure through status, matching the existing asynchronous contract. When the production queued path is enabled, `Status::OK` means the work was published to the runtime queue, not necessarily that a transport has already accepted it. Applications may observe `PENDING` for tasks that have not reached `Transport::submitTransferTasks
