items.title: [Bug][SM86] cuTile FP8 RoPE tests fail after CUDA 13 CI compiler provisioning
items.author: cindyzxq
items.body_excerpt:
## Description

The CUDA 13 nightly jobs on SM86 fail in all supported `cutile` variants of  `test_generalized_rope_quantize`.
Both CUDA 13.0 and CUDA 13.4 jobs fail with the same 48 test cases and the same error, so this does not appear to be specific to one CUDA version.

## Failed jobs
- CUDA 13.0 / SM86:
https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/actions/runs/37577314511/job/112663853459
- CUDA 13.4 / SM86:
https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/actions/runs/37577314511/job/112663853544

Both jobs report:  48 failed, 30257 passed, 576 skipped

## Failed tests

All failures come from:  tests/attention/test_rope.py::test_generalized_rope_quantize
The failing cases share these parameters:
···
  backend=cutile
  enable_pdl=False
  quant_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn
  attention_type=mla
···
  The 48 failures correspond to:  2 input dtypes × 6 token sizes × 4 MLA shapes = 48 cases

## Error
···
  ValueError: No valid config found in search space.
  Config: namespace(TOKENS_PER_BLOCK=1, occupancy=1)
  UnsupportedFeatureError: float8_e4m3fn is not supported on sm_86

  flashinfer/quantization/kernels/cutile/rope_quantize_fp8_cutile.py:
      q_rope_out,
      ^^^^^^^^^^
···
  Every autotune candidate fails because the cuTile FP8 output type is not supported on SM86. The autotuner then reports the less specific No valid config found in search space error.

## Regression analysis

 - #4939 provisioned the TileIRAS/cuTile compiler in CUDA 13 CI images.
    This changed is_cuda_tile_available() from false to true on the SM86
    runners, allowing the previously skipped tests to execute.

  - #4673 updated CI from image 20260822-9a0e83b to 20260930-b1420f1, exposing the issue in the nightly jobs.

   Therefore, #4673 is the direct CI regression trigger, while the missing  operation-specific SM86 capability gate  and was exposed by the compiler provisioning from #4939.

  ## Expected behavior

  On an architecture where the cuTile FP8 RoPE kernel is unsupported:

  1. The test should be skipped with a clear architecture-specific reason; and
  2. An explicit backend="cutile" API call should fail early with a clear unsupported-architecture error.

  It should not enter autotuning and fail with No valid config found.

  ## Suggested fix

  Add an operation-specific architecture capability check for the cuTile FP8 RoPE path.

  The check should not globally disable cuTile on SM86 because three of the newly  enabled cuTile cases pass. It should only reject or skip the unsupported FP8 RoPE path.


  ## Validation requested

  - SM86: unsupported cuTile FP8 RoPE cases are rejected or skipped clearly.
  - SM100/SM103: supported cuTile FP8 RoPE cases continue to run and pass.
  - Other cuTile operations that work on SM86 remain enabled.

items.author: mickqian

Center Q4 on MiniMax-H3 as the stress test; most of the work is model-agnostic.
   - Lossless performance: overlap TP/Ulysses communication with compute, fuse kernels under the bit-exact contract, and ship validated GB200/GB300 recipes.
   - Lossy `high` tier: extend the quality gate to all Blackwell GPUs and to substituted (LoRA) weights, then combine sparse attention, few-step distillation (PDD, Turbo LoRA, on top of FastH3 V2) and FP8/NVFP4 for at least 2x over `exact`.
   - Community H3 variants: run at least 90% of the top-50 Hugging Face derivatives (GGUF, quantized, LoRA, component repos) with a plain `sglang serve`, fail before downloading otherwise, and keep distilled LoRAs effective when merged.  
   - Serving and platforms: batching for audio-video outputs and disaggregated serving; ROCm, NPU, DGX Spark, Apple MPS and consumer GPUs.
   - Consumer GPUs (RTX 4090, RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000): default commands that run without OOM on 24–32 GB of VRAM and 32–64 GB of host memory, with weight residency planned from measured memory (layerwise streaming, decode-scoped VAE, evicting idle encoders) and faster weight streaming from host memory and disk; FP8/NVFP4 GEMMs, FP8 attention and INT8 W8A8 on SM89/SM120; at least ComfyUI's speed with the same weights.

items.title: b12x: retry instantiation with compile_directly on unplanned CuTe programs (patch)
items.author: PrblyElect
items.body_excerpt:
Since b12x moved into `flashinfer/experimental/b12x`, filing here (the archived b12x repository points development and PRs at FlashInfer).

**Problem.** Booting a CSF-packed DeepSeek-V4-Flash (TP=3, 3× GB10/SM120) with a runtime built from b12x master + the CSF kernel path, the weights-stage prepare dies with:

```
moe.w4a8.compact_micro ... unplanned CuTe program / used undeclared programs
```

Cross-session plan reuse bypasses the obligation machinery and reaches materialize with undeclared programs (compact_micro at n % 128 == 64).

**Patch.** Retry-once-with-compile at the `_instantiate` boundary: wrap it into a thin retry that fires only on the two matching error strings (`unplanned CuTe program` / `used undeclared programs`) and only when not already `compile_directly`, retrying with `expected=set(expected), compile_directly=True`. The original body moves verbatim to `_instantiate_once`.

The timing races already carry their own `no_compilation` contexts in `_measurement.py`, so this adds no unfair compilation — it does exactly what warmup's `compile_directly` path does.

- Minimal diff against `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/preparation/session.py` on current main: https://gist.github.com/PrblyElect/76456b357a257e2e8baaa6a6105a3617
- Serving context and validation (weights-stage prepare through serving boots clean; corruption batteries clean under compiled modes): https://github.com/PrblyElect/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-TP3-3x-DGX-Spark

Happy to open a PR if the direction looks right.

### Changes proposed

I've been reproducing your Table 1 cache hit rates on arxiv-trace/mooncake_trace.jsonl using LRU, and I get the same curve shape but a systematic offset at every capacity:

| blocks | 1k        | 10k     | 30k    | 50k     | 100k  | infiniti |
|--------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| paper   | 0.30   | 0.40   | 0.48   | 0.50   | 0.51    | 0.51    |
| mine    | 0.341  | 0.460 | 0.537 | 0.551 | 0.552 | 0.553 |

I compute hit rate as (sum of longest-resident-prefix blocks) / (sum of all blocks requested), replaying in timestamp order. Since the infinite-cache case is policy-free, I'd expect it to be reproducible from the trace alone, but I get 0.553 against your 0.51.

I've tried five denominator definitions (blocks vs input_length tokens, excluding the partial tail block, per-request averaging) and none closes the gap. Is the released trace the same one used for Table 1, or is there a detail in the hit-rate definition I'm missing?

items.title: [RFC][Data] Add read_hive datasource for Apache Hive
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This RFC proposes an alpha `ray.data.read_hive()` datasource for Apache Hive. It is a separate Ray Data entry point with Hive-specific planning and execution semantics; generic `read_sql()` and Ray's existing table `Catalog` do not by themselves express the HS2 and future routing contract described here.

The initial architecture uses HiveServer2 (HS2) as the compatibility path. Impyla owns HS2 protocol, authentication, sessions, query execution, result fetching, and row decoding. Ray owns datasource planning and execution semantics and converts result batches to Arrow blocks. The initial path does not access Hive Metastore (HMS), table locations, HDFS, object storage, manifests, or data files from Ray workers.

The target architecture also allows a future capability-gated direct-read path for proven table profiles. That path reuses existing Ray table or file readers and is delivered separately. It does not replace the HS2 compatibility path. `write_hive()` is outside this read RFC and requires a separate write and commit design.

## Context and motivation

Ray has generic `read_sql()` support but no Hive-specific datasource contract for table planning, Hive semantics, and future route selection. Hive relations may depend on views, transactions, table-format metadata, partitions, InputFormat, SerDe properties, authorization, and server-side functions. HS2 keeps these semantics with Hive and can use Hive's query planner and server-side optimizations, including projection, predicate, and partition pruning where supported.

Direct reads serve a different need: parallel scans through Ray workers for table profiles whose metadata and storage semantics can be proven compatible with existing Ray readers, such as the Parquet or Avro readers where their source-resolution paths support the profile. This route also changes which identities access table storage, so it requires an explicit capability and security boundary.

Ray issue [#51094](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/51094) and PR [#58253](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/58253) explored metadata-first direct reads; the PR closed without merging. The HS2-only initial boundary is also recorded in [ray-hive issue #1](https://github.com/jiangxt2/ray-hive/issues/1). This proposal takes an HS2-first approach and treats direct reading as a later extension.

## Architectural goals and non-goals

Goals:

- Add a distinct alpha `read_hive()` datasource API.
- Establish HS2 as the initial compatibility path for Hive relations.
- Stream query results incrementally as Arrow blocks while preserving one source operation and preventing transparent replay or mixed result streams.
- Align the datasource architecture with Ray Data's DataSourceV2 direction.
- Define a future route-selection boundary that reuses existing Ray readers only when table capabilities are proven.

Non-goals:

- Full Hadoop InputFormat or Hive SerDe compatibility.
- New physical-format readers as part of Hive support.
- Ray-side file parallelism for HS2 result streams.
- Automatic query splitting or runtime switching between HS2 and direct reads.
- Spark/Flink-level Hive compatibility.
- A Ray-owned TCLIService client or `write_hive()`.

## Architecture and responsibilities

| Area | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `read_hive()` | Provide a distinct Hive-oriented datasource entry point. Its exact signature and option model are implementation decisions. |
| Hive planning | Resolve the requested relation and the metadata needed to determine schema and route. Planning must not require executing the data query a second time. |
| HS2 execution | Preserve Hive-side relation semantics and consume one result stream. The initial release uses this path and does not give Ray workers direct table-storage access. |
| Direct execution (future) | Select an existing Ray table or file reader only for a proven compatible profile. Unknown or unsupported profiles remain on HS2. |
| Ray Data integration | Fit the evolving DataSourceV2 architecture and use Ray's datasource execution, block, resource, pushdown, and cancellation capabilities where applicable. The concrete adapter and integration seam are left to implementation with Ray Data maintainers. |

The initial raw-SQL scope requires that the result schema be available without a second data-query execution; schema probing by re-running arbitrary SQL is outside the initial strict path. The exact public call shape is not fixed by this RFC.

A strict HS2 read represents one Hive data query and one result stream. Results are consumed incrementally. If connection, query, fetch, or decoding fails, the read fails rather than replaying the query or appending another stream. The datasource does not claim a stronger snapshot guarantee than Hive provides for the operation.

Ray's existing `Catalog` abstraction may be reused by a future direct route when it can resolve the source and credentials required by an existing reader. Hive relation classification and capability decisions remain part of Hive planning. The RFC does not prescribe a new Catalog interface.

## Client, compatibility, and security boundaries

Impyla is an optional dependency loaded when Hive support is used. Its exact version constraint and the concrete connection configuration are implementation decisions. The initial authentication profiles are binary NOSASL, PLAIN for Hive `NONE`, and Kerberos/GSSAPI; LDAP with TLS and HTTP profiles are staged follow-ups and require corresponding real-Hive evidence. `NONE` and `NOSASL` remain distinct.

For TLS-enabled profiles, the caller must configure certificate and server identity verification through `connection_factory`. Kerberos credentials are provided by the runtime environment; the datasource does not add credential acquisition or renewal. Compatibility claims for Hive versions, authentication, result types, and lifecycle behavior are limited to profiles covered by real integration evidence.

The HS2 reader uses generic

comments.body:
> OK, what’s the reason to have both direct-read and HS2?
> 
> is HS2 primarily like read_sql? I am wondering if it makes sense to only
> have a Catalog object that we can pass into parquet/sql/etc readers?

My current thinking is that the two paths address different compatibility and performance requirements, but I agree that the boundary between HiveCatalog, read_sql(), and read_hive() needs further discussion.

For direct reads, my existing design is already Catalog-first: Hive metadata is used to resolve and classify a table, and a sufficiently validated profile can then reuse existing readers such as read_parquet() and read_avro(). This path is intended for large table scans and would only be enabled for explicitly allowlisted profiles.

I currently see HS2 as the general compatibility path, which is closer to read_sql(). It is needed for views, transactional tables, custom SerDes/InputFormats, server-side functions, and cases where direct storage semantics cannot be proven. This path is primarily compatibility-oriented and does not provide Ray-side file-level parallelism.

The open question is whether the HS2 path should be implemented as a separate read_hive() datasource or expressed through a HiveCatalog plus read_sql(). Compared with generic read_sql(), the Hive-specific path may still need Hive-relation metadata handling, HS2-specific connection/authentication configuration, and strict single-operation and incremental-read semantics.

I would appreciate your thoughts on this.

Another benefit of the HS2 path is that it can leverage Hive’s SQL planner and execution engine, including predicate pushdown, projection pruning, partition pruning, and other server-side optimizations where supported. These capabilities, together with Hive-specific semantics, cannot generally be reproduced by a pure file-level scan.

items.title: [data] Umbrella: query optimizer gaps identified by TPC-H benchmarking
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

While benchmarking Ray Data on the full TPC-H suite (sf1000), we identified a set of query optimizations that Ray Data can and should perform but currently doesn't.

Main idea: a query planner should skip shuffles it can prove unnecessary, shrink data before every shuffle using every predicate it can find or derive, and compute shared work once. Ray Data currently does none of these: every join and group-by shuffles unconditionally, and the TPC-H benchmark scripts hand-write the optimizations the planner should perform (e.g. manual `select_columns`, manual filter placement, manual `.materialize()` for common subtrees).

### Sub-issues

| # | Optimization | Queries | Priority | Issue |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Shuffle elimination for co-partitioned data (physical property propagation) | q3, q13, q18 | P0 | #66830 |
| 2 | Top-N: push Limit through Sort | q2, q18, q21 | P0 | #66831 |
| 3 | Two-sided predicate pushdown through joins | q7 | P0 | #66832 |
| 4 | Column pruning derivation through joins | every query | P0 | #66833 |
| 5 | Join `condition` slot + equi-join key extraction | q2, q5 | P0 | #66834 |
| 6 | Residual (non-equi) join predicate evaluated at probe time | q7, q17, q20 | P1 | #66835 |
| 7 | Eager aggregation (partial aggregate pushdown below join) | q3 | P1 | #66836 |
| 8 | Subplan reuse (plan-DAG CSE) | q2, q7 | P1 | #66837 |
| 9 | Broadcast join | all small-dimension joins | P1 | #66838 |
| 10 | Runtime (Bloom) filters Join | q7 | P2 | #66839 |

Are there any footguns when using TMA store?

Are there still fenceproxy requirements when using TMA store?  It seems in the `release/3.3x` branch of triton that `tl.extra.cuda.experimental_tensormap_fenceproxy_acquire(desc)` was removed?

Reason I ask is I have a kernel that is using TMA store that works on the majority of test cases of varying shape, `seqlen x hidden_size` where `128 < seqlen < 1024` and `hidden_size` is `16-byte` aligned, but randomly fails, as in the output does not match that of a reference implementation.  

If I run the tests with the same random seed several times in a row (e.g., pytest --lf ...), it succeeds eventually.

I'm using the kernel TMA descriptor API since the shape of the tensor is determined at runtime based on the number of tokens assigned to an expert (MoE) in order to predicate stores to only that expert's tokens in a persistent kernel that loops over all experts.

I've thoroughly tested my kernel without TMA store enabled, and tests always pass so I'm absolutely certain that the kernel implementation is correct.  The fact that the kernel succeeds for the majority of test cases with TMA store enabled leads me to believe that the indexing for the descriptor is correct, but confused as to why it fails randomly?  FWIW, I'm also using kernel descriptor TMA loads, and these tests always pass for these configurations.

items.title: [Bug]: ~6 s fixed per-request latency on sm120 (4x RTX 5060 Ti TP4) with Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN NVFP4 27B — 1.3.0rc29
items.author: sean640112
items.body_excerpt:
# ~6 s fixed per-request latency floor on sm120 (4× RTX 5060 Ti, TP4) with a Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN 27B NVFP4 checkpoint

## Summary

On a 4× RTX 5060 Ti (sm120) box serving a **dense hybrid GDN + full-attention 27B** NVFP4 checkpoint with `trtllm-serve` (PyTorch backend, TP4), we measure a **~6 s per-request floor on time-to-first-token that is independent of prompt length**. A 212-token request takes **6.06 s** to first token (8.0 s total), and the floor persists at every length we tested (212 → 59,571 tokens). Requests are reproducible to ±5 ms across 12 measurements in 3 separate server starts.

The same hardware, same checkpoint, same prompt, same client, served by SGLang gives **0.26–0.30 s** for the identical request. `trtllm-serve` therefore looks ~20× slower on short requests, while its *marginal* prefill throughput is only ~2.6× lower (~2,143 tok/s vs ~5,600 tok/s).

We have ruled out MTP/spec-decode, scheduler policy, `max_seq_len`, chunked prefill, the CUDA caching allocator, and thinking-mode as causes (details below). We would like to know whether this per-request floor is **expected on sm120 for hybrid GDN models**, or a bug — and which knob/diagnostic we should look at next. We are happy to run any instrumentation you suggest.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | 4× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, compute capability **12.0 (sm120)**, TP=4 |
| Driver | 610.57.04 |
| CUDA toolkit | 13.3 (`nvcc` 13.3, `CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3`) |
| OS / Python | Linux, Python 3.12.11 (venv) |
| TensorRT-LLM | **1.3.0rc29.dev202609240000** (nightly from 2026-09-24; PyPI 1.2.1 does not contain `modeling_qwen3_5.py`, hence nightly) |
| torch | 2.14.0+cu132 |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.18 |
| triton | 3.8.0 |
| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | 4.8.0.dev0 |
| tensorrt / tensorrt_cu13 | 10.14.1.48.post1 |
| MPI | OpenMPI 5.0.10 (`mpi4py` bootstrap path) |
| Model | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` — `architectures: ["Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration"]`, `model_type: qwen3_5`; 64 layers, hidden 5120, 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads |
| Quantization | ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: **FP8 per-tensor on 208 layers** (`block_size` absent) + **NVFP4 `group_size: 16` on 193 layers**, `kv_cache_quant_algo: null` |

Note on the attention backend: your hardware support matrix lists sm120 as supporting NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 (per-tensor) / FP8 KV cache, which covers this checkpoint's formats — so the quantization scheme itself should be fully supported on sm120.

## How to reproduce

Server (the `mpirun -n 1` wrapper and `OMPI_MCA_*` are needed on this host because `import tensorrt_llm` otherwise blocks in the mpi4py `MPI.COMM_WORLD` initialization, and this host's own hostname resolves to loopback only):

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3
export OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include=lo OMPI_MCA_oob_tcp_if_include=lo
mpirun -n 1 --oversubscribe trtllm-serve serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 --tp_size 4 \
  --max_seq_len 140000 --max_batch_size 8 \
  --served_model_name qwen3.8-27b \
  --free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.80 \
  --extra_llm_api_options opts.yaml
```

`opts.yaml`:
```yaml
enable_chunked_prefill: true
max_num_tokens: 8192
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: MTP
  max_draft_len: 3
  speculative_model: /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

Client — a minimal stdlib-only streaming client (this is the "probe" used for every number below; it measures the first chunk that carries `choices[0].text`/`delta.content`):

```python
import json, time, urllib.request
prompt = open("/path/to/corpus.txt").read()[:600]          # → 212 tokens
body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, "stream": True}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/completions",
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
t0 = time.time(); ttft = None
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
    for raw in r:
        s = raw.decode().strip()
        if not s.startswith("data: "): continue
        if s[6:] == "[DONE]": break
        d = json.loads(s[6:])
        ch = d.get("choices") or []
        if ch and ch[0].get("text"):
            ttft = time.time() - t0; break
print("TTFT", ttft)
```

## Measured results (same probe, same prompts, same box)

| prompt tokens | path | TRT-LLM stream TTFT | TRT-LLM non-stream total | SGLang stream TTFT | SGLang non-stream total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **212** | completions | **6.053–6.062 s** (n=5) | 7.995–8.035 s | **0.262 s** | 0.304 s |
| 222 | chat (medium template) | 12.11 – **22.21 s** (unstable across restarts) | 14.06 – 26.19 s | 0.268 s | — |
| 7,172 | completions | 10.10 s | 12.02 s | 0.243 s *cached* | 1.84 s *cached* |
| 12,131 | completions | 12.12 s | 14.06 s | — | — |
| 28,008 | completions | — | 20.13 s | — | 6.15 s *cached* |
| 59,571 | completions | — | 36.26 s | — | — |
| 65,032 | chat | 56.52 s | 56.45 s | — | — |

*("cached" = the SGLang side hit its radix prefix cache on the shared corpus prefix, so those cells are not a like-for-like prefill comparison.)*

Least-squares fit of the completions path (`total = C + N/R`, 5 points spanning 212 → 59,571 tokens):
**C = 8.10 s, R = 2,143 tok/s, R² = 0.9966** — i.e. a very large constant plus a modest rate term. (The streaming TTFT is ≈ 1.9 s lower at every point, i.e. TTFT ≈ 6.1 s + N/2143.)

For reference, an independent client (vLLM's `bench serve` against the same server) measured prefill throughput of **453 / 1,014 / 1,302 tok/s** at 8K / 32K / 64K with meanTTFT 16.15 / 29.28 / 46.44 s, i.e. the same shape: mostly a constant, with the rate part improving with length.

The SGLang side on this box (same checkpoint, TP4, DFlash2, fp8 KV, same client) measures ~5,600 tok/s marginal prefill and a per-request overhead of ≲0.3 s. So the fixed component, not the rate, is what dominates short requests for us.

## What we ruled out (each was an actual A/B on a server restart)

| Variant | tiny-request TTFT | 8K-prefill |
|---|---|-

items.title: [Feature]: VisualGen MiniMax-H3: support AdaLN-pruned checkpoints (multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned)
items.author: atokayev
items.body_excerpt:
### The feature, motivation and pitch

Please add support for the community AdaLN-pruned MiniMax-H3 checkpoint ([multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned](https://huggingface.co/multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned)) in the VisualGen MiniMax-H3 pipeline.

**Motivation.** The pruned transformer is 40 GiB instead of 66 GiB (39% fewer parameters), and the text encoder is truncated from 66.7 to 52.5 GB. In diffusers this makes MiniMax-H3 fit one 80 GB H100 (see below), which the stock checkpoint cannot do in VisualGen today (weights alone are about 104 GiB with an FP8 transformer, and there is no CPU offload for H3; see #13893).

**Current behavior (1.3.0rc29, 1x H200).** `VisualGen(model=<dir>)` detects the MiniMax-H3 pipeline and reads the weights, then `MiniMaxH3Transformer.load_weights` fails:

```
ValueError: MiniMax-H3 checkpoint is missing 55 required tensors:
time_embedder.linear_1.weight, time_embedder.linear_1.bias,
time_embedder.linear_2.weight, time_embedder.linear_2.bias,
transformer_blocks.0.adaln_proj.linear.bias, ...
  tensorrt_llm/_torch/visual_gen/models/minimax_h3/transformer_minimax_h3.py:859
```

**Why.** The pruned checkpoint stores AdaLN differently:

| | Stock | Pruned |
|---|---|---|
| Time embedding | `time_embedder.linear_1/2` (MLP) | `time_embedder.table` (precomputed, 1025 entries) |
| `adaln_proj.linear.weight` | (96768, 2688) | (96768, 8) |
| `adaln_proj` bias | `adaln_proj.linear.bias` | `adaln_proj.folded_bias` |
| Extra tensors | none | `adaln_basis` [8, 2688], `adaln_mean` [2688] (in `transformer/adaln_affine.safetensors`) |
| Transformer config | stock | custom class `MiniMaxH3PrunedTransformer3DModel` (`auto_map`), `adaln_rank: 8`, `num_layers: 50` |

The reference implementation is `modeling_minimax_h3_pruned.py` in the pruned repo. Expanding the weights back to the stock shapes would make the loader pass but restores the 66 GiB transformer, so it does not help. The useful change is a rank-8 AdaLN and time-table path in the transformer.

**Reproduction.**
1. Build a model directory with the stock `vae`, `scheduler`, `audio_scheduler`, `audio_vae`, `tokenizer`, `processor` and `modular_model_index.json` from `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3`, and the `transformer/` and `text_encoder/` from `multimodalart/MiniMax-H3-Pruned`.
2. Run `VisualGen(model=<dir>, args=VisualGenArgs.from_yaml("cfg.yaml"))` with `quant_config: {quant_algo: FP8, dynamic: true}`, `attention_config: {backend: FA4}`, resolution 480x832, 124 frames.

**Measured with the pruned weights in diffusers** (modular pipeline, 832x480, 124 frames, 28 steps, seed 42, 8 prompts, 1x H200):
- Cost: 9.5 GPU-s per video-s vs 20.9 for the stock checkpoint, both with CPU offload (2.2x). This is not a comparison with TensorRT-LLM.
- Quality vs stock: VBench composite +0.003 (95% paired-bootstrap interval -0.000 to +0.006); LPIPS 0.146, similar to the 0.149 between two stock runs on different engines. Only 8 prompts and one seed.
- Memory on an emulated 80 GB H100 (driver-reported free memory capped; real H100 not tested): peak 52.6 GiB at 960x544 and 53.4 GiB at 1344x768 with automatic CPU offload. The stock checkpoint peaks at 76.8 GiB there.

### Alternatives

- **CPU offload in VisualGen (#13893):** would also help H100 fit, but costs latency; pruning shrinks the weights themselves.
- **Quantized pruned variants** (SDNQ, GGUF, NVFP4 builds exist on Hugging Face) use formats VisualGen does not load.
- **Converter to the stock layout:** loads, but gives back the full transformer size.

### Additional context

- Related: #13893 (offloading for visual_gen) and the open PR #19772 (fuses MiniMax-H3 AdaLN RMSNorm with per-token modulation), which touches the same AdaLN code a pruned path would change.
- Open question: does the truncated 51-layer text encoder load in VisualGen? The failure occurs before that point.
- The FastH3 4-step adapter also expects the original AdaLN width, so we have not tested pruned + distilled in any engine.
- Environment: TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29 (NGC image), 1x H200, includes the MiniMax-H3 support from #18733.

<details>
<summary>Trimmed log (TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, 1x H200)</summary>

```

items.title: [Feature]: Whisper serving parity in trtllm-serve — /v1/audio/transcriptions, long-form audio, verbose_json segments, decoder biasing
items.author: ravo42-maker
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`openai/whisper-large-v3` runs on the PyTorch backend once the pending KV-cache fixes land (#19302 for #18609 / #19515, #19516 for #19514), and the engine itself is fast: on an RTX 5070 Ti, fp16, 0.34 s per 30 s clip warm (~87x realtime; ~14x for faster-whisper large-v3 float32 on the same clip). But it is still not usable as a drop-in STT service, because the serving layer is missing. Our use case is clinical dictation (10–20 minute recordings), currently served by faster-whisper and vLLM; every gap below is something those two already provide. Ordered by how blocking it is:

1. **`/v1/audio/transcriptions` (and `/v1/audio/translations`) in `trtllm-serve`.** Today audio reaches the model only through `/v1/chat/completions` with `input_audio` or the Python `LLM` API. Every OpenAI-compatible STT client uses the audio route: multipart `file`, `model`, `language`, `prompt`, `temperature`, `response_format`, `timestamp_granularities`. Nothing under `tensorrt_llm/serve/` implements it on current `main`.

2. **Long-form audio.** `WhisperInputProcessor` accepts exactly one clip of at most `max_source_positions` (1500 frames = 30 s) and rejects longer input with "chunk the audio" (`modeling_whisper.py`, the `max_audio_seconds` check). A 16-minute file needs windowing on the server, ideally seek-based — the next window starts at the last complete segment's end timestamp, as openai/whisper and faster-whisper do. Fixed pre-cut 30 s chunks lose words at mid-sentence cuts (vllm-project/vllm#58029 documents that failure mode), so this depends on item 3.

3. **`verbose_json` output: per-segment `start`/`end`, `text`, `avg_logprob`, `compression_ratio`** (and `no_speech_prob` where available). The input processor currently forces `<|notimestamps|>` in the decoder prompt, so timestamps are never produced. Per-segment `compression_ratio` is what production pipelines use to detect Whisper's repetition loops; without it the service cannot be monitored.

4. **Decoder biasing:** `prompt` (previous-text conditioning across windows) and a `hotwords`-style bias for proper nouns. faster-whisper exposes both; vLLM accepts `hotwords`.

5. **Whisper-specific input validation.** A user-supplied `max_seq_len` below `max_source_positions` should be rejected: with `max_batch_size=2` it fails at the micro-batch scheduler, but with `max_batch_size=8` it passes and silently drops phrases from the transcript (details in #19514).

Items 1 and 3 are the ones that would let a maintainer or contributor close the gap to vLLM's `/v1/audio/transcriptions`; 2 builds on 3; 4 and 5 are independent.

### Alternatives

A thin service in front of the `LLM` API that does windowing, emits segment timestamps and emulates the OpenAI response shape. That duplicates what vLLM already ships and every TensorRT-LLM Whisper user would have to write it.

### Additional context

Hardware verification runs, the rc25 + patch wheel and the repro kit are described in #18609, #19450, #19514, #19515, #19516 and in the #19302 thread. Happy to test any of the above on sm_120 and on real multi-minute dictations.

items.title: SubbyteReference breaks its offset invariant for negative offsets (constructor and operator+=)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SubbyteReference` (both the primary template and the `StorageVec` partial specialization in include/cutlass/subbyte_reference.h) mishandles **negative** offsets: the constructor and `operator+=` with a negative argument use truncating division without normalizing, leaving the object in a state that violates its own invariant.

Verified by execution on a minimal host build (Storage = uint8_t, Element = int4b_t):

```
control  -= (+3)  : storage_delta=-2 off=1   get=-3   correct
case B   += (-3)  : storage_delta=-1 off=-1            (invariant requires off in [0, 1])
FAIL: += negative breaks offset_ invariant
case C   ctor(ptr, -3): storage_delta=-1 off=-1        same broken state
```

Correct state for element -3 is one storage unit further back (`storage_delta == -2`, `offset_ == 1`). Instead `offset_ < 0`, and any subsequent `get()`/`set()` shifts by a negative bit count (undefined behavior) or reads the wrong nibble. The mirrored `operator-=` with a positive argument is correct - its borrow logic compensates - which is why only the negative-input paths were affected.

Reachability: `TensorRef::operator-(coord)` and negative `add_pointer_offset` feed this constructor through `ReferenceFactory` for sub-byte tensors. Nothing in-tree navigates sub-byte tensors backward across vector boundaries today, so this is latent public-API breakage.

### Suggested fix

Normalize negative deltas exactly like the positive path does: fold the current `offset_` in first, then use floor-style division/borrow so that the postcondition `0 <= offset_ < kElementsPerVector` always holds.

items.title: Collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on `gloo` and raise `Invalid scalar type`
items.author: sadra-barikbin
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Hi, collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on backend `gloo`. Actually `GENERATE_ALL_TYPES` macro in `torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupGloo.cpp` seems to raise `RuntimeError: Invalid scalar type`.

To reproduce:
```python
import torch.distributed as dist

tensor = torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    gather_list = [torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]
else:
    gather_list = None
dist.gather(tensor, gather_list)
```
This is also the case for `all_gather`, `reduce`, `all_reduce` and `broadcast`. Changing `dtype=torch.bool` to `dtype=torch.uint8` resolves the error, while `torch.bool == torch.uint8` evaluates to `True`.

items.title: [dynamo] torch.compile: StreamContextVariable.python_type() hardcoded to torch.cuda.StreamContext, returns wrong type for XPU/NPU
items.author: hitluo
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## 🐛 Bug

Under `torch.compile`, `StreamContextVariable.python_type()` always returns `torch.cuda.StreamContext` regardless of the actual device. This means `isinstance(ctx, torch.<device>.StreamContext)` inside a compiled function returns `False` even when `ctx` **is** an XPU/NPU stream context, and attribute lookups on the context object resolve along the wrong MRO.

The bug is **latent**: `python_type()` is only consumed during tracing when user code performs a type check (`isinstance`/`type()`) or attribute access (`ctx.stream`) on a `StreamContext` object inside the compiled function. The normal `with stream(s):` path (create → enter → body → exit) never calls `python_type()`, so the defect is invisible unless the user inspects the context object.

## To Reproduce

### PrivateUse1 backend (torch_npu on Ascend NPU) — verified

```python
import torch, torch_npu
from torch_npu.utils._dynamo import add_dynamo_methods_init
add_dynamo_methods_init()

@torch.compile(backend="eager", fullgraph=True)
def fn(s):
    ctx = torch.npu.stream(s)
    return torch.ones(2).npu() if isinstance(ctx, torch.npu.StreamContext) else torch.zeros(2).npu()

s = torch.npu.Stream()
res = fn(s)
# Expected: tensor([1., 1.], device='npu:0')
# Actual:   tensor([0., 0.], device='npu:0')  — isinstance returns False
```

#### Actual test output (torch 2.15.0.dev20260917+cpu, torch_npu 2.15.0.dev20260917, Ascend NPU):

```
STEP 1: Verify bug in source code
StreamContextVariable.python_type source:
    def python_type(self) -> type:
        return torch.cuda.StreamContext
[BUG CONFIRMED] python_type() hardcodes torch.cuda.StreamContext

STEP 5: NPU isinstance test
[BUG] NPU isinstance returned False (wrong!)
  result: tensor([0., 0.], device='npu:0')
  expected: tensor([1., 1.], device='npu:0')

SUMMARY:
  source_check                   PASS
  npu_isinstance                 FAIL/BUG
BUG CONFIRMED: StreamContextVariable.python_type() is hardcoded to torch.cuda.StreamContext
```

> Note: `add_dynamo_methods_init()` is required when using `backend="eager"` (it registers NPU stream handlers that would otherwise only be applied during inductor backend initialization). With `backend="inductor"`, the call is not needed.

## Expected behavior

`StreamContextVariable.python_type()` should return the device-specific `StreamContext` type:

| Device | `python_type()` should return | Currently returns (bug) |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA | `torch.cuda.StreamContext` | `torch.cuda.StreamContext` ✅ (correct by accident) |
| XPU | `torch.xpu.StreamContext` | `torch.cuda.StreamContext` ❌ |
| NPU | `torch.npu.StreamContext` | `torch.cuda.StreamContext` ❌ |

A device-agnostic dispatch (either runtime derivation from the stream's device module, or a subclass-override mechanism symmetric with the existing `_cpython_type` pattern) would make `python_type()` correct for all devices without hardcoding any single backend's type.

## Root cause

- **`torch/_dynamo/variables/streams.py`**: `StreamContextVariable.python_type()` hardcodes `return torch.cuda.StreamContext` for all stream context variables, regardless of device:

  ```python
  class StreamContextVariable(FxTracebackAnnotateVariable):
      """This represents torch.cuda.StreamContext"""
      ...
      def python_type(self) -> type:
          return torch.cuda.StreamContext
  ```

  The base `StreamContextVariable` is shared by CUDA and XPU (XPU has no dedicated subclass — it is created via the device-interface handler `handle_device_interface_stream` in `torch/_dynamo/variables/torch.py`), so the CUDA hardcode makes it incorrect for all non-CUDA devices.

- **No subclass override for PrivateUse1**: PrivateUse1 backends (e.g. NPU) define a `NpuStreamContextVariable(StreamContextVariable)` subclass in their out-of-tree packages, but this subclass does **not** override `python_type()`, so it inherits the CUDA hardcode. There is no extension mechanism for out-of-tree backends to supply their device-specific `StreamContext` type — the base class has no overridable slot (unlike `StreamVariable`, which already has the `_cpython_type` class attribute pattern).

- **`python_type()` consumers affected**: The method is consumed during tracing by:
  - `object_generic_getattr` (`torch/_dynamo/variables/object_protocol.py`) — attribute lookup walks the MRO of the type returned by `python_type()`, so `ctx.stream` resolves along `torch.cuda.StreamContext`'s MRO instead of the correct device's `StreamContext` MRO.
  - Type-based dispatch (`torch/_dynamo/guards.py` and `torch/_dynamo/symbolic_convert.py`) — `isinstance(ctx, torch.npu.StreamContext)` compares against `python_type()`, returning `False` when it should be `True`.

  Note: `python_type()` does **not** participate in guard evaluation (`TYPE_MATCH` records `type(value)`, not `python_type()`), so the bug does not cause guard failures or recompilation — it silently produces wrong tracing results or graph breaks.

### Versions

PyTorch: 2.15.0.dev20260917+cpu (current main branch); also affects 2.13.0+. Backend: torch_npu 2.15.0.dev20260917 (Ascend NPU). The NPU reproduction was verified on an Ascend NPU container with torch 2.15.0.dev + torch_npu 2.15.0.dev.

items.title: `AOTAutograd` ignores `guess_tangent_strides_as_outputs` under dynamic shapes
items.author: qgallouedec
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Found while trying to optimize Qwen3.5 packed training on B300 with [trl](https://github.com/huggingface/trl) (core maintainer here 👋). 

With dynamic shapes, `MemoryFormatMeta.from_tensor` only records `suggest_memory_format(t)` for tensors with symbolic sizes ("Support for symbolic shapes is not implemented yet"), so `guess_tangent_strides_as_outputs` (#173313, #184922) doesn't apply (limitation already listed in #144579): a 3D transposed output gets its tangent coerced to contiguous.
A compiled region returning `proj(x).transpose(1, 2)` (as gated-DeltaNet layers do before the causal-conv1d extension) then copies the incoming gradient into the transposed layout, and the weight-gradient GEMM reads it with leading dimension `T`, off cuBLAS' fast path when `T % 8 != 0`.

```python
import time

import torch

C, H = 6144, 2048
w = torch.randn(C, H, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)


def proj(x):
    return (x @ w.t()).transpose(1, 2)  # (1, C, T), strides (C*T, 1, C)


for dynamic in (False, True):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    f = torch.compile(proj, dynamic=dynamic)
    for T in (16384, 16383):
        x = torch.randn(1, T, H, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        g = torch.randn(1, T, C, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)

        def step():
            (f(x).transpose(1, 2) * g).sum().backward()  # eager consumer, channel-last gradient

        for _ in range(3):
            step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(20):
            step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        print(f"dynamic={dynamic} T={T}: {(time.perf_counter() - t0) / 20 * 1e3:.2f} ms")
```

```
                      T=16384    T=16383
dynamic=False         0.82 ms    0.81 ms
dynamic=True          0.88 ms    3.06 ms
```

On 2.13, the dynamic backward graph asserts `tangents_1` as `(1, 6144, s0)` with strides `(6144*s0, s0, 1)`; the static one expects the output's strides `(…, 1, 6144)`.

### Expected

Dynamic shapes behave like static ones. 

Recording the output's dim order (valid for any symbolic sizes) and laying the tangent out in that order at trace and run time does it: with a local monkeypatch of `from_tensor`, `coerce_tangent_and_suggest_memory_format` and `coerce_to_expected_memory_format`, the repro gives 0.82 ms for every `T` on 2.13, and compiled packed SFT on one B300 goes :
- 1.29x faster on Qwen3.5-2B,
- 1.26x on Qwen3.5-9B,
- 1.17x on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B LoRA, and
- 1.32x on Qwen3.5-9B DDP over 8 GPUs.

(The repro and this report were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude Code); I ran and reviewed them.)

items.title: [Serve] Upcoming Changes in Ray Serve 2.55+
items.author: abrarsheikh
items.body_excerpt:
The following changes are planned for the next several Ray Serve releases. Please review and prepare your applications accordingly.

* Pydantic v1 support will be removed. Ray Serve will require Pydantic v2. If you are still on Pydantic v1, upgrade now with pip install \-U pydantic. See [\#58876](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/58876) for migration details.  
* Sync deployment methods will run in a threadpool by default. Synchronous user code will be executed in a threadpool rather than blocking the event loop, improving concurrency for sync handlers. If your deployment relies on the current single-threaded behavior, you should set `max_ongoing_requests=1` on the deployment.  
* We are replacing the current Ray Serve HTTP Proxy with a more optimized ingress layer. This change means that the ingress deployment will no longer support model multiplexing or custom request routing. While this new ingress layer will be opt-in for several Ray versions, we strongly advise moving any multiplexing logic or custom request routing policy to downstream deployments.   
* `RAY_SERVE_RUN_USER_CODE_IN_SEPARATE_THREAD` will default to 0\. User code will run in the same thread as the replica event loop by default. If your deployment depends on user code running in a separate thread, explicitly set `RAY_SERVE_RUN_USER_CODE_IN_SEPARATE_THREAD=1`.  
* `RAY_SERVE_RUN_ROUTER_IN_SEPARATE_LOOP` will default to 0\. The request router will run in the same event loop as the proxy/replica by default. If your setup requires a separate router loop, explicitly set `RAY_SERVE_RUN_ROUTER_IN_SEPARATE_LOOP=1`.

items.title: [RLlib] MultiAgentEpisode marks the episode terminated when a new agent joins on the step the last registered agent terminates (despite __all__=False)
items.author: WiemKhlifi
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

In a `MultiAgentEnv` if a new agent's **first** observation arrives on the **same step** the last already-registered agents terminate, `MultiAgentEpisode.add_env_step` declares the episode terminated, although the env returned `terminateds["__all__"] = False`. The new agent's observation is discarded, and under `batch_mode="truncate_episodes"` the `MultiAgentEnvRunner` then steps the still-live, un-reset env with an **empty action dict** (runner declares a new episode when it's still the same one). Envs that validate their actions crash the EnvRunner (`having_actions=set() does not cover all actions in needing_actions={...}` in our case).

**Expected:** the episode stays open (the env said so) and the new agent is registered.

**Why:** the "Case 2" check runs over agents that are **already registered** ([`multi_agent_episode.py#L413-L416`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L413-L416); [`agent_ids`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L1008-L1011) is `agent_episodes.keys()`):

```python
self.is_terminated = terminateds.get("__all__", False)       # False
...
if all(aid in set(agents_done) for aid in self.agent_ids):   # newcomer not registered yet
    self.is_terminated = True                                # overrides the env
```

The newcomer is only registered later in the same method ([`#L532`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L532)), so it can't veto the check, and its first observation falls into the "already done" branch ([`#L509-L516`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L509-L516)). 

`SyncVectorMultiAgentEnv` arms its autoreset from the env's own `__all__` ([`#L140-L145`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/vector/sync_vector_multi_agent_env.py#L140-L145)), so the env is not reset, and the runner sends `{}` into it ([`multi_agent_env_runner.py#L389-L403`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_env_runner.py#L389-L403)). 
In our case we were using the `batch_mode=complete_episodes` which only hides the crash.

This looks like the case the class's own TODO already anticipates ([`#L30-L31`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/rllib/env/multi_agent_episode.py#L30-L31)): `# TODO (simon): Include cases in which the number of agents in an episode are shrinking or growing during the episode itself.`

**Suggested fix** (`multi_agent_episode.py#L415`): count agents that report an observation in this step as present.

```python
if all(aid in agents_done for aid in self.agent_ids | set(observations)):
```

This keeps the episode open at the handover and leaves the intended Case 2 behavior (every agent finished, some terminated, some truncated) unchanged. Happy to open a PR with the reproduction below as a test in `rllib/env/tests/test_multi_agent_episode.py`.


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.58.0 (also reproduced on 2.57.0)
- Python 3.13, gymnasium 1.2.2
- Tried it on both: Linux (Kubernetes) and macOS

### Reproduction script

```python
import numpy as np
from ray.rllib.env.multi_agent_episode import MultiAgentEpisode

eps = MultiAgentEpisode(agent_module_ids={"a0": "p", "a1": "p"})
eps.add_env_reset(observations={"a0": np.zeros(1, np.float32)}, infos={"a0": {}})

# One step: a0 terminates, a1 sends its FIRST observation, env says NOT done.
eps.add_env_step(
    observations={"a0": np.zeros(1, np.float32), "a1": np.ones(1, np.float32)},
    actions={"a0": 0},
    rewards={"a0": 1.0, "a1": 0.0},
    infos={"a0": {}, "a1": {}},
    terminateds={"a0": True, "__all__": False},
    truncateds={"__all__": False},
)
print(eps.is_terminated, sorted(eps.agent_ids), eps.get_terminateds())
```

Output on 2.58.0:

```
True ['a0'] {'a0': True, '__all__': True}
```

Expected:

```
False ['a0', 'a1'] {'a0': True, '__all__': False}
```

A full `MultiAgentEnvRunner` reproduction (PPO, `truncate_episodes`, a toy env that validates its action dict) that crashes on the empty action dict is available on request:

```
ActionsMissing: env step t=5: having_actions=set() does not cover all actions in needing_actions={'a1'} (live agents={'a1'})
```

items.title: [Data] Support optional query-schema inference in read_hive
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Track optional query-schema inference as a follow-up to [PR #66573](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66573). This extends the HS2 read path described in [RFC #65978](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65978) while preserving its requirement that schema inference must not execute the data query a second time.

The reader proposed in #66573 requires an explicit `pyarrow.Schema` for query reads. Its current DataSourceV2 path needs a concrete schema during planning on the driver, before the read worker executes the query. HiveServer2 provides result metadata through Impyla's `cursor.description` after execution and before fetching rows, but that metadata is not available to the current planning path.

The requested behavior is:

- Allow query reads without a caller-supplied schema and infer the Arrow schema from the result metadata of the same query execution used to fetch rows.
- Do not submit a separate schema-probing data query or execute the SQL twice.
- When the caller supplies a schema, retain it as the output schema and preserve the existing validation of column count, order, case-insensitive column names, types, and non-nullable fields.
- Preserve schema information for empty result sets.

This requires agreeing on how the DataSourceV2 path handles a schema that becomes available during execution. Query splitting, retries, direct storage reads, and additional Hive type support are outside this issue.

Related to [PR #66573](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66573) and [RFC #65978](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65978).

### Use case

Users running trusted SQL queries should not need to manually reproduce result schemas that HiveServer2 already provides, including schemas for expressions, aliases, and aggregates. Users who need an explicit output contract should still be able to supply a schema and receive validation errors when the query result does not match it.

items.title: [Data] Make null ordering consistent between Arrow/Pandas and Polars sort
items.author: viiccwen
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Ray Data's Arrow sort path uses `pyarrow.compute.sort_indices`, and its Pandas path uses `DataFrame.sort_values`. Both place null values last by default.
When `DataContext.use_polars_sort=True`, the Polars path calls `DataFrame.sort(...)` without specifying null placement. Polars places nulls first for both ascending and descending order.

As a result, changing an execution backend flag changes Dataset row order:

```text
ascending, Arrow/Pandas: 1, 2, 3, null
ascending, Polars:       null, 1, 2, 3

descending, Arrow/Pandas: 3, 2, 1, null
descending, Polars:       null, 3, 2, 1
```

This can also change the rows selected by `sort(key).limit(k)`.

### Versions / Dependencies

Sorting the same Dataset should produce the same null placement regardless of whether Ray Data uses Arrow, Pandas, or Polars. Use null-last semantics, which matches the existing Arrow and Pandas behavior.

### Reproduction script

```py
import ray
from ray.data.context import DataContext

ray.init()
ctx = DataContext.get_current()
rows = [{"a": 3}, {"a": None}, {"a": 1}, {"a": 2}]

for use_polars in (False, True):
    ctx.use_polars_sort = use_polars
    result = ray.data.from_items(rows).sort("a").take_all()
    print(use_polars, result)
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [Data] Include input file paths in JSON/JSONL parsing errors
items.author: Yin-1022
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem / Description

When ray.data.read_json() encounters malformed JSON or JSONL input, the resulting parsing error does not identify the source file that causes the failure.

This affects both reading paths:
- ArrowJSONDatasource (lines=False): The fallback to Python's json.load() raises a JSONDecodeError without including the input file path.
- PandasJSONDatasource (lines=True): Pandas parsing failures raise a ValueError without including the input file path.

This might lead to difficulty in debugging when reading multiple files, as users see the parsing error but cannot easily identify which input file is malformed.

For comparison, CSVDatasource does provide a contextual error message containing the offending file path.

## Minimal Reproduction
```
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import ray

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    root = Path(tmp)

    cases = [
        (
            "malformed.json",
            '[{"name": "A", "value": 1}, {"name": "B", "value": }]',
            False,
        ),
        (
            "malformed.jsonl",
            '{"name": "A", "value": 1}\n{"name": "B", "value":\n',
            True,
        ),
    ]

    for filename, content, lines in cases:
        path = root / filename
        path.write_text(content)

        try:
            ray.data.read_json(str(path), lines=lines).materialize()
        except ValueError as e:
            has_path = path.as_posix() in str(e)
            print(f"lines={lines}: file path in exception = {has_path}")
```

### Actual behavior (unmodified Ray):
Both cases fail during parsing, but the resulting exception messages do not include the offending input file path.

### Expected behavior:
The parsing error should identify the file that failed, while preserving the underlying parsing error details.

## Proposal
Add contextual error messages to JSON datasource parsing failures, similar to the existing behavior of CSVDatasource.

The improved errors should:
- Include the input file path that causes the failure.
- Provide a brief format hint appropriate for JSON or line-delimited JSON.
- Preserve the underlying parsing error information and existing exception types where possible.

For example:
```
Failed to read JSON file: /path/to/malformed.json.
Please check that the file contains valid JSON.
```
This would make malformed input files easier to identify, particularly in multi-file or distributed data processing workloads.

items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

items.title: feat: Add AIBrix Chat - a frontend demo portal for LLM inference
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

AIBrix provides powerful infrastructure for LLM inference, but we lack a user-facing demo to showcase its capabilities. Currently, users need to interact with AIBrix through API calls, or third-party clients, which creates friction when:

- Live demos — Presenting AIBrix at conferences, meetups, or internal reviews requires a polished UI
- End-to-end validation — Testing the full stack (gateway routing, model serving, load balancing) benefits from a real frontend client
- Onboarding — A working chat UI makes it easier for new contributors to understand the user-facing value of the infrastructure

### Use Case

Add a lightweight chat portal under apps/chat/web/ that serves as both a demo and a functional frontend for AIBrix-managed LLM endpoints.

What it includes:
- Chat interface with conversation management (create, search, delete, move)
- Project organization for grouping related conversations
- Model selector supporting multiple backends
- Sidebar navigation with chat history
- Dark-themed, responsive UI built with React + Vite + Tailwind CSS


Architecture:
```
  apps/
  ├── chat/
   │   ├── web/          # React frontend
   │   └── api/          # Backend proxy for LLM endpoints (planned)
```

### Proposed Solution

Why in-repo (not a separate project)?

1. Dogfooding — The chat portal consumes AIBrix gateway APIs directly, validating routing algorithms, model selection, and streaming behavior from a real client

items.title: QuantizedHuggingFaceStorageReader only loads the first 1/32 of each MXFP4 tensor
items.author: haydn-jones
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Was loading `openai/gpt-oss-20b` on torchtitan (uses `QuantizedHuggingFaceStorageReader`) and the model just produced garbage. The MoE expert weights are almost entirely zeros after loading.

The problem is in [read_metadata()](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/7bf52b3a9782d3440a17eb3f00983795f3b12af0/torch/distributed/checkpoint/quantized_hf_storage.py#L58-L81) I think. For the `*_blocks` tensors it rewrites size to the dequantized shape, but leaves the chunk metadata at the quantized `[..., G, B]` shape.

```
size   (32, 2880, 2880)
chunks [((0, 0, 0, 0), (32, 2880, 90, 16))]
```

So when the planner intersects the requested tensor with the stored chunks, the last dim gets clamped to `min(2880, 90)`. Each row only reads its first 90 values and everything after stays at whatever the dest tensor was initialized to.

MRE:

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.quantized_hf_storage import QuantizedHuggingFaceStorageReader

path = "<path to gpt oss>"
key = "model.layers.0.mlp.experts.down_proj_blocks"

m = QuantizedHuggingFaceStorageReader(path=path).read_metadata().state_dict_metadata[key]
print("size  ", tuple(m.size))
print("chunks", [(tuple(c.offsets), tuple(c.sizes)) for c in m.chunks])

t = torch.zeros(tuple(m.size), dtype=torch.bfloat16)
dcp.load({key: t}, storage_reader=QuantizedHuggingFaceStorageReader(path=path), no_dist=True)

print("zero fraction", (t == 0).float().mean().item())
nz = (t != 0).any(dim=0).any(dim=0).nonzero().flatten()
print("nonzero columns:", nz.min().item(), "..", nz.max().item(), "count", nz.numel())
```

Output:

```
size   (32, 2880, 2880)
chunks [((0, 0, 0, 0), (32, 2880, 90, 16))]
zero fraction 0.9724321961402893
nonzero columns: 0 .. 89 count 90
```

I think the fix is to also rewrite each `_blocks` chunk into dequantized coordinates. Sizes `[..., G, B] -> [..., G * B * 2]` and offsets `[..., g0, 0] -> [..., g0 * B * 2]`. I haven't tested this though. 

### Versions

Nightly.

cc @awgu @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @pragupta @msaroufim @dcci @aditvenk @weifengpy @kapilsh @LucasLLC @pradeepfn

items.title: [data] Track output partitioning as a physical property and eliminate redundant shuffles
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #66829.

### Problem

Every `Join` emits `JoinShuffleMap*` and every group-by emits `HashAggregateMap` unconditionally. When a group-by follows a join on the same key (or a superset of it), the data is already colocated and the second shuffle is pure waste.

TPC-H q3 (`tpch_q3.py`):

```py
ds = orders_customer.join(lineitem_filtered, on=("o_orderkey",), right_on=("l_orderkey",))
ds.groupby(["o_orderkey", "o_orderdate", "o_shippriority"]).aggregate(Sum(...))
```

```
Now:        JoinShuffleMap ×2 → JoinReduce            # shuffle 1
            → HashAggregateMap → shuffle → AggReduce  # shuffle 2, same key
Optimized:  JoinShuffleMap ×2 → JoinReduce
            → local HashAggregate(mode=Complete)      # 1 shuffle total
```

### Proposal

Operators declare the partitioning they produce and the distribution they require from their inputs; the planner inserts a shuffle only when the requirement is not already satisfied. Here are the things to do to tackle this:

- [ ] **Property plumbing**: `Join`/`Aggregate` physical ops expose an output-partitioning property; the planner checks it before planning a shuffle. Covers the exact-key case (q3).
- [ ] **Subset-key satisfaction**: partitioning on a subset of the grouping keys satisfies the requirement. Covers q18's 5-column group-by over an `l_orderkey` partitioning, and q13.
- [ ] **One-phase aggregation**: when the distribution is already satisfied, plan a single complete aggregate instead of the partial/final split, skipping the partial-state serialization entirely.

Affected queries: q3, q13, q18 (one full shuffle of the join output each).

items.title: [RFC] Training/Inference Numerical Consistency for RL Post-Training
items.author: shikicloud
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

In RL post-training, the rollout engine samples tokens and the trainer recomputes logprobs on those same tokens with the same weights. When the two disagree, PPO's importance ratio is computed against the wrong denominator; low-probability tokens can spike the ratio and blow up gradients; training can collapse.

Four causes, each with published evidence:

1. **Kernels are not batch-invariant.** The same request can produce different logits depending on what else is in the batch, because RMSNorm/matmul/attention pick their reduction strategy from batch shape ([Thinking Machines, "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference"](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/), 2025-09-10).
2. **MoE routing disagrees between engines even with identical weights** — ~10% of per-layer routing decisions differ, 94% of tokens affected in ≥1 layer, on Qwen3-30B-A3B ([R3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370), arXiv 2510.11370). R3 (#18397) is an initial solution to fix this cause.
3. **LM-head / router precision.** BF16 alone dropped train/inference token-probability correlation to ~0.9; FP32 restored ~0.99 ([MiniMax-M1 tech report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585), arXiv 2506.13585).
4. **Severity is hardware- and kernel-dependent and compounds with length.** Same code: KL ≈ 5e-4–1e-3 on one GPU, 1e-2–1e-1 on another, traced to a specific attention-kernel bug ([ByteDance Seed, "When Speed Kills Stability"](https://yingru.notion.site/When-Speed-Kills-Stability-Demystifying-RL-Collapse-from-the-Training-Inference-Mismatch-271211a558b7808d8b12d403fd15edda)).

R3 addresses cause 2. This RFC covers what's left of R3 (cause 2's remaining edges) plus causes 1, 3, and a sampling-semantics issue that compounds all of them. Other useful features like TIS/MIS/KPop remain in RL frameworks but not inference engines. Futhermore, this RFC targets on important features for TRTLLM, we will explore new features to solve this problem on an new issue.

This RFC is generated by codex with human's instructions and supervision. Also thanks @NolenLiang and @JeffPengCoder's help. CC's @joyang-nv @xuantengh @yuki-97 

## What exists today

- **Router Replay**: `LlmArgs.enable_return_routed_experts` + `SamplingParams.return_routed_experts` → `CompletionOutput.routed_experts`, `int16`, `[seq_len-1, num_moe_layers, top_k]`, pre-EPLB logical ids. Separated-routing MoE backends only; fails closed on PP>1, spec decode, fused routing(TBD).
- **`logprobs_mode`**: `RAW` (pre-sampling-params) / `PROCESSED` (post). No `raw_logits`/`processed_logits` variants.
- **`FORCE_DETERMINISTIC`**: a C++ env var, not exposed via `LlmArgs`. Covers attention multi-block, KV-cache reuse, and all-reduce workspace size. Does not cover autotuner tactic selection, FMHA library selection, all-reduce *strategy* selection, or CUDA-graph padding(TBD).
- **`MoeConfig.disable_finalize_fusion`**: CUTLASS only; the LlmArgs docstring states the fused path is non-deterministic for top-k > 2.

Two items already landed for Router Replay: per-request gating (`SamplingParams.return_routed_experts=False` now correctly attaches nothing), and the output dtype is `int16`.

Reading the PyTorch backend (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/`) turns up nine places where a numeric result depends on batch shape or token count, not just the sequence — this is what drives the Deterministic inference work below:

| # | Source | Class | Covered by `FORCE_DETERMINISTIC`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Attention multi-block/split-KV (MMHA/XQA/TRTLLM-Gen); split count = `f(SM_count, batch*heads)` | batch-dependent | Yes — but a shared-memory guard can silently re-enable multi-block regardless of the flag |
| 2 | FMHA library selection by batch bucket (`fmha/manager.py`) | batch-dependent | No — `TLLM_FMHA_LIBS` can pin one manually |
| 3 | Dense GEMM tactic selection by M (autotuner) | batch-dependent, plus profiling-noise without a persisted cache | No — `enable_autotuner=False` falls back to `tactic=-1`, but the fallback cuBLASLt path's own algorithm choice is unexamined |
| 4 | MoE grouped-GEMM tactic selection by token count | batch-dependent | No |
| 5 | MoE finalize/unpermute reduction, CUTLASS top-k>2 | non-deterministic per LlmArgs docstring | Partially — `disable_finalize_fusion=True`; TRTLLM-Gen has no unfused path |
| 6 | All-reduce *strategy* selection by message size | batch-dependent | No — only workspace *size* is fixed, strategy selection isn't |
| 7 | CUDA-graph batch-size padding ladder | batch-dependent | No |
| 8 | Chunked-prefill / KV-reuse boundary placement | depends on scheduler budget, not just the sequence | Yes — both disabled |

Two bugs found while reading the same code, independent of scope: `getBoolEnv` matches only the exact string `"1"` (`FORCE_DETERMINISTIC=true` is silently ignored), and MMHA's multi-block override under shared-memory pressure bypasses the flag entirely.

## Proposed Change.

Organized by delivery phase. Each phase lists what happens to every workstream in that phase, rather than each workstream carrying its own separate phase numbering.

### Phase 1 — config only, no new kernels, land first

- **Router Replay:**
  - Validate TRTLLM-Gen, DeepGEMM, and WideEP end to end. Today only CUTLASS has a GPU test, on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat; the other backends' support is inferred from `_supports_load_balancer()`, not tested.
  - Optional `uint8` output for `num_experts <= 256` models. `int16` already halves the naive `int32` footprint, but large payloads are a real failure mode at scale — a comparable rollout system hit ~35GB/actor, ~280GB across 8 actors, on a 96-layer MoE model with long context. Worth having the compact path ready before someone hits this on TRT-LLM.
- **Deterministic inference:**
  - Config-only surface over the gaps in the table above:

    ```python
    class TorchLlmArgs:
        enable_deterministic_inference: bool = False
        # Superset of FORCE_DETERMINISTIC=1:
        #   - autotuner f

items.title: [Bug]: Upgrade XGrammar: qwen_xml compilation errors and tool-call loops recover on 0.2.7
items.author: indrajit96
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary / requested change

Please upgrade TRT-LLM's supported XGrammar dependency from **0.1.32** to a compatible release containing the XML fixes demonstrated with **0.2.7**, and add regression coverage for empty object schemas, boolean schemas and whitespace between XML parameters.

We found user-visible failures while validating default structural guidance in [Dynamo PR #13654](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/13654). These include ordinary empty-argument calls, strings, nested objects and mixed scalar arguments. The tested TRT-LLM release is **1.3.0rc29**, whose [requirements pin XGrammar 0.1.32](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/v1.3.0rc29/requirements.txt#L72).

On the **same Nemotron-3-Super checkpoint and Dynamo PR image**, an isolated compiler/dependency upgrade recovered all five custom regression families: **30/30 focused live requests** (three repetitions in each streaming mode). A subsequent complete custom-suite rerun scored **42/48**, up from **32/48** with the original compiler. Main and PR guidance OFF scored **41/48**. All 48 upgraded requests returned HTTP 200; all original PR-ON passes remained passes.

This issue requests a supported dependency upgrade. The experimental override is not a qualified TRT release, and it does not resolve every schema limitation or task failure.

## System info

- Host architecture: x86_64; two NVIDIA H100 NVL GPUs, approximately 94 GiB each; Super served with TP=2.
- Model: `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-FP8`, revision `744b1880a37996c5d56bf454ae164dfd74d77c4e`.
- TRT-LLM: `1.3.0rc29`, PyTorch backend, explicitly configured XGrammar guided decoder.
- Original XGrammar: `0.1.32`; experimental XGrammar: `0.2.7` with required `apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.14.post1` in an isolated import path.
- NVIDIA driver: `580.159.04`; each GPU reports 95,830 MiB total memory.
- Python 3.12.3; PyTorch `2.14.0a0+4fdf77b940.nv26.8.63802676`; Transformers 5.5.4; glibc 2.39.
- Dynamo 1.6.0; Rust frontend; `nemotron_nano` tool/reasoning parsers. Tested [Dynamo source](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/commit/2f5313af9ee35ad578d3011975eca03b46305185), immutable image digest `sha256:270253a3451f91ea089eb0322f03931226fde0c84519eccc9de036a364d17dac`.
- Custom requests: temperature 0, thinking disabled, max_tokens 2048 except the nested-object case (4096), streaming and non-streaming.

Engine configuration:

```json
{"backend":"pytorch","tensor_parallel_size":2,"pipeline_parallel_size":1,"max_batch_size":8,"max_num_tokens":8192,"max_seq_len":16384,"enable_chunked_prefill":true,"kv_cache_config":{"enable_block_reuse":false,"free_gpu_memory_fraction":0.8},"cuda_graph_config":{"max_batch_size":8}}
```

The live override used `PYTHONPATH=/work/xgrammar027` and `TVM_FFI_DISABLE_TORCH_C_DLPACK=1`. No Dynamo tag, parser, schema, TRT adapter, model checkpoint or engine configuration was changed. In the five custom regression families, HTTP requests, worker prompt token IDs, tag bytes and final effective sampling/stop settings were checked against saved originals. We distinguish final sampling from early snapshots captured before the worker applied token limits and stop settings.

## Failure buckets / actual behavior

| Bucket | Affected requests | XGrammar 0.1.32 | Experimental 0.2.7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Closed empty-object XML | `named_no_argument_server_time`, both modes | EBNF compilation failure; non-stream HTTP 500, streaming without a completed call | 6/6 focused live requests pass; one call with `{}`, normal `tool_calls` finish |
| B. Boolean-schema XML | Five `strict:false` schema fixtures, both modes | `Expected JSON schema object, got boolean: true`; all ten fail compilation | All ten compile and complete with one schema-valid call; eight satisfy the exact task, two optional-only outputs add an unwanted `path` |
| B2. Open empty-object XML | Ten BFCL inference-error cases; eight saved initial Super tags checked on CPU | Empty-property tools with open schemas can break the full tag; HTTP 500 | Eight saved Super tags compile on CPU; all ten original Lightning inference errors clear in live multi-turn replay |
| C. Parameter separators / loops | Escaped string, nested object and mixed scalars; both modes | Malformed/repeated calls until `length`: 2048, 4096 and 2048 completion tokens respectively | 18/18 focused live requests pass; one correct call; normal `tool_calls` finish |
| D. Optional argument omission | `named_weather_enum_argument`, both modes | Omits requested `unit:"celsius"`; normal finish, but wrong task output | 6/6 focused Super requests include the unit; paired Lightning version controls also recover 6/6 |
| E. Regex lookahead | `lookahead` with auto, required and named choices | Compilation fails | Still fails when argument constraints are retained; relaxing with `strict:false` compiles on 0.2.7 |
| F. Other observed failures | Parallel/multiple calls, reasoning/output assertions, residual BFCL task errors | Recorded separately below | Not established as fixed by this upgrade; not attributed to a TRT compiler defect |

### A / B: compilation errors

Closed empty XML object error:

```text
EBNF parser error at line 16, column 1: Expect element, but got
```

Relaxed boolean-schema error:

```text
Expected JSON schema object, got boolean: true
```

Both reproduce on CPU with XGrammar alone; TRT execution, a model and Dynamo response parsing are unnecessary. Plain JSON `{}` and an empty constant XML body compile successfully in the closed-empty control. A constant-empty rewrite is not valid for an **open** empty-property object, since additional arguments remain permitted.

### C: valid separator rejected; malformed unfinished output accepted

The old compiled XML grammar rejects a correctly closed parameter followed by a newline:

```text
</parameter>
<parameter=next_argument>
```

It accepts the same complete call when parameter elements are adjacent. XGrammar 0.2.7 accepts and terminates the newline-separated version.
