items.title: [Testing] Triage of tests that never run: disabled specs and suites that no CI job compiles
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

A read-only sweep of the tree at `4be9a600` (2026-09-27) looked for tests that cannot protect anything because they never execute. One family is disabled in place, some of it for two years. Another sits behind build tags that no test job passes, so its suites never run. A third family quietly skips itself on CI hosts.

This is a different axis from #2805, which tracks tests that are going red right now. A skipped test cannot go red, which is how these stayed invisible. One overlap (the console catalog skip, already named in #2805 A2) is listed in the appendix instead of repeated as an item.

The sweep grepped for skip markers across the Go and Python trees and cross-referenced every test file behind a build tag against every workflow under `.github/workflows`. Line numbers are against `4be9a600`.

If you want to take one, please comment on the item first so two people do not end up on the same thing, and link the PR here when it is up. Small focused PRs are the easiest to review.

## Items

- [ ] A1. The oldest in-place skip: the rayclusterfleet reconcile spec, skipped since 2024-09.
- [ ] A2. Roleset and StormService scaffold specs skip themselves in `BeforeEach` (2025-06).
- [ ] A3. ModelAdapter controller suite: all 18 specs parked behind `XDescribe` (2025-08).
- [ ] A4. OpenAI compatibility e2e: `TestCompletionStreaming` carries a bare fix-me TODO with no explanation (2025-10).
- [ ] A5. Two kvcache Python files skip at import time with no reason string (2025).
- [ ] A6. One storage factory test skips because a network probe is treated as flaky (2026-06).
- [ ] B1. `-tags zmq` test suites (9 files, 48 test functions) are run by no CI job (needs a wiring decision).
- [ ] B2. `-tags integration` tests under `pkg/controller` have no runner (needs a decision on where they belong).
- [ ] C1. Three rate limiter tests skip themselves in CI because no Redis is listening.

Grading:

- A: the skip is unconditional in the source; the fix is to re-enable and repair, or remove.
- B: no CI entry compiles the tag; the fix needs a wiring decision first.
- C: the test runs but skips itself under CI conditions; a green run hides it.

## A. Disabled in place

### A1. rayclusterfleet: the oldest skip

`pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/rayclusterfleet_controller_test.go:112` is the only spec of its suite, and it skips under a deferral note that waits for the integration test to land:

- Acceptance: the spec runs in `make test` again, or it is deleted together with the TODO. If part of the reconcile is out of reach for the unit environment, say which part and where it is covered instead.
- Verify: `go test ./pkg/controller/rayclusterfleet/... -v` (the suite uses envtest, so run it via `make test` or with `KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS`).
- Size: S.

### A2. Roleset and StormService scaffold specs

`pkg/controller/roleset/roleset_controller_test.go:45` and `pkg/controller/stormservice/stormservice_controller_test.go:45` both skip inside `BeforeEach` with `Skip("skip this test and revisit once main logic is implemented")`. Both skips came in `8fd23efa` (#1226, 2025-06-25) and were never revisited. Each file has exactly one spec, so the skip takes the whole suite to zero.

- Acceptance: the specs pass against the current controllers, or the scaffold specs are deleted so the suites are empty on purpose.
- Verify: `go test ./pkg/controller/roleset/... ./pkg/controller/stormservice/... -v`.
- Size: S; both files share one origin, so one PR can carry both.

### A3. ModelAdapter: 18 specs behind XDescribe

`pkg/controller/modeladapter/modeladapter_controller_test.go:37` disables the whole suite with `var _ = XDescribe("ModelAdapter Controller", func() {`, under the comment "Disable Ginkgo tests that require Kubernetes environment". The package already has an envtest entry point: `suite_test.go:46` `TestControllers` with `testEnv *envtest.Environment` (`:44`). A separate integration suite lives at `test/integration/controller/modeladapter_test.go`.

items.title: [Feature][ModelClaim][Residency] Add per-claim Sleep Policy overrides
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

Related umbrella RFC: #2290.

ModelClaim idle sleep is currently configured on the warm-pool Deployment through
the `pool.aibrix.ai/policy` annotation. When the pool sets
`lifecycle.sleepAfterSeconds`, every eligible vLLM ModelClaim engine owned by that
Deployment uses the same timeout. An individual claim cannot declare that it:

- must remain awake;
- needs a different idle timeout from the pool default; or
- should sleep after an idle period even when the pool has no lifecycle policy.

This prevents latency-sensitive and long-tail models from sharing one warm pool
with different availability policies. The current workarounds are to disable idle
sleep for the entire pool or move always-on models into a separate GPU pool. The
first loses HBM reclamation; the second reduces the value of high-density pooling.

### Use Case

One B300 warm pool hosts:

```text
online-chat  -> must remain awake
batch-coder  -> sleep after 10 minutes idle
evaluation   -> sleep after 2 minutes idle
```

The pool should continue to own the GPU Pods and KV-reclaim policy while each
ModelClaim can express its own sleep requirement.

### Proposed Solution

Add an optional sleep policy under `ModelClaimSpec.residencyPolicy`:

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: PoolDefault
```

Initial modes:

| Mode | Semantics |
| --- | --- |
| `PoolDefault` | Inherit the Deployment lifecycle policy; do not sleep automatically when the pool has no lifecycle policy |
| `Never` | The pool policy must not automatically sleep this claim |
| `AfterIdle` | Use the claim's own `idleTimeout` |

Examples:

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: Never
```

```yaml
spec:
  residencyPolicy:
    sleepPolicy:
      mode: AfterIdle
      idleTimeout: 15m
```

Effective-policy precedence:

```text
ModelClaim sleepPolicy
    > Deployment lifecycle policy
    > no automatic sleep
```

The claim sleep policy overrides lifecycle sleep only. It must not change the
pool's KV-reclaim policy.

### API Validation

- `mode` is one of `PoolDefault`, `Never`, or `AfterIdle`.
- `AfterIdle` requires a positive `idleTimeout`.
- `PoolDefault` and `Never` reject `idleTimeout`.
- `AfterIdle` initially supports vLLM only.
- Existing claims without `residencyPolicy` retain their current behavior.

### Implementation Boundary

This is an API/controller change:

- add ModelClaim API types, CRD schema, and generated artifacts;
- add an effective sleep-policy resolver;
- resolve the claim policy before issuing Sleep;
- skip automatic Sleep for `Never`;
- use the claim timeout for `AfterIdle`, including when the Deployment has no
  lifecycle annotation;
- preserve existing request-metric, ClaimRef UID, status, and topology safety
  checks.

No Python runtime change is required. The runtime already exposes idempotent
Sleep, activity metrics, phase, ClaimRef, and last-transition observations. No
Gateway behavior change is required for this track.

### Priority

1. **P1: `Never`** — solve the concrete opt-out requirement for critical models.
2. **P1: compatibility and safe convergence** — unset policies remain unchanged,
   and controller restarts must not sleep a `Never` claim.
3. **P2: `AfterIdle`** — add claim-specific idle timeouts.
4. **P2: observability, documentation, and E2E coverage**.

The issue is P2 while ModelClaim remains experimental, but should become P1
before production readiness or GA.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Unset policies and `PoolDefault` preserve current pool behavior.
- [ ] A `Never` claim is never selected for automatic Sleep.
- [ ] Other claims in the same pool can still sleep normally.
- [ ] `AfterIdle` uses the claim's `idleTimeout`.
- [ ] `AfterIdle` works without a Deployment lifecycle annotation.
- [ ] Claim sleep policy does not affect KV reclaim.
- [ ] Invalid combinations are rejected by CRD validation.
- [ ] Controller restart preserves the effective policy.
- [ ] Unit and integration tests cover mixed policies in one pool.
- [ ] No Python runtime wire-protocol change is introduced.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: [CI] Installation E2E test step grew from ~9 min to ~41 min since July
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
**Area:** Testing (E2E)

## Summary

In the `Installation Tests` workflow, the `Run installation e2e tests` step went from 9m15s in mid-July to 40m36s now, and the whole workflow from about 20 minutes to 54. The `installation-test` job has a 75-minute timeout.

Measured on two runs of the same workflow:

- July 13: https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/29281096831/job/86923371188
- October 8, `a228471` (main at #2930): https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/37735233267/job/113174859334

## Numbers

| | Jul 13 | Oct 8 |
|---|---|---|
| Whole workflow | 20.5 min | 54 min |
| `Run installation e2e tests` step | 9m15s | 40m36s |
| Test packages | 1 (`./test/e2e`) | 13 |
| Top-level tests | 44 | 180 |
| Sum of test time | 486s | 2,123s |
| Compile time before the first test | 47s | 3m08s |

October 8 time per package. All packages run one after another (`go test -p 1`):

| Package | Time |
|---|---|
| gateway/routing | 527s |
| controller/roleset | 360s |
| controller/stormservice | 257s |
| gateway/pd | 218s |
| controller/podset | 206s |
| controller/modeladapter | 169s |
| controller/modelclaim | 163s |
| controller/raycluster | 117s |
| controller/modelwarmup | 46s |
| gateway/api | 32s |
| controller/modelrouter | 25s |
| controller/autoscaling (+ external-metrics) | ~5s |

## Why it grew (about +31 min)

### 1. New controller lifecycle E2E tests: about +19 min

Controller tests went from about 204s (only `TestRoleSetInPlaceUpdate`) to 1,348s. Every new package runs on the same kind cluster, one after another, so each one adds its full time to the step.

| Change | Package time now |
|---|---|
| StormService E2E (#2733, Sep 16) | 257s |
| PodSet lifecycle E2E (#2751, Sep 20) | 206s |
| ModelAdapter E2E no longer skipped (#2657, Sep 3) | 169s |
| ModelClaim E2E (#2460 Jul 18, expanded through #2929 Oct 8) | 163s |
| RayClusterFleet lifecycle E2E (#2753, Sep 20) | 117s |
| ModelWarmup E2E (#2769, Oct 2) | 46s |
| ModelRouter lifecycle E2E (#2743, Sep 19) | 25s |
| RoleSet historical-node (#2628) and drain (#2736) tests enabled in CI | roleset 202s → 360s |

### 2. Gateway tests: about +8 min

Gateway tests went from about 282s to 777s.

- **Each request to the mock is about 3.3× slower (#2383, Jul 14).** That change turned on capacity-aware latency in the mock by default. A request with no `max_tokens` now sleeps about 0.03s + 2ms × `randint(10, 500)` output tokens. That averages about 0.55s, where it used to be a fixed 0.2s.
  - 30 pod-discovery requests: 6.3s → 20.8s.
  - The 8 routing tests present in both runs: 163s → 351s in total. `TestRandomRouting` went 21s → 67s; the VTC tests went from about 21s to 52–61s.
- **New tests:**
  - power-of-two routing: 137s
  - PD failure, bucketing and watchdog tests: `gateway/pd` is 218s now
  - backend-request and API endpoint tests

### 3. Build overhead: about +4 min

#2676 (Sep 8) split the suite into packages and added `go test -p 1`. The `-p` flag limits concurrent compile actions as well as test binaries, so all compilation is now serial:

- compile time before the first test: 47s → 3m08s
- about 5–9s of compiling and linking before each of the 13 packages

items.title: [Perf] SM107: mm_mxfp8 cute-dsl backend never uses Sm107BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel (only SM100 kernels are autotune candidates)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On SM107 (Rubin), `mm_mxfp8(..., backend="cute-dsl")` never uses the Rubin-specific CuTe DSL kernel `Sm107BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel`. The cute-dsl MXFP8 runner only imports and autotunes the SM100 kernel family. So on Rubin the backend runs the SM100 kernels, which skip the SM107 subclass's Rubin-specific overrides.

### Where

`flashinfer/gemm/gemm_base.py`, `_cute_dsl_gemm_mxfp8_runner` (main @ `58171ea83`):

- It imports only `Sm100BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel` and `Sm100BlockScaledSplitKGemmKernel`.
- It builds tactics from those two kernels only. The SM version (`sm_major`/`sm_minor`) is passed in but never used to select a kernel family.
- `forward()` launches `Sm100BlockScaledSplitKGemmKernel` when the tactic has `split_k_slices > 1`, and `Sm100BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel` otherwise.

`Sm107BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel` (`flashinfer/gemm/kernels/dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm107.py`, a subclass of the SM100 kernel) documents MXF8 as a supported input type:

> MXF8: A/B: Float8E5M2/Float8E4M3FN + SF: Float8E8M0FNU + sf_vec_size: 32

That is exactly the `mm_mxfp8` problem.

### Inconsistency with `mm_fp4`

The FP4 path already handles this. `_cute_dsl_gemm_fp4_runner` imports `Sm107BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel` when `sm_version == 107`, adds an `"sm107"` kernel type to its tactic space, and gates each candidate on `Sm107Kernel.can_implement(...)`. #4856 added the SM107 family to the FP4 autotune candidates. The MXFP8 runner never received the equivalent change.

### Expected

On SM107, `mm_mxfp8(backend="cute-dsl")` should include `Sm107BlockScaledPersistentDenseGemmKernel` tactics in its autotune candidates. The SM100 kernels can stay as additional candidates, the same way the FP4 runner keeps them. That way the autotuner can pick the Rubin kernel where it is faster.

### Notes

- Autotuning itself works. The issue is only that the candidate set lacks the SM107 kernel.
- Impact is not yet measured. A before/after comparison of `mm_mxfp8(backend="cute-dsl")` on SM107 would be part of the fix.
- Related: on SM107, `backend="auto"` for `mm_mxfp8` resolves to `cutlass` only (`_heuristic_func_mm_mxfp8`), so cute-dsl is reached only when requested explicitly.
- #6076 (open) refactors the same runner factory but does not add the SM107 kernel; whichever lands second will need a rebase.

### Environment

- FlashInfer main `58171ea83` (2026-10-05); also present in 0.7.0
- Arch: SM107 (cc 10.7)

items.title: [ModelClaim] Add operational metrics for pooled runtimes and policy actions
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

ModelClaim exposes basic desired/ready/activation metrics and runtime KV/HBM gauges, but operators cannot currently tell whether an engine is repeatedly restarting, was re-adopted after an agent restart, exhausted its restart budget, or whether the pool KV policy applied or skipped a decision.

ModelClaim is still experimental, so this issue is limited to additive observability. 

### Use Case

When several model engines share one GPU, an operator needs to distinguish a healthy dense pool from a pool that is silently converging through engine restarts or repeatedly failing policy actions. The signals must support alerts and post-incident diagnosis without requiring runtime snapshot or controller log inspection.

### Proposed Solution

Add low-cardinality Prometheus metrics covering:

- engine restart attempts and restart-budget exhaustion;
- runtime agent re-adoption outcomes;
- engine state counts by phase (`active`, `sleeping`, `restarting`, `failed`);
- pool-policy evaluation and action outcomes (`applied`, `skipped`, `failed`) with a bounded reason label;
- requested and successfully applied KV limits per model;
- sleep and wake operation count and duration;
- duration for which a ModelClaim has no ready engine.

Keep labels bounded to namespace, model, pod/pool where necessary, action/result, and an enumerated reason. Do not expose free-form errors, operation IDs, PIDs, or claim UIDs as metric labels. Detailed errors should remain in logs and Kubernetes Events.

Add focused unit tests for registration, values, cleanup of deleted gauge series, and bounded label values. Document metric names and semantics alongside the ModelClaim runbook.

### Acceptance Criteria

- Metrics are exported from the existing controller-manager or runtime `/metrics` endpoints.
- A terminal engine failure, successful re-adoption, successful/failed KV update, and sleep/wake operation are observable without reading logs.
- Policy skip reasons are from a fixed enum and cannot introduce unbounded cardinality.
- Existing ModelClaim APIs and reconciliation behavior remain unchanged.

items.title: moe_cute_util.cuh: util_convert_type returns a tensor that points at a local array
items.author: BwL1289
items.body_excerpt:
In `cpp/tensorrt_llm/cutlass_extensions/include/cutlass_extensions/gemm/kernel/moe_cute_util.cuh`:

```cpp
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
return cute::make_tensor(cute::make_rmem_ptr<To_type>(&frag), tensor.layout());
```

The returned tensor is a view of `frag`, a local of `util_convert_type`. `frag` is gone once the function returns, so
reading the result is undefined behaviour. Both routines in `fused_moe_kernel_routine.cuh` read it
(`util_convert_type<...>(accum)`, then the copy to shared memory).

With nvcc this happens to work. With clang (device code at -O3, sm_121a) the conversion and the SwiGLU that feed it are
removed, ptxas then removes the MMAs whose results are no longer used, and the kernel stores registers nothing wrote.
SASS counts (HMMA / LDSM / F2FP / FMUL) for the bf16 32x128x64 SwiGLU instantiation of
`fused_moe::run_global<Fused_Moe_Kernel_sm80<...>>`:

- nvcc (NVIDIA's flashinfer-jit-cache 0.7.0+cu130 wheel): 96 / 64 / 12 / 72
- clang: 64 / 40 / 0 / 48
- clang with the change below: 96 / 64 / 12 / 72

A bf16 or fp16 MoE call through this kernel (DeepSeek-V2-Lite shapes, 256 and 8192 tokens) then gets every row wrong
(NaN or values up to 1e37), and the output changes from call to call. With the change, the output matches the nvcc build
to every printed digit (max abs error against a float32 reference: 1.6e-05 for bf16 at 256 tokens, as with nvcc).

Suggested change, which returns a fragment that owns its registers (same layout, same element order):

```cpp
static_assert(cute::cosize_v<Layout> == numel, "util_convert_type: the fragment must be contiguous");
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
auto out = cute::make_tensor<To_type>(tensor.layout());
CUTLASS_PRAGMA_UNROLL
for (int i = 0; i < numel; ++i) {
  out.data()[i] = frag[i];
}
return out;
```

To see the lifetime problem without a GPU: compile the function against small stand-ins for the CuTe/CUTLASS types it
uses, read the returned tensor after the call, and run it under AddressSanitizer with
`ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1`. The current code is reported as a stack-use-after-return; the change
above is not.

FlashInfer's own `include/flashinfer/attention/hopper/utils.cuh` (`convert_type`) has the same pattern.

items.title: [Bug] calculate_nvfp4_global_scale returns wrong per-token scales for hidden sizes above 8192 that are not multiples of 8192
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 wheel, torch 2.9.1+cu130, A100 80GB PCIe (driver 610.57).
- The kernel is unchanged on main `b031dbe`: `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/quantization.cu` and `cpp/tensorrt_llm/common/reduceKernelUtils.cuh`.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)` on a bf16 `x` of shape `[m, n]` should return `448 * 6 / max|x[i]|` for each token. When the hidden size is above 8192 and not a multiple of 8192, many tokens get a wrong scale once a CTA handles more than one token (for a 2-D input, `m` above the SM count).

A minimal script:

```python
import torch
import tensorrt_llm  # registers torch.ops.trtllm

m = 512
torch.manual_seed(0)
rows = torch.arange(m)
amp = 2.0 ** ((rows * 5) % 11 - 3) * (1 + (rows * 3 % 8) / 8)  # per-token maximum
for n in (12288, 8192):
    x = (torch.rand(m, n) - 0.5) * amp[:, None]
    x[rows, torch.randint(n, (m,))] = amp
    x = x.bfloat16().cuda()
    ref = 2688.0 / x.double().abs().amax(1, keepdim=True)
    got = torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)
    bad = ((got.double() - ref).abs() > 1e-4 + 2e-6 * ref.abs()).sum().item()
    print(f"n={n}: {bad} of {m} tokens have a wrong global scale")
```

On an A100 (SXM4 80GB) it printed:

```
n=12288: 309 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
n=8192: 0 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
```

Results with the 1.2.1 wheel:
- each call was checked in full against a float64 reference;
- a call counts as wrong if any token's scale is non-finite or off by more than 1e-4 + 2e-6 · |ref|.

| x shape (bf16) | wrong calls | wrong tokens in sampled calls |
|---|---|---|
| [512, 12288] | 914302 / 914302 | 301–318 of 512 |
| [256, 28672] | 920766 / 920766 | 101–114 of 256 |
| [512, 8192] | 0 / 924832 | |
| [1024, 4096] | 0 / 914518 | |

For example, in the first call at [512, 12288], token 3 got 28.0 instead of 42.0.

### Expected behavior

Each token's global scale is `2688 / max|x[i]|`, for any `n` the operator accepts. The launcher checks only `n % 256 == 0`.

### actual behavior

In `computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel` (`quantization.cu:351–374`), `getMaxAbs` calls `blockReduceMaxV2`, which contains a `__syncthreads()`, inside the per-thread loop:

```cpp
for (int vecIdx = threadIdx.x; vecIdx < n / ElemsPerVec; vecIdx += blockDim.x)
{
    float4 vec = reinterpret_cast<float4 const*>(input + tokenIdx * n)[vecIdx];
    float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);   // blockReduceMaxV2 -> __syncthreads()
    perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
}
```

The launcher uses `blockDim.x = min(n / 8, 1024)`. When `n / 8` is above 1024 and not a multiple of it, threads with `threadIdx.x < (n / 8) % 1024` run one more iteration per token than the others. CUDA requires a `__syncthreads()` in conditional code to be reached by all threads of the block, and here it is not.

The warps with fewer iterations run ahead. Each barrier instance then joins warp 0's reduction of one token with the other warps' reductions of later tokens handled by the same CTA. After those warps exit, it joins with the values they left in shared memory. The reduced maximum mixes tokens. In a standalone copy of the kernel, run without Compute Sanitizer, every wrong value matched the one predicted from this pairing.

A second, smaller problem: `blockReduceMaxV2` has no barrier between warp 0's read of `shared[lane]` (`reduceKernelUtils.cuh:281`) and the next call's write of `shared[wid]` (line 269). On the standalone copy, Compute Sanitizer racecheck reports hazards between these two lines at every shape we tested, including `n` = 4096 and 8192. Under racecheck or synccheck, those two shapes also returned wrong scales (one launch each), though they were correct in every plain run.

### additional notes

Suggested fix: reduce once per token, after the loop, followed by a barrier.

```diff
@@ -343,7 +343,6 @@ __device__ float getMaxAbs(float4& vec)
     {
         absMaxVal = static_cast<float>(cuda_max(absMaxVec.x, absMaxVec.y));
     }
-    tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&absMaxVal);
     return absMaxVal;
 }
 
@@ -365,6 +364,11 @@ __global__ void computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel(
             float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);
             perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
         }
+        // Reduce once per token, outside the per-thread loop: threads make different numbers of loop iterations
+        // when n / ElemsPerVec is not a multiple of blockDim.x.
+        tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&perTokenMaxAbsVal);
+        // blockReduceMaxV2's shared slots are rewritten by the next token's reduction.
+        __syncthreads();
         float globalScaleVal = 448.f * 6.f / perTokenMaxAbsVal;
         if (threadIdx.x == 0)
         {
```

A standalone copy of the kernel with the equivalent change gave no wrong scales on A100 and A40, and is clean under racecheck and synccheck.

**Reach.** Callers in the tree:
- the opt-in NVFP4 low-precision MoE combine in `nccl_ep.py:460` (`use_low_precision_moe_combine`, default off). It requires NVFP4 and a hidden size that is a multiple of 512, so sizes such as 10240 or 12288 can reach it. Its input is `[ep_size, max_tokens_per_rank, hidden]`, so a CTA handles several tokens once a rank receives more than SMs / `ep_size` tokens;
- `deep_ep_low_latency.py:386`, which runs this combine only for hidden sizes 4096, 6144 and 7168, and is not affected;
- `visual_gen/.../cute_dsl/fmha.py:626`, which caps rows at 8192 and is not affected; its comment calls 8192 "the largest dimension compatible with the same routine".

The operator's unit test (`test_fp4_calculate_global_scale.py`) use

comments.author: peter941221
comments.body:
Independent repro and a fix proposal for this one.

Setup: RTX 5090 (sm_120), CUDA 13.0, standalone harness built from current main
(edfc6672) with the kernel, getMaxAbs and blockReduceMaxV2 code verbatim, plus
a fixed variant. Result: confirmed, and the exposed range is wider than the
title - there are two independent defects here.

D1 - divergent block collective. getMaxAbs() calls blockReduceMaxV2(), which
contains __syncthreads(), from inside the per-thread vector loop. With
blockDim = min(n/8, 1024) for bf16, per-thread trip counts are uniform only
when n <= 8192 or n % 8192 == 0. Threads that finish early advance to the next
token and enter the collective again, mispairing barriers and mixing data
across tokens. The reported n=12288 case: 295-323 wrong of 512 over 50 runs
here (A100 report: 301-318; consistent across machines).

D2 - shared-buffer reuse in the same helper. blockReduceMaxV2() stages warp
maxima in a function-local static __shared__ buffer, and warp 0 reads them with
no barrier after those reads; the next call's lane-0 stores can overwrite slots
while warp 0 is still reading. So uniform shapes fail as well: n=16384 (exactly
2 iterations for every thread) measured 108-171 wrong of 512 over 300 runs,
while n=8192 (1 iteration) was clean over 300 runs. Measured criterion: all
tested n <= 8192 clean; all tested n >= 16384 affected (11008, 12288, 16384,
24576, 28672, 32768), non-multiple shapes hit hardest.

Discriminating experiment: adding a trailing __syncthreads() inside
blockReduceMaxV2 (experiment build only) makes 16384 and 24576 fully clean
(0/0/0, 50 runs each) but leaves 12288 broken (256-273 wrong of 512) - the two
defects are independent. Hoisting the collective out of getMaxAbs to once per
token, uniformly reached by all threads, clears all of it: 0/0/0 on 11 shapes
(4096, 8192, 11008, 12288, 16384, 24576, 28672, 32768 plus three
gridDim.y = m variants), 50 runs each, plus 300-run stability at 12288 and
16384; max relative error 4.5e-08 against an fp64 reference.

Error shape (test data: uniform noise plus one planted per-token maximum): for
n=16384 the wrong scales are exactly 2x the reference - the planted maximum is
lost and the result falls back to the noise floor at half amplitude. For
n=12288 the error goes both ways, including scales about 7x and 14x too small
when a larger amplitude from another token leaks through the mismatched barrier
- that direction pushes values outside the representable FP4 range, which is
the more dangerous failure.

Proposed minimal change (getMaxAbs has a single call site in this file):

    template <typename T>
    __device__ float getMaxAbs(float4& vec)
    {
        ... unchanged ...
        return absMaxVal;      // blockReduceMaxV2 call removed from here
    }

    // in the kernel, after the vector loop:
    tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&perTokenMaxAbsVal);
    float globalScaleVal = 448.f * 6.f / perTokenMaxAbsVal;
    if (threadIdx.x == 0) { globalScale[tokenIdx] = globalScaleVal; }

Only thread 0 writes globalScale, and thread 0's value is the block maximum
under both layouts (in blockReduceMaxV2, only warp 0 ends up with a meaningful
value), so the write semantics are unchanged.

A trailing barrier inside blockReduceMaxV2 would close D2 as well, but by
itself it does not fix D1 (measured above), and I have not audited its other
call sites (kernels/unfusedAttentionKernels.cu has one), so I kept the change
inside the kernel.

Is there any in-flight work on this? If not, I can send a PR with a regression
test for n=12288 and n=16384 in
tests/unittest/_torch/thop/parallel/test_fp4_calculate_global_scale.py.

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

`export_to_c` fails on the plain C path (no `--enable-tvm-ffi`) when the function was compiled for a different arch than the current GPU. For example, `--gpu-arch sm_90a` on a B200:

```text
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, _cudaDeviceGetAttribute, _cudaFuncSetAttribute, _cudaGetDevice, _cudaKernelSetAttributeForDevice, _cudaLaunchKernelEx, _cudaLibraryGetKernel, _cudaLibraryLoadData ]
error: Error dumping object file: Failed to dump object file with PIC relocation
```

The same export works for the native arch, and it also works if I load the runtime libraries `RTLD_GLOBAL` first. My guess is that no execution engine gets built for an arch the GPU can't run, so `libcute_dsl_runtime.so` never gets loaded before the object dump.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

```python
import ctypes, sys, tempfile

import cuda.bindings.driver as cuda
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import make_fake_stream


@cute.kernel
def noop_kernel(x: cutlass.Int32):
    pass


@cute.jit
def noop(x: cutlass.Int32, stream: cuda.CUstream):
    noop_kernel(x).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1), stream=stream)


if "--preload" in sys.argv:
    for lib in cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries(enable_tvm_ffi=False):
        ctypes.CDLL(lib, mode=ctypes.RTLD_GLOBAL)
fn = cute.compile(noop, cutlass.Int32(0), make_fake_stream(), options="--gpu-arch sm_90a")
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    fn.export_to_c(tmp, "noop", function_prefix="noop")
print(f"cutlass-dsl {cutlass.__version__}: exported", flush=True)
```

```console
$ python repro.py
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, ... ]
$ python repro.py --preload
cutlass-dsl 4.8.0: exported
```

**Expected behavior**

`export_to_c` works for any `--gpu-arch` the compiler accepts, with no manual preloading.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 and 4.7.0 (cu13), cuda-python 13.4.1
 - B200, driver 580.159.03, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.12

**Additional context**

#2859 had the same error on the TVM-FFI path and was fixed in 4.3.3; the TVM-FFI path does export cross-arch now. The plain C path still fails. Workaround: preload `cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries()` with `RTLD_GLOBAL`.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 TMA GEMM mainloops rely on elect_one_sync() electing lane 0 (TMA issuer vs. PipelineTmaAsync is_leader)
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

Most SM90 TMA GEMM mainloop collectives work only if `elect.sync` elects lane 0. Paths and lines are at main `0b55a2f`.

Two threads are chosen by different rules.

**The TMA issuer is the elected lane.** These collectives call `producer_acquire` and issue the TMA copies only inside `if (lane_predicate)`, where `lane_predicate = cute::elect_one_sync()`, that is, `elect.sync` with a full mask:

| Collective (`include/cutlass/gemm/collective/`) | elect / `producer_acquire` lines |
|---|---|
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 320 / 374 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 318 / 372 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized.hpp` | 401 / 457 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 415 / 458 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 426 / 469 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 370 / 425 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 368 / 422 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8_blockwise_scaling.hpp` | 463 / 543 |

The non-warp-specialized `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` (lines 365 and 504) and the SM90 implicit-GEMM conv collective (`conv/collective/sm90_implicit_gemm_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp:558–559, 612`) have the same pattern.

**The producer's arrival comes from warp-group thread 0.** `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_acquire` performs `arrive_and_expect_tx` only when `params_.is_leader` is set (`include/cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:533–535`, and 555–557 in the token overload). This arrival is the stage's only producer arrival. The kernels set `is_leader = warp_group_thread_idx == 0`:
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:324`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp:471`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_pingpong.hpp:463`;
- the array cooperative and pingpong kernels, lines 522 and 531;
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:334`.

The mainloop warp is warp 0 of the producer warp group, so warp-group thread 0 is its lane 0.

**Why lane 0 matters.** PTX ISA 9.4 (§9.7.15.15, `elect.sync`) promises only that the election is deterministic, with the same leader for the same `membermask` every time. It does not say which lane. If another lane were elected:
- that lane would call `producer_acquire` without being the leader, so nothing arrives on the full barrier;
- lane 0 would not enter the `if` at all;
- the TMA's complete-tx would only drive the transaction count negative.

The phase would never complete. Consumers would block in `consumer_wait`, then the producer in `producer_acquire` once every stage is used, and the kernel would hang.

The kernels run today, so current hardware evidently elects lane 0 here. The code also states that intent:
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:356` says "Set predicate for the lowest lane_id in the warp";
- `sm90_pipeline.hpp:286` says "We have exactly one thread elected in the Producer as the 'leader'";
- CuTe's fallback without `elect.sync` returns `(threadIdx.x % 32) == 0` (`include/cute/arch/cluster_sm90.hpp:197`).

**Unaffected collectives.** Some collectives call `producer_acquire` from all 32 lanes and issue TMA only from the elected lane, so lane 0 always arrives:
- the mixed-input collectives (`sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized_mixed_input.hpp:684/694`, and the array variant at 774/784);
- the non-array FP8 blockwise collective (577/587–588).

The epilogue's TMA loads are also unaffected, because one elected lane both posts the expect-tx and issues the copy.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Found by reading the source against the PTX ISA. There is no runtime reproduction.

**Expected behavior**

The lane that issues the TMA loads is the lane that arrives with the expected bytes. In-tree code already derives the leader from the election:
- on the same `PipelineTmaAsync`, `examples/88_hopper_fmha/kernel/fmha_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:205, 210` and `sm120_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative_asymmetric_dma.hpp:443, 448`;
- in the SM100 kernels, e.g. `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:465`.

For the SM90 kernels, that would be:

```cpp
mainloop_pipeline_params.is_leader =
    warp_group_role == WarpGroupRole::Producer &&
    producer_warp_role == ProducerWarpRole::Mainloop && lane_predicate;
```

Restrict it to the mainloop warp. The `MainloopAux` warp in the blockwise kernels also has the Producer role and calls `producer_acquire` from all lanes. Giving it a leader would add a second `arrive_and_expect_tx` per stage.

This works because the kernel's `elect_one_sync()` and the collective's later one use the same full mask, and PTX guarantees the same leader for the same mask. Two more changes go with it:
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` would need `lane_predicate` computed before `is_leader` is set;
- the debug-build `brkpt` checks in `producer_acquire` (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:542–544` and 564–566), which fire when the leader is not lane 0, would need to go. They already assume lane 0 for the FMHA and SM120 kernels above.

The alternative is to gate the TMA issue in each affected collective on lane 0 instead of `elect_one_sync()`.

**Environment details**

Source analysis; no runtime environment involved. Hopper (sm_90a).

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: [data] Push Limit through Sort (Top-N execution)
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #66829.

### Problem

`sort(...).limit(k)` materializes a full global sort: sample boundaries, range-shuffle every row, sort each partition, then take k rows. TPC-H q2/q18/q21 end with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 100`.

```
Now:        sample boundaries → range-shuffle ALL rows → sort each partition → Limit
Optimized:  per-block top-100 heap → gather 100 × num_blocks rows to one task → final top-100
```

No range shuffle at all; cost drops from O(n log n) + full shuffle to roughly one scan.

### Proposal

Teach `LimitPushdownRule` (`python/ray/data/_internal/logical/rules/limit_pushdown.py`) to push a `Limit` through a `Sort`, planning a dedicated Top-N physical op. Needs a per-block bounded heap and a single merge task; the sort key and direction come from the `Sort` op.

items.title: [data] Plan-level common subtree reuse (CSE on the logical DAG)
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #66829.

### Problem

A subtree consumed twice executes twice. TPC-H q2 works around it manually:

```py
# tpch_q2.py — "Materialize to avoid recomputing the region->nation->supplier chain
#  in both Branch B and the main pipeline (Ray Data has no CSE)."
regional_suppliers = nation_region.join(supplier, ...).materialize()
```

```
Now:        the region→nation→supplier chain executes twice (or user adds .materialize())
Optimized:  compute once → feed both consumers (plan-DAG CSE)
```

We do have `CommonSubExprElimination` but this is only inside one `Project`; this issue is on the subplan level. We can work around by manually identifying a common sub plan and running that part and reusing it, but that would make our resource accounting wrong and give additional overhead as it is now another dataset.

items.title: [data] Broadcast hash join
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #66829.

### Problem

Ray Data has no broadcast join; both sides of every join are hash-shuffled, even when one side is a few rows. For example TPC-H q7 at sf1000:

```
Now:        2-row nation (filtered) and 150M-row customer BOTH hash-shuffled on nationkey
Optimized:  broadcast the 2-row side to every map task → map-side hash join, customer never moves
```

### Proposal

A `broadcast=True` join: materialize the small side, replicate it to all map tasks, build the hash table locally, stream the large side through without any shuffle.

items.title: [data] Runtime Bloom-filter pushdown to Join
items.author: owenowenisme
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #66829.

### Problem

A join's selectivity is data-dependent and invisible to static pushdown. TPC-H q7: after static pruning the orders side is ~8% of orders, but lineitem still shuffles every date-surviving row (~60% of 6B), and 92% of them find no match at probe time.

```
Now:        lineitem → shuffle 3.6B rows → Join (92% discarded at probe)
Optimized:  small side → bloom_filter_agg(o_orderkey)
            → lineitem scan: Filter(might_contain(l_orderkey)) → shuffle ~8% of rows
```

### Proposal

When a join has a selective build side and a much larger probe side, run the build side first, aggregate its keys into a Bloom filter, and inject a `might_contain` filter into the probe side's scan. False positives are harmless (the join still does exact matching).

**One thing to be cautious about: because Ray Data stream-executes the shuffle map stage, the big side of the table might start running before the Bloom filter of the smaller table is ready. We can probably fall back to a vanilla join when the filter isn't available and only filter after it's available.**

**Also need to research when we should use this.**

items.title: External routing does not support prefill/decode disaggregated Pods
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Feature Description and Motivation

The current external routing implementation supports single-target replica selection. It can receive candidate Pods with prefill/decode role attributes, but one external decision returns only one target Pod.

As a result, prefill/decode disaggregated Pods are not currently supported by the external routing path: selecting one role-labelled Pod does not select a P/D pair or invoke AIBrix's existing P/D orchestration and handoff flow.

This issue tracks that missing capability as a future external-routing enhancement. The existing single-target behavior remains valid and should stay backward compatible.

## Use Case

Operators may want to use an external decision service for workloads deployed as separate prefill and decode Pods, while retaining AIBrix's P/D execution flow.

Today they must use the built-in `pd` strategy; the `external` strategy cannot represent or apply the coordinated P/D decision.

## Proposed Solution

Investigate how external routing can support prefill/decode disaggregated Pods and integrate with the existing P/D router.

The implementation approach is intentionally left open. Follow-up design work should determine the protocol shape, compatibility with the current single-target API, target validation, fallback behavior, and reuse of the existing P/D orchestration path.

Related P/D work: #1134 and #1223.

## Area

Gateway

items.title: [Train] STRICT_SPREAD runs can wait forever when the autoscaler packs coordinator bundles onto one node
items.author: justinvyu
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Since #66002, Train V2 waits for the AutoscalingCoordinator to reserve capacity before it creates the worker placement group, then pins each worker to a reserved node. For `placement_strategy="STRICT_SPREAD"` on an autoscaling cluster, that reservation may never cover the worker group, so the run never starts.

**Why**

- `_AutoscalingCoordinatorActor._merge_and_send_requests` (`python/ray/data/_internal/cluster_autoscaler/default_autoscaling_coordinator.py`) collapses `STRICT_PACK` bundles into a single summed bundle, so the autoscaler is asked for one big enough node. `STRICT_SPREAD` gets no equivalent treatment. Its bundles go to `ray.autoscaler.sdk.request_resources` as independent bundles, and that API can't express "one bundle per node".
- So for 8 workers × `{"GPU": 1}`, the autoscaler can satisfy the request with a **single 8-GPU node** if the cluster config offers that node type. After that, it considers the demand met and won't launch more nodes.
- `_compute_reservations` honors `STRICT_SPREAD` (at most one bundle per node), so that node yields **1 of 8** reserved slots.
- Train never creates the placement group, because it's still waiting for the reservation. So the strategy-aware pending placement group demand that used to drive autoscaling before #66002 never reaches the autoscaler.

**Result**

- `FixedScalingPolicy(num_workers=8)`: on master, it polls for 60s, raises `WorkerGroupStartupTimeoutError`, and retries indefinitely with the default `controller_failure_limit=-1`. With #66763, it waits in the controller loop indefinitely, logging "Waiting for reserved resources: 1/8 workers are covered…".
- `ElasticScalingPolicy` with `min_workers > 1`: waits indefinitely, since 1 < `min_workers`.

**Expected**

The autoscaler launches enough nodes to satisfy `STRICT_SPREAD`, as it did when the placement group itself drove autoscaling.

**Possible fixes**

1. Forward the strategy to the autoscaler for `STRICT_SPREAD`. This needs an autoscaler API that can express spread or anti-affinity, which `request_resources` can't.
2. Skip reservation pinning for `STRICT_SPREAD` in Train (`ScalingPolicy._should_pin_to_reservation`, or `can_pin_to_reservation` on master), letting the placement group drive autoscaling as before. The cost is losing protection from concurrent runs sharing capacity for that strategy only.
3. At minimum, detect a reservation stuck below what's needed and log that `STRICT_SPREAD` may not be satisfiable through autoscaling.

Related: the elastic policy requests `max_workers` bundles and the coordinator reserves `STRICT_PACK` all-or-nothing, so elastic + `STRICT_PACK` only starts once `max_workers` fit on one node, and `min_workers` has no effect.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray master (`5808b33e30`), Train V2.

### Reproduction script

Not reproduced on a real autoscaling cluster yet. This was found by reading the code while reviewing #66601 / #66762. Expected repro:

```python
import ray
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer

# Cluster config whose only GPU worker node type has 8 GPUs, starting with 0 GPU nodes.
trainer = TorchTrainer(
    lambda: None,
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(
        num_workers=8, use_gpu=True, placement_strategy="STRICT_SPREAD"
    ),
)
trainer.fit()  # expected: one 8-GPU node launches; the run never starts
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to find and write up this issue.

items.title: [Core] Don't prestart one worker per CPU when num_cpus is autodetected
items.author: ctcjab
items.body_excerpt:
(Posted by Claude on my behalf)

### Description

When the first driver connects, the raylet prestarts one idle Python worker per CPU (`--num_prestart_python_workers=num_cpus` in `services.py`). Those workers stay up, because they fall within the idle-worker soft limit, which also defaults to `num_cpus`. If `ray.init()` starts a local cluster without `num_cpus`, it uses the host CPU count, so a large machine pays for a worker pool sized to the hardware rather than to the work.

The prestarted workers don't import task code, so they save little. In a 96-task fan-out whose tasks import a large module, they saved ~3.5s on the first fan-out and nothing afterwards, while `ray.init()` took ~2s longer.

**Proposal:** when `num_cpus` is autodetected rather than given, don't prestart, or cap prestart at a small number. Clusters started with an explicit `num_cpus`, such as `ray start --num-cpus=N` on sized nodes, keep the current behavior.

<details><summary>Repro (96-CPU host, Ray 2.55.1, Python 3.13, RHEL 9)</summary>

```python
"""Idle-worker cost of prestart on a local cluster. Usage: python repro.py [--no-prestart]"""

import sys
import time

import psutil
import ray

kwargs = {"include_dashboard": False}
if "--no-prestart" in sys.argv:
    kwargs["_system_config"] = {"prestart_worker_first_driver": False}

t0 = time.monotonic()
ray.init(**kwargs)  # no num_cpus: the node advertises every host CPU
init_s = time.monotonic() - t0
time.sleep(20)  # let prestarted workers come up

node = ray._private.worker._global_node
procs = {psutil.Process()}
for infos in node.all_processes.values():
    for info in infos:
        p = psutil.Process(info.process.pid)
        procs |= {p, *p.children(recursive=True)}
idle = sum(p.cmdline()[:1] == ["ray::IDLE"] for p in procs)
threads = sum(p.num_threads() for p in procs)
rss_gb = sum(p.memory_info().rss for p in procs) / 1024**3
print(
    f"cpus={int(ray.cluster_resources()['CPU'])} init={init_s:.1f}s "
    f"idle_workers={idle} threads={threads} rss={rss_gb:.1f}GB"
)
ray.shutdown()
```

```
$ python repro.py
cpus=96 init=5.9s idle_workers=96 threads=5170 rss=9.6GB
$ python repro.py --no-prestart
cpus=96 init=3.8s idle_workers=0 threads=465 rss=1.3GB
```

A second pair of runs on the same host gave `threads=5188 rss=10.3GB` with prestart and `threads=465 rss=1.8GB` without.

</details>

### Use case

Several developers, or several concurrent test processes, each start a local cluster on the same large host. Each `ray.init()` adds about 5,000 threads, which counts against the per-user process limit (`ulimit -u`). Once that limit is reached, unrelated processes fail to create threads and abort. We set `_system_config={"prestart_worker_first_driver": False}` for our own local clusters, but every caller of `ray.init()` has to know to do that.

items.title: Experimental tracking: FROST low-latency FP8 projections
items.author: YangXu1990uiuc
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @YangXu1990uiuc

Track an experimental `backend="frost-low-latency"` implementation of the existing `flashinfer.bmm_fp8` API for small-M FP8 projections. No new operator signature or model/checkpoint dependency is needed.

The proposed kernel uses vectorized E4M3 loads, packed BF16 products and FP32 accumulation. It avoids tensor-core setup and partition reduction for shapes where those costs dominate. A measured B200 example is `(M,K,N)=(1,1024,1024)`: 1.977 us for the fastest measured existing provider (cuBLAS), versus 1.563 us for this implementation in warmed CUDA graph replay. At M=8, the same kernel loses (1.990 us versus 2.469 us). This is a narrow component optimization, not a general serving-speedup claim.

The experimental path is appropriate because performance depends strongly on shape and cache residency, and the kernel has no reuse across activation rows. It remains explicit-only, even when experimental automatic backends are enabled. Existing default selection is unchanged.

Initial execution contract: SM100/SM107, BMM batch dimension one, `1 <= M <= 64`, positive `K % 512 == 0`, positive `N % 8 == 0`, contiguous row-major A / column-major B, 16-byte-aligned E4M3 inputs, scalar CUDA FP32 scales and BF16 output. This is the correctness range; the profitable dispatch region is substantially smaller. Kernel code, admission and compilation stay in `flashinfer/experimental/` with a thin core handoff.

Graduation target: the first release on or after **2026-11-04**, subject to maintainer review. Before graduation:

- Establish reproducible wins against all applicable existing FP8 providers, with both warm and evicted weights.
- Define a conservative shape/device/cache-policy dispatch region, or retain explicit selection if automatic dispatch cannot be justified.
- Validate numerical behavior, storage/stream rebinding, CUDA graph replay and memory safety on each admitted architecture.
- Decide whether this schedule belongs in an existing low-latency backend instead of retaining a separate backend name.
- Graduate or remove the experimental implementation if its maintenance cost exceeds the demonstrated coverage.

The implementation PR will include a runnable example, a crossover benchmark and scoped correctness tests. This issue tracks qualification and API integration; model-specific decoder fusion is outside its scope.

items.title: SM120 (RTX PRO 6000) MoE backend gaps: MoeConfig.backend schema missing MegaMoE entries, and no EP-capable path for this hardware
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

items.title: [Feature]: Wire SM107 into nvfp4_gemm CuTe DSL dispatcher (cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin has no caller)
items.author: farazkh80
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`trtllm::cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin` (added in #19272) has no caller. The generic `nvfp4_gemm` dispatcher's CuTe DSL backend is still SM100/SM103-only, so SM107 (Rubin) can never select the Rubin NVFP4 CuTe DSL kernel through `nvfp4_gemm`.

## Details

- In `tensorrt_llm/_torch/custom_ops/torch_custom_ops.py` (`NVFP4GemmUnifiedRunner`), the `cutedsl` tactics are only collected when `get_sm_version()` is 100 or 103. On any other SM, an explicit `cutedsl`-only request raises "CuteDSL NVFP4 backend requires SM 100 (B200) or SM 103 (B300)". The `cutedsl` forward branch always builds `CuteDSLNVFP4BlackwellRunner`.
- On SM107 the only NVFP4 CuTe DSL path in use is the locality-domain inplace op (`cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_locality_domain_inplace_rubin`), reached from `Linear` when `enable_locality_domains` is set.
- `cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin` is registered but unreachable.

## Proposed work

- Add SM107 support to the `nvfp4_gemm` CuTe DSL dispatcher: SM gate, tactic collection, and a forward branch that uses the Rubin runner.
- Make sure the SM100/SM103 path is unchanged.
- Add a test covering SM107 selection through `nvfp4_gemm`.

## References

- Review thread: https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/19272 (comment on `cute_dsl_nvfp4_gemm_rubin`, where the author agreed to a follow-up PR)

shortlist.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
shortlist.author: akshathtiwari
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \

shortlist.title: [Bug] Disconnected streaming client leaves a zombie request that decodes to max_tokens and floods "state was deleted in TokenizerManager" (regression from #34160 revert)
shortlist.author: wkgcass
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

> Submitted by GLM-5.3

When a streaming client disconnects mid-generation, the scheduler-side request
is never aborted and keeps decoding until `max_tokens`. Every output batch for
that request logs:

```
Received output for rid='...' but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager.
```

at a high rate (observed ~15 lines/s per request, sustained for the entire
remaining generation — in production two zombie requests burned GPU for 15+
minutes and occupied both `--max-running-requests` slots, blocking all new
requests from being scheduled).

Root cause (verified on current `main`):

1. `TokenizerManager.generate_request` has an `except BaseException` cleanup
   that calls `_discard_pending_req_states(obj)`. It was added for failures
   *before* the request reaches the scheduler (e.g. input-length validation),
   but a client disconnect raises `asyncio.CancelledError` — also a
   `BaseException` — so the state of a request that **is running on the
   scheduler** gets popped immediately at disconnect time.

2. The delayed safety net then doesn't fire: `create_abort_task` (attached to
   the `StreamingResponse` as a background task, runs ~2s after teardown)
   calls `abort_request(rid)`, which early-returns on
   `tokenizer_worker_num == 1 and rid not in self.rid_to_state`. The
   `AbortReq` is never dispatched, so the scheduler never learns the client
   is gone and decodes to `max_tokens`; each `BatchStrOutput` for that rid
   hits the deleted-state error path.

This is a regression of 71043b9dbb ("Revert parallel request lifecycle
tracking from #32588", #34160). Before the revert, #32588 handled this
correctly: `_discard_pending_req_states(obj, request_lifecycles)` dispatched
`AbortReq` for every rid whose state had `dispatched == True` **before**
removing the state. The revert deleted the `dispatched` markers and the
abort-then-remove ordering, leaving the orphan window. Presumably not covered
by CI because it requires killing a streaming client mid-generation.

(The `HEALTH_CHECK`-prefixed rid skip next to the error log is a different,
known race — unrelated, see #11925.)

Suggested minimal fix (verified in production, restores the pre-revert
invariant without reintroducing full lifecycle tracking):

1. In `generate_request`, treat cancellation separately and only discard
   state if the request was never dispatched:

```python
        dispatched = False
        try:
            ...
            self._send_one_request(tokenized_obj)
            dispatched = True
            async for response in self._wait_one_response(obj, request):
                yield response
        except (asyncio.CancelledError, GeneratorExit):
            # Client disconnect mid-request: keep the state of a dispatched
            # request so the delayed background abort still finds it; the
            # scheduler's abort echo deletes it cleanly. Discarding here
            # orphans the scheduler-side request, which then decodes to
            # max_tokens.
            if not dispatched:
                self._discard_pending_req_states(obj)
            raise
        except BaseException:
            self._discard_pending_req_states(obj)
            raise
```

2. Add a `force` flag to `abort_request` that bypasses the
   `rid not in self.rid_to_state` early-return, and pass `force=True` from
   `create_abort_task` (the scheduler's `abort_request` handler scans by rid
   prefix and no-ops unknown rids, so force-dispatching is safe — it just
   closes the window where the state was already deleted elsewhere):

```python
    def abort_request(self, rid: str = "", abort_all: bool = False, force: bool = False):
        if not abort_all and not rid:
            ...
            return
        if (
            not abort_all
            and not force
            and get_serving().tokenizer_worker_num == 1
            and rid not in self.rid_to_state
        ):
            return
```

With this patch: disconnect → decode stops within the 2s abort window, zero
error lines; normal streaming completions (`[DONE]`) unaffected.

### Reproduction

Any model; the bug is in the tokenizer-manager layer and is
hardware/model-independent.

1. Launch a server:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model <any-model> --port 30000
```

2. Start a long streaming generation, then kill the client mid-stream:

```bash
curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<any-model>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Count from 1 to 5000, one number per line."}],"max_tokens":16000,"stream":true}' &
sleep 10 && kill -9 %1
```

**Actual**: `sglang:num_running_reqs` stays 1 and the request decodes until
`max_tokens`; the log floods with the message above (same rid, repeated many
times per second).

**Expected**: the request is aborted shortly after the disconnect (within the
2s background-abort window) and decode stops.

### Environment

- sglang `main` (regression introduced by 71043b9dbb / #34160, still present
  as of a1f9508dd4; no commit has touched `tokenizer_manager.py` since —
  `except BaseException` cleanup and the guard are at current lines ~825
  and ~1952)
- single GPU, TP=1, `--max-running-requests 2`; speculative decoding enabled
  (DSPARK) on our instance, but nothing here is spec-specific
- reproduced and root-caused on a fork whose `tokenizer_manager.py` is
  unmodified upstream code

comments.author: eug3
comments.body:
### Additional production evidence + a working workaround (2x DGX Spark, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4)

We hit this exact bug in production today on **SGLang TP=2 across 2 DGX Spark nodes** (`Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, speculative NEXTN, `--tokenizer-worker-num 1`). Sharing our numbers and a working mitigation in case it helps:

**Observed symptoms (identical to #36333 and #36876):**
- 3 zombie requests accumulated over hours (first at 11:58, then 13:02, then 14:41), each from a client that disconnected mid-stream.
- GPU pinned at ~95% for 2+ hours with **zero completed requests**; `sglang:num_running_reqs` stuck at 3.0.
- Log flooded with `Received output for rid=... but the state was deleted in TokenizerManager` — **~148,000 lines** sustained across hours.
- `POST /abort_request` returned 200 but had **no effect** (confirmed the `abort_request()` early-return: with `tokenizer_worker_num == 1` and `rid not in self.rid_to_state`, the `AbortReq` never reaches the scheduler — exactly as #36333 describes).
- New requests queued behind the zombies; spend/completion never logged for the zombies.

**Our workaround (patched `tokenizer_manager.py` in the running image, verified):**
1. `abort_request()`: removed the early-return when `rid not in self.rid_to_state` — always dispatch `AbortReq` to the scheduler (scheduler-side abort is safe for unknown rids; it scans queues and no-ops when absent).
2. `_handle_batch_output()`: when output arrives for an already-deleted state (orphan), proactively re-send `AbortReq(rid, abort_all=False)` to reap the scheduler-side task.

**Verification:** simulated client disconnect (kill curl 2s into a streaming responses call): `num_running_reqs` → 0 within 10s, GPU → 0%, subsequent requests unaffected. Concurrent test (3 streaming, 2 killed mid-stream, 1 completed): all slots reclaimed, the completed one finished normally. 60s observation window: zero growth of "state was deleted" after the initial reap.

**Note on #36876:** even with the AbortReq reaching the scheduler, `Scheduler.abort_request()` only sets `to_finish = FINISH_ABORT()` for requests found in `[running_batch, last_batch]` — during batch transitions (overlap scheduling / speculative decoding) a request can be in neither, leaving the same zombie. Our orphan-output reap (fix 2) happens to cover that window too, but the two fixes should ideally both land upstream. Happy to provide the full patch or a minimal repro script if useful.
